Now begins the Śrīvāmakeśvarīmata, accompanied by the commentary composed by the venerable Rājānaka Jayaratha.
First Chapter:
Her ninefold essential nature consists of being composed of the Wheel of the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*), which is the unfolding of the relationship between the self and its Lord.
By means of the contemplation of their own syllables as being the self of all, they cause the three cities to appear within the bowless [space]. || 1 ||
Victorious are my former gurus, headed by the venerable Dīpikācārya, who are overflowing with the nectar of the supreme non-dual realization. || 2 ||
Today, this effort of mine is undertaken to dispel even slightly the blindness caused by the cataracts of others' false imaginings, and to illuminate the venerable *Vāmakeśvarīmata*.
In this context, indeed, the introducer of the Tantra— intent on wishing to favor others and desiring to cause them to enter into the womb of this secret scripture—
performs repeated salutations to those worthy of worship according to the degrees of their devotion,
[addressing] her who takes the form of Gaṇeśa, the planets, the lunar mansions, the Yoginīs, and the zodiac signs.
I bow to the Goddess, who consists of mantra, who is the Mother (Mātṛkā), and whose form is the sacred seat (Pīṭha). || 1 ||
"Here— in this [system]—
there is no other Mātṛkā-vidyā" (Svacchandatantra 11.199);
thus, elsewhere [it is said that] the Blessed Lady Mātṛkā, whose true nature is unknown by the bound souls (paśus), [is not found].
That power of the Creator of the universe which was described as "inherent" (*samavāyinī*) by [the passage] beginning with *Mālinīvijayottara* 3.5,
is also mentioned here.
(2) O Dear One, Tripurā is the supreme primordial Śakti; from her, through the division of the gross and the subtle, the Mātṛkā [arises] as the mother of the origin of the three worlds. (4.4)
[This refers to] that which will be described by such [passages as] "the supreme speech (parā vāk), whose nature is self-reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa), arises spontaneously even in the gurus;
this is the primary sovereignty, the supreme lordship of the Self."
That throbbing Great Being, which is undifferentiated by space or time, is declared to be the very essence;
it is the Heart of the Supreme Lord.

The Supreme Goddess Parā, whose essence is the supreme reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), who is the mother of the universe consisting of both the signified and the signifier, and who is the power (*śakti*) whose nature is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), as described in passages such as (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.5.10).
"— I do not delight in being alone. From this statement,
[it follows that] if Maheśvara were to remain with a body of a single form, [there would be no such statement].

And by the reasoning stated in such passages as, "The state of Maheśvara and the state of pure consciousness would have been abandoned like a jar or other objects" (Tantrāloka 3.100), [the power] is unfolding with the desire to manifest externally, as formulated by the illustrious Naravāhanadatta.

The eight groups (gaṇas) are the classes [of consonants] beginning with *a, *ka, *ca, *ṭa, *ta, *pa, *ya, and *śa; they are [respectively] presided over by Gaṇeśa, the planets, the lords of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the lords of the zodiac signs (*rāśi*), and the Yoginīs, as indicated by such expressions.
The [planets] are the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Mercury, Venus, Saturn, and so forth.
The groups have been described in sequence as being joined with the six planets; furthermore,
due to their conjunction with the bright and dark fortnights of the moon’s face, they are said to produce pleasure and suffering respectively.
By such statements, the planets are its lords;
among them, the Sun is the lord from Leo through half of the twelve zodiacal signs (maṇḍala-bhagaṇa),
while the Moon is the lord from Cancer in reverse order, and the others likewise by their respective gifts.

Because of this statement, the constellations (*nakṣatras*) are its support both indirectly and directly; the Yoginīs, because they participate in the conjunctions with those respective planets and so forth; the lunar days (*tithis*) such as the first day (*pratipad*), which arise by revolving in dependence upon that [constellation]; the [six] Brahmī goddesses and others as well; and the zodiac signs (*rāśis*).

The meaning is: "shining forth as the nature of Time (kāla), whose characteristics have been declared by the Great Guru [in the passage]: 'Aries and the other signs, which possess that form, are Time—the movement of the sun and so forth... It is not merely thus.
He says "having the form of the *pīṭha*" (*pīṭharūpiṇīm*) because she shines forth even as the nature of space (*deśarūpatayā*). Regarding the word *pīṭha*, it is said:
"The *pīṭha* is declared to be the *mātṛkā*...

Thus, although the term primarily denotes the substratum of the entire universe, here, because [the *mātṛkā*] is inseparable from it, space is implied; therefore, she is also [described] as having the nature of space.

The meaning is "appearing. This is the intended sense here: for it is Supreme Consciousness alone that, through its sovereignty, first desires to manifest the universe and, by means of the diversity of forms, manifests spatial succession.
Due to the manifestation of the variety of actions, the Lord [also manifests] the succession of time.

According to this principle (*Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* 2.1.5), by manifesting the diversity of forms through its manifestation as the subtle, the intermediate, and the gross— consisting of the *kalās*, *tattvas*, and *bhuvanas*—

it illuminates the path of space (*deśādhvan*). Furthermore, by manifesting the diversity of action through its manifestation as phonemes (*varṇa*), mantras, and words (*pada*), it also illuminates the path of time (*kālādhvan*).
It manifests as the totality of the universe, consisting of the sixfold path. As they say in that regard: "That which is the manifestation of activity is called the path known as Time (kālādhvan).
Within this, there clearly exists a triad of paths designated as phonemes (varṇa), mantras, and words (pada)."
That aspect which consists of the manifestation of form is determined as the path of space (deśādhvan);
here, the triad known as kalā, tattva, and pura is included within it.
"In each of these three triads there exists a gross, subtle, and supreme form; because of this, this entire path is said to be sixfold. (Tantrāloka 6.36, p.

Thus, he says "consisting of mantra" (*mantramayīm*) to indicate that she alone also appears as the presiding subject (*adhiṣṭhātṛtvena*) of this [universe]. Here, by the word "mantra," all seven subjects (*pramātṛ*), beginning with Śiva and ending with the *sakala*, are implied; the meaning is that she appears as consisting of all the Rudras, individual souls (*kṣetrajña*), and so forth. Therefore, even while consisting of the agitation (*kṣobha*) of subject, object, and the rest, her primordial nature remains entirely undiminished.

The word "this" refers to what was called "the Goddess. Even so, the meaning is: "I bow to Her who shines as the very self of supreme self-luminous consciousness, whose sole nature is that of the supreme subject; I enter into Her as the cognizing subject (*cit-pramātṛ*), with the limited state of being a subject consisting of the body and so forth rendered subordinate.
Here, as long as the subject matter at hand has not reached its final rest, it is simply not logical even to mention a further subject to be introduced; and therein—

That [explanation] is devoid of the actual meaning of the word, obscured by arduous conceptualization, and for the most part incoherent; it is even more difficult than the difficult, in that regarding the explanation of the word *Gaṇeśa*, since the letter *ga* denotes merely the number to be counted as three, it lacks the capacity to convey the meaning "three" because there is no expression of the number characterized as "three-ness. Even in that case, it would be by the word *svāmin* alone...

This inclusion is redundant because its meaning has already been conveyed; for there exists only a single wheel-component characterized by three spokes to be established, and that is accomplished by this much alone—so what is the purpose of this inclusion? As the scripture states:
"Therein, one [spoke] is in the middle, eight at the end of the two [sides], and fourteen at the ends of the four."
O Maheśvarī, there are fourteen, ten pairs, and eight cavities.

Thus [it is said]. Now, if it is argued that by the word *svāmin* (lord) the middle [spoke] is denoted, while by the word *varṇa* (color/letter) the three-spoked [wheel] is denoted, we say no; for in either case, this very meaning is established by itself precisely through the non-distinction from the middle. Nor is there, on account of its falling within the axle (*akṣa*), a single part of the ten spokes, because—just like [the spokes] falling within the directions (*dik*)—it lacks the status of being a designator of the number characterized as "ten."
The mind alone is the single lord of the ten senses; since that [intellect] arose from the Taijasa [ego], the mind was born as the ruler of the senses. (Māṭharavṛtti 2.31, p.

Thus [it is said]. You yourself have also stated that the mind is the lord of the group of the sense organs (*buddhīndriya*). Furthermore, the term "lord of the group" (*gaṇapati*) denotes the object to be counted (*saṃkhyeya*), not the number itself; therefore, it has already been explained that this term does not denote fourteen spokes.
By the phrase "as the lords of two groups" (*gaṇayor īśārṇatayā*), two sets of sixteen spokes are expressed. And in this context, this is not intended to refer to only one.

Regarding the sacrifice of the sixteen-spoked [wheel]: as for the word *gaṇeśa*, let us set aside for now the question of by what operation it denotes this meaning, since there is much to be said on that matter. Even so, it conveys only the object to be numbered (*saṃkhyeya*), not the number itself; thus, once again, the intended meaning remains untenable, and the direct presentation of all the components of the wheel would not be established. Furthermore, *gaṇeśā*...

There are eight *grahas* and twenty-seven *nakṣatras*. How are there nine wheels and nine arts (*kalās*)? *Aṇimā*, *laghimā*, *mahimā*, *īśitva*, *vaśitva*, *prakāmatā*, *bhukti*, *icchā*, and *mokṣa*—these are declared here in the *tantra* as the *siddhis*.

By such statements as these, they are able to describe the ten *siddhis*, the *mudrās*, and the eight *vidyās*— by way of their lordship, their colors, their [forms as] the *nandis* and so forth, their status as the lords of the directions starting with the East,
their forms as Gaṇapati and the lunar days (*tithi*), and as the *vidyeśvaras*, both in sequential and non-sequential order.

In the Gaṇayoga, by virtue of being the letter of Īśa (the letter *i*) and likewise by virtue of being a Lord of the World (*lokeśa*), the term "Gaṇeśa" consists of nine, three, eight, ten, ten, eight, eleven, and eight syllables respectively within the Navacakrī.
The lords of the Gaṇas are in the arts of the wheel, the planets are the speakers within the wheels,
the lunar mansions are in all nine supernatural powers, and the mudrās are in the vidyās.

Since it has been stated thus, and since such a claim regarding those who are considered great by the world would appear harsh to the ears of everyone, let this suffice according to the maxim of the "sample from the cooking pot" (*sthālīpulāka-nyāya*). Likewise, the explanation of [the mandala] having forty-three corners and so forth through the calculation of Gaṇeśa and the other [deities] is almost entirely like leftover food; what is the use of this further elaboration that only increases the bulk of the book?

What is deliberated upon that is not useful for the subject at hand? Furthermore, regarding the vital points (marmasthāna), if one were to engage in such scrutinizing out of envy at every step, the very activity would become corrupted;
therefore, enough with excessive prolixity. || 1 ||
Thus,
homage to Śambhu, who is the sole cause of saṃsāra, yet the sole adversary of saṃsāra; who has the form of saṃsāra, yet is himself beyond saṃsāra.

Thus, according to the perspective taught by the Great Guru (*mahāguru*) in [Utpaladeva’s *Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā* 1.8], having manifested this kind of transmigratory existence in the form of the sixfold sacrifice (*ṣaḍvidhādhvara*), He again conceals it by His own will;
in order to demonstrate Her power to accomplish what is exceedingly difficult to achieve, he says:
I bow to the Great Goddess, the Mother, the Supreme Sovereign,
who brings an end to the turbulent agitation of the surging waves of Time.
Beyond that as well, O Goddess, there is an immeasurable time which constitutes the ultimate limit;
it is eternal, eternally risen, incapable of being impaired, and cannot be diminished.
And he should project everything below, from the pervasive power (vyāpinī) down to the earth,
as well as the path of the goddess consisting of moving and non-moving beings, by means of the powers such as the *tuṭi* and others.
The tumultuous roar (*hallohala*) of Time, whose essential nature has been defined in such passages as (Svacchandatantra 11.311),
is that Time which is designated as "Equilibrium" (*sāmya*). — (Svacchandatantra 11.309).

Thus, its specific state consists of an indivisible nature characterized by equality, devoid of the aforementioned excellence or lack thereof; its surging waves are another, the sixteenth time-period, while the seventeenth is the supreme.
But that time which is beyond the supreme, O Dear One, is the Lord, the eighteenth.
The "vibrations" (*visphūrjitāni*) mentioned in such passages as (Sva0 4.329)— consisting of *tuṭi*, *lava*, *nimeṣa*, and so forth— are the conceptualizations (*kalanā*) of that [Power] which,

by being primarily characterized by succession and non-succession brought about through the distinctions of various appearances, constitute limitations (*avaccheda*). [She is the one who effects the pacification] of those [limitations].
Even the differentiation of appearances everywhere would have to follow a temporal sequence;
the appearance of the void and so forth is fragmented, whereas that of the subject does not occur simultaneously.
By means of the reasoning stated in such passages as (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 2.1.6), through the dissolution of the limited subjectivity of the void and so forth, [the supreme state is attained].
For one who fully understands that "all this is my own manifestation," there is liberation even amidst the proliferation of conceptual constructions regarding the universal self.

She causes those beings who are to be graced and who engage in such contemplations as "ī0 pra0 4|1|6" to rest within the supreme abode— the indivisible, perfectly full, and transcendental consciousness-self, which is beyond the divisions of time; for this very reason, she is the Great Goddess (*mahādevī*), by virtue of her greatness consisting in the singular density of undivided, supreme consciousness.
The meaning of the sentence is: "I bow to Mātṛkā, who is radiant, and for that very reason the Supreme Goddess, endowed with the sovereignty that accomplishes even the most difficult tasks. || 2 ||

To reveal that she is not only thus, but is even intent on bestowing various specific siddhis, he says: "When even a single syllable of this [mantra] is mastered, a man vies with the Sun, Garuḍa, the Moon, Kandarpa, Śaṅkara, Agni, and Viṣṇu. (3)

The meaning is that even a human being, when even a single syllable at the beginning of this [Vidyā]—starting with the *vāgbhava*—is perfected through the procedure for accomplishing each individual syllable as will be described, competes with the Sun and other luminaries and becomes equal to them. As he will say:
"From that, O Goddess, one indeed becomes like another Vainateya" (4.45).

Thus, O Goddess of the gods, for those who pride themselves on all manner of amorous charms and are full of passion, the practitioner, O Goddess, becomes an overcomer of even the most intense love. (4.38)
Thus,
surrounded by hosts of wicked disease-demons, many *ḍākinīs* in various forms,
and floods of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*, he appears as if he has three eyes. (4.50)
"Resembling a blazing fire by the assembly of all the yoginīs," thus [it is said].
Having first propitiated this very Vidyā, the Enchantress of the Three Worlds...
And as it is said: "The Lord Hari assumed a form that deludes the three worlds" (4.67).
Since such statements apply specifically to Anala and Kandarpa, the same sense is established for Ravi and Indu as well; thus they are not mentioned separately.
Because of the use of the plural number, the sense of "and others" is also obtained, so that Vākpati and the rest are also included. As he will say:
"He too becomes eloquent, like another Vācaspati" (4.26).

For this very reason, one should not claim here that the inference of [the state of] being a lord of speech (*vākpati*) is baseless or inconsistent; rather, it is intended to demonstrate the fruit of merely attaining the perfection of the syllables, according to the maxim of the "gourd from the stalk" (*kāṇḍakūṣmāṇḍanyāya*).

One might ask: what occasion is there for stating the fruits of propitiating the three wheels? To this it must be said: for here [is described] Vaiśvānara, the ten-fold one, the lord of days endowed with a hundred rays;
the moon that gladdens the world; and Garuḍa, who destroys the poison of the ten classes [of beings].

Even Madana possesses ten states; even Vāgīśa is endowed with the ten branches of knowledge; Śambhu is the lord of the ten directions; and Śambhu assumes a body consisting of the hundred Rudras in ten ways.

Viṣṇu, who possesses ten incarnations and is the creator of the manifold great elements; Brahmā, born from the lotus; and Śiva, the lord of speech—though not explicitly mentioned here, they are to be inferred.
Having propitiated the three wheels consisting of ten, ten, and fourteen constituent forms,
these three triads are established here through the causal agency of the Left-hand Guru.
Indeed, the Goddess herself, whose nature consists of the three *piṇḍas*, has attained the state of being the womb of the universe;
therefore, it is said that even the accomplishments (*siddhis*) pertaining to the wombs reside within the *piṇḍas*.
Since the previously mentioned [qualities] such as the ten *kalās* and so forth result in the Goddess being the womb (*yoni*) consisting of the three *piṇḍas*, their status as causes is inconsistent;

therefore, why do you say that all this is like a web of falsehood for the Great-Souled Ones? Furthermore, if only the seven [elements] beginning with *kha* (ether) were taken as the material cause, then only a set of seven qualities—such as brilliance (*tejas*), strength (*bala*), and so on—[would result].
It cannot be a definitive [proof], because it is inconclusive due to the possibility of other such qualities as well;
for in that regard too,
there are light, strength, clarity, form, knowledge, and purity.
And exertion for the sake of others—these are the seven most excellent qualities.

In this regard, because there is an absence of such abundance, because it is illogical, and because there exists an adherence to the sequence beginning with the Sun (Ravi) and others, its artificiality is suspected; let this matter rest. And as for what has been stated here by others [in the *Kālahallola-sūtra*] from the *Ravitārkṣya-ādi-sūtra*:
The two sciences consisting of one syllable and three syllables have been indicated by me.

Thus, by making [the letters] victorious through the logic of Viśvāmitra, having established a ninefold creation consisting of both the signified and the signifier, the letters *ka*, *ha*, *e*, *ka*, *ma*, *i*, *ha*, *ka*, *la*, *ra*, and *i* are sequentially implied by the words *ravi* and so forth; therefore, it is stated that the primary convention of the mantra is also hinted at here. Regarding this, we [proceed] to refute...

What can we say when we are not even bold enough to attempt such a composition? Or rather, why be angry with this poor ascetic, since even the author of the Vārttika has performed the extraction of mantras in exactly this manner for every single word? Enough of this lack of reflection! 3.
This [power] does not act only upon the practitioner alone; rather, he states that this entire world, consisting of both the moving and the non-moving, is likewise permeated by it:
"Since the three worlds are adorned by the moonlight of the syllable..."
I bow to the Goddess who is the Sovereign of All, the Great Śrī Siddhamātṛkā. || 4 ||
As the Śruti says: "When the sun has set, O Yājñavalkya, and the moon has set, what is the light of the person? "Speech is his light," the Emperor replied.
(Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.5)
Thus [it is said]. The former teachers also [state]:
"This very same designation (saṃjñā) of transmigrating beings exists both externally and internally. (p. 10)
"Since this [body] is seen to be unconscious upon departure, like a piece of wood or a wall" (Vākyapadīya 1.128);
otherwise, "this entire triple world would become blind darkness."
If the light called sound were not to shine throughout the duration of saṃsāra, [then...]

And thus: in this very way, by that splendor characterized by the vibration of consciousness— which is of a single essence because it lacks the quality of appearing through repeated interruptions (like lightning and the like), and which manifests in an uninterrupted form through the vision "this Self is once and for all manifest" (sakṛdvibhāto'yamātmā)— [he perceives].
But regarding the primordial knower, whose form is eternally manifest and who partakes in all cognitions—
what new manifestation could there be as a means of knowledge for him?

According to this principle, because she is not an object within the scope of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that deals with previously unknown objects, the Supreme Power (*parā śakti*), designated by such terms as Mahātripurasundarī, is established from the very beginning as self-evident; she is the Mātṛkā who bestows life upon all things, even those which are themselves the means of valid cognition.
"Of them too, the supreme life-force is that very Supreme Lord" (Tattvasaṃgraha 1.55).

According to such statements, she is the Goddess because she bestows life upon all subjects, means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, and so forth; therefore, I bow to—that is, I enter into—the Goddess whose nature is to sport by assuming the forms of those respective subjects and the rest. || 4 ||
It is established that these three worlds have arisen from this very supreme Śakti and are animated by her alone;
to demonstrate that she is also their substratum, he says:
"These three worlds are strung upon the great thread of the Imperishable."
I bow to that perfected Mātṛkā, which extends from the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa) to the outer shell of the universe (Kaṭāha). || 5 ||

This all-pervasively radiant shell of the cosmic egg is the Egg of Power (*śaktyaṇḍa*). Within it exists the triple world—consisting of the moving and the unmoving, and characterized by existence, non-existence, both, and neither—which is nothing but the imperishable syllables. These constitute the Great Sūtra, capable of pervading all things; strung upon it and woven through it, the entire universe remains fixed as if adhering to its very foundation. This is that primordial, established Mātṛkā.
"I pay homage"—this is the meaning of the sentence. || 5 ||
O Goddess, that Mātṛkā who is endowed with supreme splendor—
by her all this is pervaded, as far as the end of the world of Brahmā.

"Thus indeed is the manifestation of sound; the moving and the unmoving are pervaded by sound. Having stated this, he speaks again in another manner in order to further elaborate upon how this entire world is strung together by these syllables.
That which arises from the three corners of the seed-syllable of the eleven supports is the universe, seen even today, from the cosmic egg down to the shell of the world.
She whose letters consist of the groups beginning with *a*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *na*, *pa*, *ya*, *śa*, and *kṣa*;
she who dwells in the head, the limbs, the arms, the heart, the back, the hips, and the feet.
I bow to that Great Goddess, who is both transcendent and immanent, whose essence is the extraction of the syllable *tāṃ*, and whose form is supreme bliss.

He says that this Mother, the Blessed Great Goddess, who has set forth, is shining with the greatness just described— the nature of consciousness— and consists of the primary phonemes whose essence is the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*); for, according to the Vedic revelation that "Bliss is the form of Brahman," the very state of being consciousness would not exist without having bliss as its form.

[She is] of the nature of bliss, whose second syllable is primarily the power of bliss; thus, through the extraction of the third seed-syllable *i*, which consists of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*)— arising from the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) characterized by the desire to emit (*sisṛkṣā*) through the state of the fusion (*lolībhāva*) of consciousness (*cit*) and bliss— and which is the "support of the essence" (*sārādhārā*), being the supreme support because it possesses the radiance of the entire universe, and for that very reason, because it is the abode of the state of power (*śaktidaśā*).

I bow down most deeply to that supreme Parāparā who possesses such a form. Thus, precisely because she is oriented toward emanation, her two powers of Absolute Consciousness (anuttara-citi) and Bliss (ānanda-citi) are joined within the power of Will (icchā-śakti).
"Triangular," they call that [center], beautiful with the fragrance of emission (*visarga*).

According to such statements as these (*Tantrāloka* 3.94), the eleventh triangle arising from the conjunction of those three seed-syllables is called the *bhaga*; situated in the sky (*viyat*), it is the secret maṇḍala.
The Triangle of Will, Knowledge, and Action.

Because of this statement: the "support" (ādhāra) is the support of birth; that which is its nature is the single-syllable essence (*ekārātman*), which is the seed. Its three corners, consisting of will (*icchā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and action (*kriyā*), have given rise to this entire common world, from the element earth up to the power (*śakti*). This is seen even now, at all times—not merely at some specific time—since no particular qualification is mentioned, and it is perceived by everyone as having that very nature.

This is the meaning. Indeed, there is not even a single part of this world that is not permeated by these three powers. For nothing that is not intended to be done, not known, or not to be accomplished can possibly sustain the skill required to carry out worldly activity; all ordinary people are witnesses to this fact. And in the same way, according to the reasoning set forth in the *Śrī Tantrāloka* and other works, [this applies] precisely to the primordial phoneme and so forth.

The meaning is that she bears the likeness [of the alphabet] through the eight groups (vargas) beginning with *ka* and *ca*, which have been mentioned. By the term "the eldest limb" (*jyeṣṭhāṅga*), the head is indicated; by that, the three parts consisting of the crest-lock (*śikhā*), the forehead (*lalāṭa*), and the space between the eyebrows (*bhūmadhya*) are implied. By the two "arms" (*bāhu*), the throat situated at their base is meant. Through the repetition of the word "heart" (*hṛd*), the navel is signified by the compound "heart-and-back" (*hṛtpṛṣṭha*). And by the "hips" (*kaṭī*), the generative organ (*janmādhāra*) is indicated. As the author of the Vārttika says:
The space between the eyebrows is the forehead-peak (*bhālacūlā*); the neck is located at the root of the upper arms, which is the eldest limb;
the heart is the chest, and the navel is said to be situated on its back.
The birthplace is the waist; likewise, according to the sequence of placement, A-Ha-Ka is the foot.
Thus [ends verse 8].
To demonstrate that this [reality] cannot even be conceptualized by the gods, he says (p.
"Even now, the deities do not know even the slightest bit of it."
"What is this? From what? Where? By what?"—thus one should contemplate its nature and its lack of form.
I bow to that Goddess, whose form consists of imperishable *kṣa* syllables,
who flashes forth amidst the surging waves of the *kula*, and who is born from the supreme *auli*.

Even the deities beginning with Brahmā, Indra, and Upendra have, even to the slightest degree, not yet—up to this very day—abandoned their own mental activity fixed upon the fourfold conceptualization regarding Her nature, cause, object, and purpose (asking: "Who is She? From what? Where?
By what?"), nor have they resolved how Her nature—which is both existence and formlessness, being and non-being—comes to be.
The meaning is that they are unable to determine its certainty. For this [consciousness], which consists of the form of "I," having withdrawn the entire universe, dissolves into the Anuttara;
thus, this universe resides within the Śakti, and she [resides] in the state of Anuttara.
It is true that there is an encapsulation by the All-pervasive Lord within that [consciousness],
for even the universe that shines within consciousness indeed exists through consciousness.
This triad, having attained a state of union through the conjunction of pairs,
becomes the single supreme form of Bhairava, whose essence is the "I."
By the reasoning stated in such passages as *Tantrāloka* 3.207, because all phonemes are subsumed through the grasping of the first and last letters,

she consists of the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃ-parāmarśa*) and is of the singular nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*) according to the sequence of phoneme-subsumption (*pratyāhāra*). Thus, she cannot be identified as "this," for she does not tolerate being an object of the reflective awareness of "this-ness" (*idantā*).

How is the determination of these [phonemes] made by way of their being "sentient" (sattva) or "non-sentient" (asattva)? If it is argued that even so, its form is established as necessarily consisting of forty-nine phonemes, and therefore the reflective awareness (parāmarśa) must be determined precisely according to that nature— this too cannot be the case, because this [Mother], being of the nature of the imperishable letter *kṣa*, abides in her own innate form which is of the nature of a *kūṭa* (syllabic unit), and thus that which is imperishable...

The meaning is that even the letter *kṣa* has that same nature. For the letter *kṣa*, by virtue of being the essence of the *anuttara* (the letter *a*), the *visarga*, and the *sa-kāra* and *ka-kāra* as a collective contraction (*pratyāhāra*), simultaneously encompasses the entire alphabet (*mātṛkā*).
Thus, because it again possesses the aforementioned manifold forms—such as being a single letter and so forth—it is impossible to determine its existence or non-existence with any fixed certainty.

It is not an object to be established; nor can its cause be determined, for this supreme *aulija*—this supreme, full *aulirovalli*—is that non-conceptual knowledge (*avikalpaka-jñāna*) which is beyond all mental activity and is *unmanasa*.
From that... [it is] the primordial, born from the beginning... (4.4).

Thus, according to the perspective to be explained, [the Goddess] is born from Śiva, who is established from the beginning; and he too, because his nature is free of conceptual construction (*avikalpa*), is indeed beyond being conceptualized, as has already been largely stated. The object is likewise: that which is Kula, the state called Nameless (*anāmākhya*).

Thus, in the supreme consciousness itself—which is of the nature of the *kula*, indefinable, and the ultimate *kalā*—this [manifestation] surges forth like the waves of the ocean, yet rests within that very [consciousness], appearing as nothing other than it; such is the path already described. In this way, even while abiding in various forms, there is no fixed purpose for this [manifestation]; what then is its determination? It is the Goddess herself.
The meaning is that she has the nature of sporting in various forms. As the scripture says:
"In Śiva there is no desire, nor is there any desiring in Śakti;
yet the Supreme Goddess of Śiva has arisen by her very nature."
Thus, the meaning is: "I praise—that is, I enter into—that supreme Śakti who is designated by such terms as *mātṛkā*. || 10 ||
Now, in order to introduce even the convention of worship, he says:
"I bow to her, the mistress of the eight great siddhis arising from the eight groups, in whom the eight mātrās abide according to the sequence of the classes. (11)

I bow to that Blessed Mother Mātṛkā, who— by her very nature— is the sovereign of the eight great and unlimited supernatural powers (siddhis), such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, which have arisen from her as her own essential forms, like the eight groups of consonants; she who is solely intent upon bestowing them.

"Joined with the eight deities according to the sequence of the *vargas*" (1.60). According to the perspective that will be stated hereafter, by connecting [the letters] with the sequence of the *vargas*, the group of eight Mothers—Vaśinī and the rest—is established; although not distinct from [the central deity] herself, they appear as if distinct, constituting her inner retinue, because they generate the respective supernatural powers (*siddhis*) such as *aṇimā*.
The meaning is that it is manifested as being worthy of worship in the first outer circle. || 11 ||

In this context, by the mere mention of the group of eight beginning with Vaśinī, the sequence for the complete worship of the entire cakra has been introduced, owing to their association with the eight accomplishments (siddhis) worshipped in all cakras; now, however, he speaks in order to also introduce the symbolic worship of the primary triangle (mūlatrikoṇa), because of its preeminence.
I bow to the venerable Tripurā, who dwells within the Śrīpīṭha known as Kāmapūrṇaja, and who is the treasury of the fourfold commands (ājñās). 12.

According to the principle stated in *Tattvaprakāśa* (1.132), "For here, everywhere, the word 'I' denotes only pure consciousness," even though the body and so forth exist, [the self] is of the nature of the Supreme Self, which is a single mass of consciousness, possessing the characteristics described and to be described.
The venerable Tripurā, designated by the term *mātṛkā*, whose legends are renowned in our own philosophical system— the venerable Mahātripurasundarī— who,

although she resides eternally in all four seats (*pīṭhas*) situated in the directions beginning with the East, has become a treasury because her command of grace (*anugrahājñā*), which was fading away due to the power of time, has been repeatedly brought down [to earth] by the foremost among the various *siddhas*, *yoginīs*, and others.
The meaning is "a place that is like a treasury" or "a source of extraction. As it has been said:
"O fair-faced one, at the conclusion of the loss of knowledge, by your command, your lineage shall flourish in Karālā through a diversity of names."

Thus, the meaning of the sentence "I bow to her who is eternally present in Kāmarūpa and other [sacred sites], being intent on desiring to favor the entire world" is as follows. By this, the indication of the secret convention (*saṅketa*) for the worship of the eighth and ninth wheels (*cakra*) is also hinted at; therefore, I shall conclude. And as for that which has been said here by others...

It should not be suspected by the learned that because [the opponent's view] was left unrefuted— on the grounds that "whatever is explained word-for-word as a fabrication of difficulties, as a non-lexical meaning, as a misinterpretation, or as a corruption is understood by all those of little learning on their own, and thus it is neglected"— and therefore "the opponent's position, being unrefuted, is indeed accepted," since that [view] is being refuted by restating it word-for-word due to its irrelevance to the present subject.
We have not attached ourselves to this point in vain, thinking that it results merely in the burden of voluminous writing;
rather, it should be understood that by stating what is contrary to that [position], it is thereby refuted. Enough of this digression; let us now address the matter at hand. || 12 ||
Having thus revealed that this tantra is preceded by praise, he begins the introduction itself with the words:
"The Śrī Devī said. To the inquiry of what she said, he replies:
"O Blessed One, all mantras have been revealed to me by you."
And thus,
there are sixty-four tantras which are indeed the most excellent among those of the Mothers.
Mahāmāyā, Śambara, Yoginījālaśambara, the god Tattvaśambaraka, and also the eight Bhairavas. || 14 ||
The eightfold Bahurūpa-jñāna, the eightfold Yāmala, the Candrajñāna, the Vāsuki, and likewise the Mahāsaṃmohana; || 15 ||
Mahocchuṣma, Mahādeva, Vāthula, Nayottara, Hṛdbheḍa, Mātṛbheḍa, Guhyatantra, and Kāmika. || 16 ||
Kālapāda, Kālasāra, and likewise another, Kubjikāmata; Nayottara, Vīṇā and others, Trotula, and Bhrātulottara. (17)
The *Pañcāmṛta*, the *Rūpabheda*, the *Bhūtoḍḍāmara*, as well as the *Kulasāra*, the *Kuloḍḍīśa*, and the *Kulacūḍāmaṇi*. || 18 ||
O God, there is the Sarvajñānottara, as well as the Mahāpicumata;
O God, the Mahālakṣmīmata and the Siddhayogīśvarīmata. (19)
O God, the Kurūpikā-mata and the Rūpikā-mata, O God, the Sarvavīra-mata and the Vimalā-mata; || 20 ||
Aruṇeśa, Modaneśa, and Viśuddheśvara—
these and likewise other scriptures, numbering in the tens of millions (koṭi).
"O Lord, you have described to me those things consisting of all-knowledge,
beginning with the lute and ending with the *vīṇāśikha*."
However, O Lord of Gods, although these sixteen branches of knowledge are included within all the scriptures, they have been merely indicated and not fully revealed.
Therefore,
O Śaṅkara, I now wish to hear their names,
as well as the complete worship of each individual wheel in its entirety.
Together with the hosts of mantras and mudrās of many deities, Śrī Bhairava spoke right here in order to provide an answer. To explain what he said, [the text] states on page 18: "What did he say?"
Listen, O Goddess, to this great knowledge consisting of the sixteen syllables of the Vidyā. (24)
I have not explained this to anyone; it is concealed within all the tantras.
And because it is difficult to fathom, its exposition here is by means of the ocean.
He says that very thing:
"In that regard, first of all, the first is the eternal Mahātripurasundarī. (25)
Then there are Kāmeśvarī Nityā, Bhagamālinī Nityā, as well as Nityaklinnā, Bheruṇḍā, and Vahnivāsinī.
Mahāvidyeśvarī, Dūtī, Tvaritā, Kulasundarī, Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, and Sarvamaṅgalā. || 27 ||
And [the goddess] Jvālāmālivicitrā—thus there are sixteen Nityās.
"The first" means the principal one. "Dūtī" means she who runs to Śiva; the meaning is that "Nityā" is indeed her name.
In that regard,
O Goddess, first hear about Tripurasundarī, the Great Eternity.
"O Goddess, when she is realized, the agitation of the universe arises.

Now, even though the Blessed One promised, 'Listen to the Nityā Mahātripurasundarī,' why has he begun to speak of the extraction of the *cakra* so abruptly? This is indeed so; however, the Blessed Goddess, the Supreme Mistress, is truly the Nityā."
Desiring to manifest externally in various forms through the majesty of its own sovereignty, it first flashes forth as the nature of the support (ādhāra) and the supported (ādheya).
For how could there be an external manifestation of the supported without a support? Thus, at the very outset, the Supreme Lord speaks in order to define the essential nature of the *cakra*.
Having pierced one power with another by means of power, he then [pierces] it again with the city of fire.
Having encapsulated [the energy], one should extend the all-pervading upper power downward.
Indeed, in this context, it is the triangle itself— due to the predominance of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and its outward orientation— that is called "power" (*śakti*), as it faces downward.
Because of the predominance of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) and because it is inward-facing, fire is said to be "upward-facing" (*ūrdhvamukha*). As the scripture states:
"That pentad of powers [is] through emanation; through dissolution, it is the fourfold fire.
Our venerable supreme gurus also [state this].
"The Śakti, triangular and single-peaked, oriented toward emanation"—
thus [it is said];
"by the city of fire" means by the upward-facing triangle, which is primarily characterized by withdrawal (saṃhāra).
Thus, by means of the two upward- and downward-facing triangles named Vahni and Śakti;
and so it is said. There are others as well.
In this [yantra] consisting of four fires, five powers reside within the center of the whirl;
it is upward-facing, with its mouth directed toward emanation.
Thus [it is said]. Others, however, desiring to demonstrate the difference between power (*śakti*) and fire (*vahni*), state:
"Having divided the entire square enclosure by three [lines], one should fashion a triangular field with threads situated toward the east and so forth."
"It is stated that the field has the shape of a *bhaga*, with its rear corner at the tip of the triangle.

This [statement] is not consistent here, because it is directly observed that the intent is merely to establish the formation of the triangle. Furthermore, if one were to insist on a forced interpretation, even though it is not the literal meaning, [one might claim it refers to] the upward- and downward-facing [triangles].
The two types of triangles are explained; yet even there, the intended designation as "fire-power" (*vahni-śakti*) would not be established.
Furthermore, the designation by terms such as "bhaga," "yoni," or "triangle" is seen everywhere else as well. As the scripture states:
"The triangle situated between the upward and downward faces, extending to the two junctions (*marman*)."
Thus,
20) the wise one should lay down six lines each by means of single staff-lines.
By which all wombs are born, together with their equal joints.
The compartments are forty-nine in number, in the form of the female organ (bhaga);
and thus it is said: "The Gurus also [state that] the end of the triangle is the pentad, consisting of the four fires and five powers."
Thus,
by means of six lines each extending along the vicinity of every single corner of the entire triangle, there shall arise a [mandala] consisting of seven sets of seven yonis.

And so it is said. In that regard, the designation "triangle" (*tryaśra*) applies to the downward-facing triangle in the first case, while the terms "womb" (*bhaga*) and "source" (*yoni*) apply to the upward-facing triangle in the latter case; thus, this [explanation] does not have a coherent meaning at all—enough of this prolixity.
Therein, in the intended field, one should first delineate the power (*śakti*) of the downward-facing triangles below.
With another such power, one should pierce through from the center by means of a transverse entry, so that the production of the root triangle occurs;

and furthermore, having enclosed those two powers with a fire-city— an upward-facing triangle— by forming a casket of their mutually facing tips, [one proceeds] from the tip of the root triangle at a slight interval.
One should worship the fourfold [group] in the center of the wheel in sequence, starting from the west, north, east, and so on, ending with the south,

according to the perspective that will be explained [in verse 1.156]. Having thus established [the deities], one should [proceed] by means of the sequence of horizontal entry into the interior of that very lower energy (*śakti*).

Having first produced three corners on the outside, at the bottom, and on the two sides, as well as two corners on the two sides by moving upward— preceded by the touching of those vital points (*marman*)— and having made them conjoined through the expansion for the production of further corners above, there arises an eight-spoked [wheel] with two powers and a single fire within a triangle; such is the nature of the eight-spoked [wheel] as defined by the Great Guru.

One should act [in this manner]. Furthermore, having said, "We have been mocked by certain rogues who, while not even perceiving other compositions of extremely difficult words that have been directly realized, abandon the calamity of such difficult word-compositions and instead join sentence with sentence," they themselves— by their own power— having pierced through the form of the triangle facing them with the city of fire (vahni-pura), [proceed as follows].

"Having encapsulated that Śakti by means of the upward-facing triangle"—thus, words are explained by words themselves. As for how much is mocked regarding their terminology, let this suffice: because of their audacity, there is simply no end to those who speak in such a manner. Likewise, one should extend downward, by way of spreading out both sides, that Śakti which has been delineated by relying on the uppermost point of the entire wheel.
The meaning is that one should form the third power, which initiates the first ten-spoked wheel, by means of the contact between two spokes from the lower eight-spoked wheel.
In the same manner, one should pierce that very [channel] upward by means of the fire-wheel (vahnicakra). || 30 ||
In the same manner, by means of the fire-wheel (*vahnicakra*)— which consists of upward-facing triangles through the process of extending both sides like the initial power (*ādyāśakti*)— one should,

after first generating the apex of this [triangle], move upward by specifically touching the four corners situated on the two sides above the eight spokes of that very power which was extended immediately prior.
One should cause it to split so that a second fire may also be accomplished. || 30 ||
By means of which one should gradually expand the power situated above that upward;
immediately after that, the very same power situated above that was first delineated.
Having first broken the knot of confluence above the second fire of the third power,

one should extend [the thread] upwards by following the sequence characterized by equality with the corner of the first city of fire, so that this ten-spoked wheel may have two pairs of fifth and seventh spokes.
Then again, O beautiful one, having extended the first fire-wheel downward from that as well; || 31 ||
By means of the very process of breaking the knot (*granthi*), one should pierce the primordial *Śakti*.

The first [circle], which is the fire-circle (*vahnicakra*) designated by the term "city of fire" (*vahnipura*) and is the initiator of the eight-spoked wheel, is extended on both sides for the sake of accomplishing the second fire.

(p. 22) Furthermore, by means of the very process of piercing the knots at the junctions below the second fire and the third power (*śakti*), one should expand downward and specifically pierce—that is, unite—the first power (which is in fact the third power relative to this wheel), making it equal to the tip of the corner of the second power; thus is the accomplishment of the ten-spoked wheel (*daśāracakra*).
From there, in that same manner, one should extend the power that reaches up to the fire at the very summit downwards. || 32 ||

Above all, at the end— that is, in the vicinity— of that second fire which revolves above the ten spokes, one should extend downward the primordial Śakti who resides precisely above all; by means of a process of expansion on both sides,
through contact with the four corners belonging to the lower two sides of the ten spokes, she initiates the second set of ten spokes.
The meaning is that it generates the fourth power. || 32 ||
In that manner,
one should pierce that [fourth power] with fire from below the initial wheel upward;
that fourth power which was just described belongs to the ten-spoked wheel established immediately following the initial wheel.

The third power below, by means of the first fire indicated by it, having performed an expansion toward both sides, should specifically pierce upward— preceded by contact with the four upper corners of the ten-spoked [mandala]— so as to equalize the corner-points of the two fires; the meaning is that one should thus generate the third fire.
Then again, as before, one should expand the primordial Śakti and cause it to pierce through. || 33 ||
The upward-flaming [fire]— [omitted]—

the primordial power (śakti) first inscribed, just as it was previously expanded for the sake of accomplishing the fifth and seventh spokes of the first ten-spoked wheel by means of piercing the knots of the power and fire, in that very same way, her again...

Having expanded the third fire situated above, one should pierce it from the center by means of a horizontal entry; having drawn a clear line (p. 23), the meaning is that one should form three spokes at the top. || 33 ||
Likewise— [filling in the gaps]—
having expanded [the syllable] devoid of fire in the midst of the downward fire,
one should pierce the power from below with the upward fire. (34)
Having omitted the second [triangle], which initiates the first ten-spoked wheel of the upper fire as it was previously inscribed,

and disregarding its utility, one should expand the third [triangle]— which initiates this second ten-spoked wheel of the lower fire and was inscribed later— into the middle, which consists of the two locations of the knots below.

By implication, having made the two side-lines extended upward from the [central] line, one should pierce the fourth power situated below; then, as just described, one should produce the three spokes below as well—thus is the accomplishment of the second ten-spoked [lotus]. || 34 ||

Thus, from this central power (*madhya-śakti*), one should extend the upward power (*ūrdhva-śakti*) downward. The central [power] is that which differentiates the first power; it is situated above the beginning of that second power.
The third power initiates the first ten-spoked wheel; above that, one should extend the fourth power, which pertains to the second ten-spoked wheel, by means of spreading it out toward both sides.
The meaning is that one should form the fifth power, preceded by contact with the four side-spokes of the second ten-spoked wheel.
"What would be gained by that? he says:
"In that very same way, O Goddess of the Gods, one should enclose the entire wheel. (35)
The particle *eva* is displaced [in the sentence]. By it, [it is meant] "the entire wheel indeed. And this is stated as the fruit in its entirety. || 35 ||
Then,
O Great Goddess, one should pierce that [center] with that wheel of fire.
By the process of breaking the knots, [one proceeds] from below, from the highest of all, and from the outermost of all. || 36 ||
Up to the middle and the upper power—[omission]—that very fifth power just described stands outside of the entire wheel, and not within;
it rests supported above the entire wheel upon that third fire-wheel, and not the first. By this, [it follows that]...
By that same power, one should pierce and unite— by means of spreading out from both sides through the sequence of breaking those two knots which consist of a union at the very base of that [power]—
the fourth and first [powers], namely the power and its counterpart, located in the middle and above the wheel respectively;
one should do so by touching the four upper corners until that fourth fire is accomplished.
Likewise—
[filling the space] up to the beloved limit of the primordial power (ādi-śakti)—
one should then cause the power above to expand from the end of the external power to the root of the internal power. || 37 ||

Immediately after that, one should cause the fourth power, which is within the interior of the fifth power situated externally, to expand upward from the limit of the first power (Ādi-śakti) down to the end of the first power; having extended it on both sides, one should join it with that [fifth power], so that there may be two spokes consisting of the sixth and tenth [units] for this wheel. || 37 ||
Then,
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, one should extend the primordial Śakti upwards as well, from the upper fire down to the lower fire. (38)

Above the entire wheel, there is a fourth fire; reaching down as far as the third fire below it, by means of being joined to its tip, one [perceives] the primordial, initial power (*śakti*)— which has been repeatedly extended for the sake of accomplishing the two sets of ten spokes.

Likewise, preceded by the expansion of both sides, one should extend it upwards in the form of a clear line, so that by the process of piercing the fourth fire, the three upper spokes of the fourteen-spoked [wheel] may be accomplished. || 38 ||
From there as well,
O Dear One, she should pierce the wheel of fire situated at the very top,
reaching as far as the knot at the lower portion of that supreme fire. (39)
Having expanded the external power (*bāhyaśakti*), one should cause it to pierce down to the very bottom;

this should be understood—like the eye of a crow—to extend as far as the knot located at the lower portion of the fire situated at the very top. Consequently, [one should pierce] those two [knots] which consist of the piercing union of the third fire’s lower portion with the fifth power of the fourth fire situated above all others.

By means of that very manner [of expansion] just described—namely, the unfolding in the form of a triangle and so forth—reaching its ultimate goal, one should pierce and unite with the fire-wheel (vahnicakra), designated by the term "fire-city" (vahnipura), which stands at the beginning above all four fires as the perfect originator of the eight spokes; thereby, the accomplishment of the third thirteen-spoked wheel of this [mandala] shall occur. And thus:
Above all the fires, for the purpose of achieving the eight-spoked [mandala], one first draws [the lines];
then, on the lower part of that fire which was just joined, there are two knots consisting of the union of the fifth power and the third fire.
Extending as far as those—that is, spreading the two side-lines—one should pierce the outer fifth power at the very bottom, so that...
The completion of this entire wheel—which consists of the four limbs of the five powers—would be achieved once the three lower spokes of the fourteen-spoked [wheel] are perfected. (p. 26)
He concludes this very point by first establishing the pervasion:
"Therefore, through emanation, the great wheel is first the fire. (40)
In the center, however, there is a pair through abiding, and the fifth is that which is withdrawal;
thus is this great wheel, consisting of the Great Śrī Tripurā. (41)

In this manner, as it has been stated, because it possesses such an exceedingly marvelous configuration, it manifests as a form shimmering before one; because it is distinct from the other *cakras* described in various other scriptures; because it "makes great" (*mahat*) by causing the universe—which consists of subject and object—to abide for a long time through its expansion; and because it "cuts" (*kartana*) by means of the direct realization of one's own Self, resulting in a complete dissolution on all sides.

If, by means of the principle of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining one while discarding the rest), through the attainment of satisfaction—which is a synonym for fullness—and by way of the forms of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), maintenance (*sthiti*), withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), and the ineffable (*anākhyā*), it is designated by the term "Wheel" (*cakra*); therefore, [she] pervades this entire universe, which consists solely of the unfolding of her own sovereignty, by being woven warp and woof; and because she possesses her own essential nature as a mass of unsurpassed consciousness and bliss, she is primarily Śrī. These three...

That Tripurā, who is designated by the term Mahātripurasundarī and whose true essence is the ineffable Supreme Consciousness alone, manifests the cities— characterized by creation, maintenance, and dissolution, which contain within them infinite triads, which fill their respective divisions, and which are the flashes of her own self-consciousness— which, though non-different from her own substrate according to the analogy of a city in a mirror, yet appear as if distinct; she who is the reality of pure Supreme Consciousness beyond all description.

"Consisting of that nature" means having the very same undivided essence [as that], as in the expression "the form of the support and the supported. For instance, first of all, that which is great by virtue of having fourteen spokes—

The wheel (*cakra*) is characterized by that creation; for external creation is indeed fourteenfold—namely, the ten and four worlds of *saṃsāra*. Therefore, in the center, according to the propriety of the ten spokes, it has the nature of fire.
The pair of wheels constitutes the form of persistence (*sthiti*). The sense is that persistence must indeed possess the nature of both [origination and dissolution]. As they say:
"The sequence called 'descent' (*avatāra*) is that which has become merged within the interval between origination and dissolution.
With respect to the root wheel, the second wheel is also eight-spoked.
"O Maheśānī, in the first wheel... (1.157).

This refers to that which is primarily characterized by withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), designated as "first" with the intention of emphasizing the abundance of the *vadarā* [fruit] as will be explained later;
for this is also stated in the *Śrīyogasañcāra* and other texts.
— — — — — — — — — — — Those which are the black and white circles situated in the center;
thus,
by means of the sixteen and twelve spokes, [they are placed] in all respects within the eight-spoked wheels.

By these and other such statements, it is stated that even the Aṣṭāra primarily consists of withdrawal (*saṃhāra*). Therefore, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is established as a matter of course that the Mūlatrikoṇa also possesses the nature of the Inexplicable (*anākhyarūpa*) due to its indivisible essence. For this very reason, the pentad of wheels (*cakrapañcaka*) is said to be the cause of all auspiciousness, the accomplisher of all aims, the creator of all protection, the remover of all diseases, and the source of all bliss.

And since the designation [of the stages] is indeed appropriate to the fourfold sequence beginning with emanation (*sṛṣṭi*), that which has been stated is alone correct. As for the fact that others disagree here regarding the reading and so forth, that is mostly due to them and should simply be disregarded; for while a difference in reading does exist here, it is merely imagined through the confusion of students and is not original. Furthermore, whether such a reading is accepted or rejected is based solely on its correctness or incorrectness.
"Excellence (*sādhutva*) consists in the skill of carrying out the intended meaning by avoiding cumbersome procedures; otherwise, it is different.
As they say:
'In this case, whether there is a variant reading or something else, it does not matter from the perspective of the root.'"
However, because of the error of the students, that demonstration by him was due to ignorance.
Thus,
when one intends to adopt a reading after deliberating upon the study of various manuscripts,
that which is indeed correct should be adopted because it is not contradicted by the consensus of the virtuous.
And as it is said [in the text]: "Thus [it is]. Why then do you prattle on here, claiming that this [text] exists [here], merely because of obtaining a superior position or a better recension?
On the contrary, this fault belongs to you alone, insofar as you [ignore] both the completion of the wheel and its pervasion by means of the extent of the text provided by us.

This has already been explained; by that much alone, you have merely established the formation of the *cakra* through an elaborate procedure. Furthermore, there are others here who avoid excessive prolixity and serve as witnesses; therefore, enough with considering that point as well, since this very [explanation] constitutes the rebuttal here. Moreover, we do not perceive anything at all regarding the impropriety of the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*).
Just as fragrance is in a flower, oil in sesame seeds, the soul in the body, and nectar in water,
even so is the Kula established within all scriptures.

Thus, there is no disagreement that this Kaula knowledge, consisting of two states, exists everywhere as the inner vitalizing force; otherwise, nothing at all would bestow either worldly enjoyment (*bhukti*) or liberation (*mukti*), as has been stated many times elsewhere. Therefore, in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
Even within the scriptures of the bound souls (pāśava), that [power] was shown by the Great Lord,
like a sudden flash of light in the midst of a terrible, blinding winter night.

By these and other such statements, it is declared therein that the knowledge of the Kula serves as the vitalizing breath even for those on the lower and lower levels. With this very intention, you yourselves have also spoken of her as the "Wave," the "Enjoyress," the "Kubjā," and the "Kuleśvarī."
I bow to that Goddess who is known as Śrī Kālakarṣaṇī and also as Kuṇḍalinī.

Thus it has been stated. In this supreme scripture, which is to be accepted by all as the direct Kula teaching, how could there be any lack of conformity with such a pervasiveness (vyāpti), or anything even touched by contradiction? And the Supreme Lord himself will state this at the beginning of the fourth chapter; therefore, enough with the exposition of these secret meanings. On the contrary—
Setting aside this kind of pervasion (vyāpti) which was stated by one's own throat [in the previous verse],
[there are] the wheel of the Point (baindava), that which consists of Ambikā, and Vāmā— these three are the delusions (bhrama).
O Mother, he who perceives these four lines outside in the city of Purandara as Jyeṣṭhā,
and who, contemplating this mass of triangles of Śakti and Fire as Raudrī,
meditates upon that uncreated support of worship— he is your true worshipper.

Whatever has been stated by those who, for the purpose of demonstrating pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, have imagined various methods—claiming that there is some established basis for the extraction of the initial letters and so on, namely that these [vowels] alone possess such an arrangement—that is not so. For this is the complete accomplishment of the fifty [phonemes]. If it were the case that these alone possess such an arrangement in the extraction of the initial letters and so forth, then here...

This is stated as a refutation of [the opponent's] delusion. Even so, since the fact that these [energies] possess such a specific arrangement is not absolute in that context, how could it apply here as well— namely,
that Raudrī is proclaimed as the head of Ambikā (the letter *a*), and Vāmā as her face?
Ambikā is said to be the arm, and Jyeṣṭhā is remembered as the weapon.
In this context, the state of the arms being clearly straight has been described; for when that subtle *kalā* known as Kuṇḍalinī arises,
the Bindu, consisting of four *kalās*, becomes the Lord residing within the womb of Śakti.
O Dear One, through the application of the churner and the act of churning, straightness is produced;
that is known as the Jyeṣṭhā Śakti, situated in the very center between the two points (bindus).
She is proclaimed as the "Threefold Path" (Tripathā) and is sung of by the name Raudrī;
Ambikā has the form of a crescent of the moon and is like the half-moonlight.
Thus, the one supreme Śakti arises in a threefold manner.
And here, the state of having the form of the crescent moon consisting of the letter *u* is [implied], yet even the name of Vāmā has not been touched upon. Here too,
as will be explained later,
she has attained the state of being a sprout from all seeds and so forth that have been swallowed whole.
Then the Vāmā and Jyeṣṭhā [energies] assume the form of a triangle (śṛṅgāṭaka).
"Raudrī, however— [text missing]—

," (4.9) and so forth; thus, in the case of Ambikā, as well as in the *Śrīsarvavīra* and other such works, there are nine new [forms] for each of these [goddesses], even in the extraction of the various phonemes in those respective places.

Since the arrangement has been made clear, it is certain that even in cases where there is merely the extraction of other phonemes (*varṇa*), such as in these instances where their form is not fixed, what can be said of other similar cases? Thus, the conclusion is that there is no established basis whatsoever here.
Alternatively, this is simply the fault of the author of the *Vārttika* himself, since you have proceeded by relying upon him; enough of this prolixity. (41)
Now he speaks of its very majesty:
"O Great Goddess, it effects moistening, liquefaction, agitation, as well as delusion, attraction, paralyzing, and likewise immobilization. (42)
It is the supreme pacifier of those who inflict disease, the destroyer of all misconduct, and the bringer of peace, nourishment, wealth, health, and the perfection of mantras. (43)
It bestows enjoyment and liberation, O Goddess, and it brings about the state of moving through the sky; it provides protection from all things and likewise produces all bliss.
It performs all rites and accomplishes the purpose of every task;
O Goddess, it brings about all types of possession and, furthermore, effects all types of piercing.
O Goddess, it brings about all reality, likewise it is the abode of all commands;
it is endowed with all supernatural powers and is the supreme bringer of all welfare. (46)
O Goddess, it consists of all mantras, and furthermore, it consists of all sacred fords;
it consists of all vows, and likewise, it consists of all nectars.
It is the pacifier of all suffering, the remover of all grief, the inducer of all ecstatic states, O Goddess, and consists of the essence of all the lords of yoga. 48.
(31) O Goddess, it consists of all sacred seats; O Beloved, it consists of all knowledge.
O Goddess, it consists of all deities and is the cause of all delight. || 49 ||
The wheel that pacifies all misfortune, wards off all obstacles, bestows all accomplishments, and fulfills all hopes. || 50 ||
It is the devourer of the floods of fierce, malevolent, and violent supreme mantras;
it attracts the accomplishments of others, as well as the commands of others. || 51 ||
It is the paralyzer of enemy armies, the deluder of the higher knowledge of others,
the paralyzer of the speech of others, and the supreme stunner of weapons.
O Goddess, it produces great wonder, promotes great enjoyment, brings about great subjugation, and bestows great good fortune. (53)
O Goddess, it is the supreme remover of great fevers, the remover of great poisons, the pacifier of great death, and the destroyer of great fears. || 54 ||
O Goddess, it causes a great agitation of the city, bestows the auspiciousness of great bliss, consists of great fortune, and grants great blessings. (55)
It is endowed with great power and destroys great sins.

The reason for the separate mention of "moistening" (*kledana*) and "liquefying" (*drāvaṇa*) is their common nature. "Paralyzing" (*stambhana*) alone is elaborated upon by the phrase "paralyzing the enemy's army" and so forth. Elsewhere, it is described as "the entry into all" (*sarvāveśa*) due to its division into fifty varieties and so on.

It has been stated: "The All-Veda" is spoken of in various ways in different places as being the nature of the resonance (*nāda*) of mantra and so forth. "The All-Holy Place" (*sarvatīrtha*) and "The All-Vow" (*sarvavrata*) [are so called] because they bestow the respective fruits thereof. Suffering (*duḥkha*) is agitation (*kṣobha*), a specific form of demerit (*adharma*) that is the opposite of happiness; whereas grief (*śoka*) is merely the lamentation for oneself and others. "The Great Enjoyment" (*mahābhukti*)... [p. 32]

This is with regard to worldly conventions (*lokadharma*). Furthermore, it should be understood that by introducing such terms as "bestowing all bliss" (*sarvānandakara*) and so forth, the author intends to reinforce the very non-duality of the empowerer and the empowered; thus, even the ninefold wheel (*cakranavaka*), which is esteemed for its worshipability, is also implicitly indicated.
And he says that its power is not limited to this much:
"In this way, the power of this wheel has been described by me. (56)
O Great Goddess, it is not possible [to describe this] even in hundreds of millions of aeons.
Is there anything else to be done outside of this? To which he replies:
"One should draw an eight-petaled lotus situated outside of this. (57)
O Goddess of the gods, outside of that as well, there is likewise a sixteen-spoked [wheel],
endowed with a surrounding halo and adorned with four gates.

"Sixteen-spoked" (*ṣoḍaśāra*): the word *ara* (spoke) is a synonym for *dala* (petal). As it is said regarding the great sixteen-petaled lotus: "— — — — — — — — — — —. "In the same way" means "the lotus itself. "Encompassing" (*pariveśa*) refers to the line of the sky (*vyomarekhā*). Furthermore, this is stated in the *Śrīrasamahodadhi*: [text follows].
It has also been stated by way of introducing the composition of the Sūtra with the intention that it is easy to perform:
"Therefore, I shall now fully explain the determination of the wheel-marked [diagram].
For that purpose, O Goddess, one should prepare an excellent mandala measuring three cubits."
One should fashion the pericarp, marked with a wheel, as one-third of that;
the two lotuses as half of that; and the area of the gates as equal to those.
Having first laid the Brahma-thread from the center of the pericarp-circle,
one should lay seven threads situated there, extending from south to north.
33) Then, having removed the fourth cord, the middle portion shall consist of two parts;
having divided the third and fifth portions, they are each diminished by three parts.
Furthermore, one should increase the middle portion by that same measure;
[this applies] to the ends of the third, the second, and the first sūtra.
Then one should extend two pairs of threads positioned further and further downward,
meeting at the seventh thread in the circle and at the Brahma-sthāna.
One should extend two threads each for the three lower positions down to the fifth;
likewise, there are six triangles formed by another two threads each.
In this manner, the fourteen-spoked [wheel] and the ten-spoked [wheel] are established;
from the second and sixth lines, on both sides of the Brahma-line.
Two pairs of threads should be laid out, extending downward and upward;
then, one should extend a pair of threads connecting their ends.
Thus has this third ten-spoked wheel been described.
From the fifth tip of the thread upwards, one should lead two other threads.

One should lay down a third thread from the center, situated between the upper and lower points, reaching as far as the two joints of the triangle, so that it intersects the other two at their mutual junctions.
Thus, the fourth, the eighth, and the letter *e* as the fifth—
by these, the wheel situated within the pericarp is perfectly established.
That pentad of powers arises through emanation, and the tetrad of fires through dissolution;
from the union of the five powers and the four fires, the emergence of the *cakras* occurs.
Among those, O Maheśvarī, one [group] consists of eight in the middle; then two, ten, and fourteen;
then fourteen, two tens (twenty), and eight, and finally one.
Through the yoga of emanation and withdrawal, the stations of power are situated in sequence within the wheel of Tripurā; by awakening to which, one becomes immortal.
Outside, one should draw two lotuses with eight and sixteen petals;
then, having provided a square, one should fashion four doors.
Thus, the supreme maṇḍala shall be provided with four corners;
the wheel should be filled with red powder, while the three [triangles] above should be white.

Thus [it is said]. This is the meaning here: "by its half" means by half of that third part, which is to say, by a sixth part. By that, two lotuses are to be made in an area measuring twelve finger-breadths on each side. For others, however, the reading is simply "by a third part. As they have said:
In that three-cubit sacrificial ground, one cubit should be designated for the doorway;
and in the sixteen-petaled lotus of the earth, the pericarp is one-third of a cubit.
Thus, this should also be applied with the intention of the two readings, "equal to that" (*tatsamam*) and "equal to it" (*tena samam*). Furthermore, regarding this three-cubit field thus divided,
prior to the establishment of its squareness— by means of the laying down of seven lines, one extending east-west along the *brahmasūtra* and six extending north-south from the center of the circle—
the [field] is first divided twenty-four times, as otherwise the mention of terms such as "parts" (*bhāga*), "words" (*śabda*), and so forth would be inexplicable.

It is established that the division must be performed in such a way that all of this is consistent with the *karṇikā*-field of the *hāstika* being divided into eight parts. Consequently, there shall be two lotuses on each side, each occupying two parts, and the door shall occupy four parts on each side. And thus, having placed a point (*bindu*) in the station of Brahmā, in accordance with that—

The explanation that there is a prescription for three circles for the sake of the two lotuses of the *karṇikā*, followed by the rule for the square, and subsequently the construction of forty-three triangles within the *karṇikā* using threads, serves only to demonstrate the extreme ridiculousness of this eminent teacher’s lack of proficiency in the work of drawing lines; enough, therefore, with these manifestations of the clarity of Caryānandanātha’s instruction.
Having been discussed together [on page 35],
the adoption of the specific sūtra is intended solely to demonstrate its utility for the completion of the circle; and thus,
from among the sūtras extending east-west and north-south, it is specifically the Brahma-sūtra [that is adopted].
The utility [of the fourth line] consists merely in producing the equality of the tips of the *śakti* and *vahni* lines at the corners.

Although the fourth line was initially drawn for the purpose of counting the divisions of the thread to determine the location of Brahma, its deletion is again prescribed so as to demonstrate its fitness for the formation of the specific components of the *cakra*. As for the other lines, however, [their utility pertains] to the completion of the *cakra*.

Fearing that if the expansion of the Sūtras were to begin from the end of the second and sixth [Sūtras] and conclude with the repose in the station of Brahman— resulting in the direct application [of the teaching] alone— the very completion of the Cakra would not occur,
the Supreme Lord, at the very outset, demonstrates therein the relinquishing of the form of the parts characterized by the three aspects.
He teaches the certainty of their positions in brief by means of the third [sūtra] and so forth.

Because of the proximity of that word "third," it refers to the third part itself; and as for the fifth part, since the expansion of the third, fifth, and subsequent sūtras will be explained at the very end, one should understand them to be at the end according to the *tantrayukti* known as "anticipation of what is yet to come" (*anāgatāvekṣaṇa*).

Having first subtracted one-third of the portion— since it measures three finger-breadths (*aṅgula*)— from the front by means of that finger-measure, and having likewise established [the mark] from the back in the same way, one should then expand the middle section toward both sides at each of those respective places, specifically at the three locations consisting of the second, the Brahma-line, and the sixth line, by means of that very path characterized as one-third, with reference to the fourteen and ten spokes.

The meaning is that one should effect an increase of one *aṅgula* in measure. This is what is intended: here, indeed, having excluded one *aṅgula* from the first, second, sixth, and seventh threads according to their respective positions, and having added one *aṅgula* in the middle of the second and sixth threads, one should place a dot (*bindu*) at each of those points for the purpose of demarcation.
Having stretched the threads both downwards and upwards, their resting points should be established here and there according to the perspective to be described.

However, even at the location of Brahmā for the first thread, one must add exactly one finger-breadth; and the third [thread] should be led to the number of arrows (five), both downwards and upwards by a finger-breadth.
As for the interpretation that it is "upwards by a finger-breadth," that does not accord with the literal meaning of the words, and thus it is not applicable to the formation of the wheels (*cakra*).

On the contrary, it is detrimental because it produces a confusion of the wheels (*cakras*) and so forth, and because it causes the vital points (*marmas*) to disintegrate on all sides; thus, it should be disregarded.
Likewise, [this applies to] those [works] from the *Śrīrasamahodadhi* which are filled with a multitude of well-guarded secrets.
A few drops of verses, though extremely difficult to obtain, have been successfully cast forth.
Having abandoned the impurities of conceptual thought through the Vāmakeśvara-āgama,
and having performed the piercing [of the centers] by means of the movement [of the breath], they will benefit all.
Having thus reflected and having conquered the heavy and profound envy of his elders,
Viśvāvarta set these [teachings], obtained from the true guru, into motion.

Even while you assert such things, having hidden the "five persons" (pañcapuruṣī) within the house and guarded them there, and having produced hundreds of mere sounds by the mere existence of those [persons], you have even today not understood so much as a single drop of the essence of the Sūtra. Beyond this, what indeed could be a greater occasion for folly or ridicule? On the contrary, having scorched your own face, you rely upon [the Sūtra] at every step.

This is said by those great souls, the supreme teachers, who draw various designs according to their own intentions; however, it cannot be claimed that because this division into thirty-two parts and so forth is not based on scripture, it is therefore invalid—enough with such chatter with the talkative! "At the two ends" means at the limits defined by a measure of one finger-breadth as it revolves according to the stated method. Thus, finally...

This should also be understood here. Even when the place of Brahmā is increased by one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), [the measurement applies] to the three situated below—that is, those consisting of the fifth, sixth, and seventh. From the phrase "from the second," meaning from the sixth; thus, according to the stated method, it is increased by one finger-breadth at a time.
