By the phrases "on both sides of the Brahma-thread" and "above and below," [the directions] above and below are indicated.
The production of equality between the triangular and the corner [of the square] is thus reinforced. "Below and above" is according to their respective order.

The phrase "joined to its extremity" (*tatkoṭisaṅgatam*) should be applied according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣinyāya*); therefore, one should extend these two lines—one below and one above—from the extremity of that previously established decagon, until they meet at the extremity of the fourth part, which serves as the intended point of junction.

The meaning is "it should be so. Likewise, at the ends (*koṭi*) of those four previously mentioned sūtras, another pair of sūtras, fifty [units] in extent, should be laid down; this is the connection with what precedes.
Regarding the word "above" (*ūrdhva*): it refers to the triangle produced by the two sets of three triangles—the first and the third—which are situated above and below and positioned in the middle.

"Produced by mutual interpenetration" refers to the two vital points (*marmadvaya*); the meaning is that one should take as the target that which extends up to and including that limit. "That" refers to the wheel (*cakra*).

The purpose for concluding the five wheels through the processes of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) is the welfare of the disciple. "Externally" means on the pericarp (*karṇikā*) marked with the wheel. Furthermore, by the employment of the two terms "red" and "white," the exclusion of the intermediate *rajas* (passion/quality) is indicated.
If here, due to the incompatibility of other pigments, this much alone suffices for the purpose; then,
having prepared the center of the pericarp within the wheel by applying *gorocanā*,
one should fill that intervening space with black pigment or alternatively with musk or milk.
"Having cast that [into the fire], one should anoint it with wheat"—

one should not say such things, for enough of this prolixity. With this very intention, even other great teachers, without having seen the meaning of this scripture, have [expounded] its method according to their own intuition, following the manner of the aphorisms, like the analogy of a painting in the sky.
In a region where the divisions are equal to ten, there is a cessation of wealth and peace on all sides;
furthermore, due to the loss of two parts in each pair of the eastern flanks, there is likewise a cessation.
Then, by discarding one-quarter, half, and three-quarters [of the previous value], and subsequently [discarding] one and a half,
two, four, eight, sixteen, and thirty-two parts, one should divide it into three groups of three.
Thus, afterwards, however, by discarding one part out of four from the first three [squares],
nine and a half [squares] should then be drawn on both sides within.
From the abandonment of the portion of the sages (7),
one should first take nine and a half units from the east, and subsequently, from the side, three and six (9) units, forming a triangle.
Having thus constructed the wheel and placed the two [halves of] the sky within it,
the teachers should fashion the wheel so that it has the weight of an axe and is free from modification.
On the three outer parts, one should construct doors provided with corners,
marked by lotuses, and endowed with both *śobhā* and *upaśobhā*.
Thus has this new path been described in accordance with the teaching of Śiva,
by which the mandala becomes easy to construct, perfectly symmetrical, and most beautiful.

Thus, the correction has been made by these and other [passages]. However, there is this much fault here consisting of a contradiction with the meaning of the scripture (*āgama*): namely, that half of the field is a semi-circle, and the lotus and so forth have sixteen petals; furthermore, a wheel is placed in the position of the lotus, and the door is provided with a *kalāṭaka* lintel, and so on.
Even though our own teachers, who proceeded by relying upon this [text], did not perceive [the error], since the lack of vision was no different [for them].

The turning of the wheel has been summarized as being in accordance with those scriptures whose meaning is established by the power of intuitive knowledge (*prātibha-jñāna*), so that it does not contradict them. For example, one should describe the rotation within a field consisting of twelve parts, such that there is a revolution in the center at the eighth part;
and therein, the triad of powers [is located] from the two sides and from the fourth part in front.

From the wandering [longitude], by subtracting one part of fire (30°) and one part devoid of qualities (0°), and from the first part, one should generate [the signs] starting with Libra (7) and ending with Sagittarius (7); and likewise, beyond that, for the fire-born [signs], starting from the part endowed with qualities (30°).
However, from the portion of Yama (the south), the fire [element] occupies the third part; then the fourth part belongs to the arrow (five) portion.
Or, the Veda (four) portions, doubled, likewise extend to the sixth part for the power of water.
With arrows at its end and a spear as the third, through the piercing of the spear and fire,
the adept thus easily attains the wheel endowed with four, three, five, and three [spokes].
Following that, in each pair [of squares], there are two lotuses with eight petals;
in the remaining squares of the quadrangle, there is the door—such is the sacrificial layout.
Thus, enough with this prolixity; let us address the subject at hand. || 58 ||
Thus, immediately after the determination of the nature of the substratum, the author states the determination of the nature of the superstratum, as its opportunity has now arisen:
"But Mahātripurasundarī is established in the Great Wheel."
Regarding this, he says (p. 39): "Pay close attention to the procedure for worship being described for her, who abides here as the presiding deity."
Listen, O Goddess, to how she is worshipped by the most excellent practitioners. || 59 ||
By means of the sequential order of the groups, it is conjoined with the eight deities;
for this [mantra] possesses the eight deities because of its internal nature.
He shows its very sequence of groups:
"O Goddess, the first group is the *avarga*; therein, the deity is Vaśinī. (60)
The guttural class (ka-varga) is devoted to that [Kāmeśvarī], and Kāmeśvarī resides therein;
Modinī resides in the palatal class (ca-varga), and likewise Vimalā is in the retroflex class (ṭa-varga).
Aruṇā resides in the *tavarga*; Jayinī is situated in the *pavarga*; Sarveśvarī is in the *yavarga*, and Kaulinī is in the *śavarga*. (62)
O Goddess, these eight deities indeed constitute the eight groups;
when worshipped, they quickly bring the entire world under the control of a person. (63)
Since worship without mantras does not take place, he first extracts the eight seed-syllables of these [goddesses].
One should extract the letter *ra* first; below that, the letter at the end of the "crooked" (*kuṭila*) group [the letter *ṇa*];
and that too, situated upon the seed-syllable of the earth [the letter *la*], conjoined with the sixth vowel [the letter *ū*]. (64)
O Supreme Goddess, one should cause it to be enriched above with a half-moon and a bindu;
this is that seed-syllable of Vaśinī, which resides in the mouths of the Yoginīs. (65)
The letter *pha* is curved; its "end-goer" (*antaga*) is the seed-syllable of the Earth (*avanibīja*), which is *la*. The sixth vowel is *ū*.
By means of the half-moon and so forth, the presentation of all the Mothers and their objects of cognition is accomplished. Thus: *rblū*.
Having thus stated the seed-syllable of Vaśinī, he also speaks of Kāmeśvarī:
O Maheśvarī, from the first [letter] of the second group, one should extract the letter mounted on Indra (the vowel *e*);
below that, one should extract the seed-syllable of the ether (the vowel *u*) situated in the fire (the consonant *r*). (66)
Conjoined with the fourth vowel and adorned with the dot (bindu) and the crescent moon (khaṇḍendu),
this is the seed-syllable (bīja) of Kāmeśvarī, which causes the agitation of the three worlds.
From the second class, the *ka*-group, take the first letter *ka*; from the *aindra* [class] take *la*; the *nābhasa* seed-syllable *ha*; the *āgneya* [letter] *ra*;
and the fourth vowel *ī*. Thus: *klhrīḥ*.
Thus he spoke also regarding Modinī:
"O Dear One, one should place the seed-syllable of Varuṇa below the fifth [syllable] of Aruṇā;
and below that, the seed-syllable of Indra, which is superior to all above."
This is the seed-syllable *tanmodinī*, which brings all principles (*tattvas*) under control.

By the metaphorical treatment of non-difference between the presiding deity and that which is presided over, the word "aruṇa" refers to the fifth letter of the *tavarga* (the *na*) presided over by that [deity]; "vāruṇa" is *va*; the "seed of Indra" is *la*; "above all" is the bindu; and "following *i*" is *ī*. Thus: *nvlī*.
Then [one should visualize] the seed-syllable of Vāyu, situated within the seed-syllable of Indra, conjoined with the sixth vowel. || 69 ||
Crowned by the head of a half-moon and adorned with a bindu—
this, O Goddess, is the supreme, pure seed-syllable (vimalā-bīja) that I have declared to you.
It causes the destruction of all sins and the eradication of all calamities. The Vāyavya syllable is *ya*, Indra is *la*, and the sixth vowel is *ū*. Thus: *ylū*.
The letter *ja* is mounted upon the letter *ka*, and beneath that is the letter of fire (*ra*). (71)
Pervaded by the fourth vowel and endowed with the bindu and nāda—
this is that seed-syllable Aruṇa, which is red and deludes all.
*Kāla* is *ma*, the fiery syllable is *ra*, and the fourth vowel is *ī*. Thus, [the seed-syllable] is *jmrī*.
Because it "goes toward" (*iyarti*) the dawn (*aruṇa*), according to the derivation of its meaning, it signifies that which has knowledge as its primary essence.
O Supreme Goddess, having joined the seed-syllable of Śiva situated at the beginning with the syllables of Indra and Varuṇa below, and the syllable of Vāyu pierced above; 73.

This very seed-syllable of Jayinī is adorned with Nāda and Bindu. O Supreme Goddess, one should extract the fourth letter of the Modinī group [ḍha] preceded by Śiva’s seed (Ha), then that [Sa], Indra’s [La], Varuṇa’s [Va], Vāyu’s [Ya], and the letter above [Ū]; thus [HSLVYŪ]. (74)
Below, one should sequentially assign the elements of Time (Kāla), Fire (Agni), and Wind (Vāyu),
conjoined with the seed-syllables of Long Life (Dīrghāyus) according to their proper order.
O beautiful goddess, when these [syllables] ending with the *īśvara-bindu* are joined together as one, this is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Sarveśvarī, which is invincible everywhere. (76)
The *modinī* group is the *ca*-group; its fourth is *jha*, *kāla* is *ma*, *agni* is *ra*, *vāyavya* is *ya*, and the seed-syllable of long life is *ū*;
thus, [the mantra is] *jhmyrū*. || 76 ||
O Goddess, one should place the Kaulinī as the fifth, situated above the seed-syllable of Time (Kāla);
likewise, one should join the seed-syllable of Fire at the very bottom.
Joined with the fourth vowel and adorned with the bindu and nāda,
this supreme seed-syllable, O auspicious lady, abides in the form of Kaulinī.
The fifth letter of the group beginning with *śa* (the *kaulinī*-presided-over class) is *kṣa*; the seed-syllable of Time (*kālabīja*) is *ma*; the seed-syllable of Fire (*vahnibīja*) is *ra*;
and the fourth vowel is *ī*. Thus, [the mantra is] *kṣmrī*. || 78 ||
He summarizes this very point:
"In this way, O Maheśvarī, these eight seeds have been declared in sequence,
O Mahādevī..."
In the word *devī*, the reading *etāni* is a corruption; for even if one were to apply the elision (*cheda*) in the word *maheśvarī*, the tautology would not be removed.
It is said that not only have the mantras of the eight deities who constitute the internal retinue been taught, but others as well shall now be stated:
"Listen to those whose forms are the limbs of the Vidyā. (79)
In the phrase "saiṣa dāśarathī rāmaḥ," there is a *sandhi* (euphonic combination) here.
He indicates those very [mantras]:
the vidyā that purifies the hands, as well as that which is established in the ritual placement upon the limbs (aṅganyāsa),
that which resides on the seat of the self, and likewise that which is situated on the seat of the wheel.
Seated upon the throne of all mantras, established on the seat of the goal to be accomplished and the seat of attainment; [recite] the vidyā for the invocation of the goddess— [and so forth]—
and not merely this alone, as far as...
"Listen"—this is the connection with what precedes. || 81 ||
He extracts this very [mantra] in sequence:
O Goddess, the first is Vāgbhava, the second is Kāmarāja;
it is joined with the end of Śānta (the letter *ma*) conjoined with the *kādi* group (the letter *śa*), and joined with the end of the one whose end is *aikāra* (the letter *au*). (82)
O Maheśānī, this Vidyā is known as that which effects the purification of the hands.

The phrase "one should extract" (*uddharet*) is to be connected with what precedes. Of the letter *śa* (palatal), the end is the retroflex *ṣ*; of that (*ṣ*), the end is *sa*; of *ka*, the beginning is the visarga; of the diphthong *ai*, the end is *o*; and of that (*o*) as well, the end is *au*. Thus, [the syllable] is *sauḥ*.
(43) But surely, O Goddess, here too the Vāgbhava is first, and then the Kāmarāja.
The end of "śānta" (the letter *sa*) is joined with the letters beginning with *ka*, and is further conjoined with the end of that which ends in the vowel *ai*.
Thus, when the instruction is being given in a general manner, just as described in the eighth chapter:
first, here, is the Vāgbhava, which is the letter *a*, well-known in the world;
the second is Haṃsadeva, and the third is Vahniveśmaka.

Thinking that those of delicate intellect might become confused if there were no distinction between the Vāgbhava and other [seeds] due to such views, the Supreme Lord, out of compassion and with the desire to explain the specific details, himself analyzes and declares these two seed-syllables:
"The seed situated between 'E' and 'O' is intended solely for the manifestation of Speech. (83)
In the Rudrayāmala Tantra, however, the supreme syllable is specified as follows: the letter *mā* (ma), joined with *śakra* (s), and combined with the fourth vowel (*ī*). (84)
Above [the letter *ka*] is enriched with a crescent moon and a bindu—[this is the seed-syllable *aiṃ*].

Situated between the letters *e* and *o* is *ai*; the bindu is the absolute void (*śūnya*). By that [is formed] *aiṃ*. *Mādana* is *ka*; *Śakra* is *la*; the fourth vowel is *ī*. Thus the *śakti*-seed-syllable *klīṃ* is explained. In this way, [the mantra is] *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ*. As it has been said:
O Goddess, O beautiful one among the gods, one should extract the eighth [syllable] from the first in the Śrīnityākula;
it is conjoined with the head of Kāla and situated above the half-moon.
O Goddess, this is that Vāgbhava, which initiates the state of mastery over speech;
it is the first seed-syllable of the group of Yonis, joined with Paurandara (the letter Ra).
O Great Goddess, Kāmarāja is adorned with Mohinī upon its head and embellished by the Bindu and the crescent moon; it bestows the attainment of all desires.
O Goddess of the gods, having extracted the Lord of the Night (KṢ) and joined it with the tenth vowel, this is declared to be the seed-syllable of Śakti, which marks the end of creation.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the *Śrī Rasamahodadhi*:
"The letter situated between 'o' and 'ja' is struck by the head above 'jha';
the letter situated between 'aṃ' and 'ga' is seated upon the throne between 'va' and 'ra'."
This second [syllable] is said to have the letter *ā* in the middle with a bindu;
it has the letter *va* in the middle with the letter *ha* situated below, and is marked by the letter *aṃ* in the center.

"First, the three-syllabled Vidyā is known as the purifier of the hands. Thus: *ai* is that which is situated between *o* and *ja*, above *ai* and *jha*, and [the vowel] *aṃ*; by this, *aiṃ*. *Klīṃ* is formed thus: *ka* with respect to the city of fire (*vahnipura*) situated between *aṃ* and *ga*; *la* in the middle of *va* and *ra*; *ī* in the middle of *ā* and *ū*; thus, *klīṃ*. *Sa* is in the middle of *va* and *ha*; *au* situated below *ā*; [and] *ha* in the middle of *aṃ* and *ka*.
Aḥ, likewise Sauḥ. In accordance with that, having first constructed there an auspicious square city measuring twenty-four finger-breadths,
one should draw a thread from the northeast (Īśāna) toward the west, and again from the southeast (Agni) toward the west.
Having established the first sūtra, one should erase the remaining three;
this is known as the Yoni of the triple staff, which possesses three māyās and is the triple deity.
On each individual column, the wise man should lay down six lines each,
by which all the womb-places (yonis) arise with their joints perfectly aligned.
There are forty-nine square compartments in the form of vulvas;
starting from the letter 'a' in the northeast (īśa), they extend to Vināyaka in the west (vāruṇī).
One should arrange the entire Mātṛkā, beginning with Viṣṇu and ending with Śiva;
this cakra should be drawn on an auspicious cloth or on a firm wooden board.
In a triangular [mandala] with three bases, characterized by the piercing of the phonemes (varṇotkīlita),
success arises within six months for one devoted to worship and recitation.
"Therefore, O Goddess, listen to how the mantras are to be extracted.
45) Thus there is the *prastāra*, the arrangement of which is as follows:
Having thus extracted the *vidyā* that purifies the hands, he extracts the second one as well, which is established through the ritual placement (*aṅganyāsa*)— namely,
[the mantra] beginning and ending with that supreme [syllable].
Of this very [mantra]— (1.88).

By the power of the emphatic particle *eva* as it will be stated hereafter, at the end— that is, in close proximity to— the first syllable of this three-syllabled vidyā which effects purification of the hands, namely the vāgbhava, one must subsequently place the third seed-syllable of Śakti, which follows immediately after that aforementioned kāmārāja; by means of which [the purification is effected].
(p. 46) There should be an inversion of the *kāmarāja* and *śakti* seed-syllables, as in *aiṃ sauḥ klīṃ*. Even in the subsequent recitation, this is the very same meaning.
And out of compassion for this matter, the Supreme Lord says [the following] so that no one might suspect that the supreme syllable of that Kāmarāja is the letter *la* or the vowel *i*:
"Joined with the *ka*-group, ending with the peaceful [letter], and conjoined with the end of that which ends in *ai*. (85)
The meaning has been explained. || 85 ||
Thus, this knowledge is a great knowledge, the source of great prosperity for yoginīs;
it is the family-knowledge (kulavidyā), O Great Goddess, which accomplishes the purpose of all undertakings. 86.
As it is said in that very same place:
"O slender-waisted one, having reversed the two [syllables] while indeed omitting the original seed-syllable,
this is the second Vidyā for the rite of ritual placement upon the limbs."

Thus: "by the first seed-syllable" means by the Vāgbhava; "of the two" refers to the remaining second and third [syllables]; therefore, after the Vāgbhava comes the Śakti seed-syllable, and after that the Kāmarāja. || 86 ||
He demonstrates the purpose of this [vidyā] in the context of the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa):
"By means of this vidyā, O Gaurī, one should effect protection for oneself.
For this very reason, it is called the "Kula-vidyā" and so forth.
He also characterizes the third Vidyā, situated on the seat of the Self, as belonging to this very same Vidyā and possessing Śiva, Māyā, Agni, and Bindu. (87)
Having joined the seed-syllable (*bīja*) to the first word, she takes the form of the seat consisting of the nature of the effect (*kāryātman*).

*Śiva* is *ha*, *Māyā* is *ī*, and *Agni* is *ra*; thus, it is *hrīṃ*. This is for the first *vidyā*, which effects the purification of the hands (*karaśuddhikarī*), and not for the second *kulavidyā*, which is a modified form of this, nor for the *vāgbhava* at the beginning of that [second *vidyā*].
The meaning is that, having removed that [seed-syllable] from its place and joined this *māyābīja*, the Vidyā residing on the seat of the Self (*ātmasana*) should be employed; thus:
*hrīṃ klīṃ sauḥ*. This is stated in the *Ṣaḍardha*: "The *piṇḍa* situated above, adorned with *ā*, *au*, and *anta*."
In the place of Vāgbhava of the first [syllable], she is the embodiment of the seat consisting of three syllables.
The letter *ṣ* is at the bottom, *t* above that, and *r* above that; because it is composed of these two syllables, it is called a "piṇḍa.
The letter *ī* is the end of *ā*, and *aṃ* is the end of *au*; thus, *hrīṃ*.
He further spoke of the fourth [syllable] situated on the wheel-throne, which follows the first of the vidyās, containing the inner end and joined with Śiva. 88.
That Vidyā, which deludes the three worlds, is situated upon the seat of the wheel (cakrāsana).

Furthermore, regarding the purification of the hands: after the first seed-syllable of the very first Vidyā, which is the Vāgbhava, and the Kāmarāja which resides within the interval between them, and the Śakti-seed which is the final one—above this triad [is the next].
"One should make it joined with the auspicious letter *ha*," so says the venerable Īśvaraśivācārya. Thus: *haiḥ*, *hklīṃ*, *hsauḥ*.
As it has been said:
"Having taken each single letter from the first and the third of the first [group]..."
At the end of that, above, by means of the sixfold [mantra], the Vidyā is situated upon the seat of the wheel.

Thus [it is said]. Here, having taken the first syllable of the first and third vidyās—which are respectively the Vāgbhava and the final syllables characterized as the Kāmarāja and Śakti-bījas—and having joined each of those single syllables above with the letter *ṣādhena*, meaning the letter *ha*; the meaning is that one should make all three syllables conjoined with the letter *ha* above. Furthermore, by means of the first syllable of the third vidyā...

Immediately after this *māyābīja* has been extracted, one should again take the first *vāgbhava* of that very same *vidyā* used for the purification of the hands; then, placing the *śaktibīja*— which is the end of that same initial *vidyā*— between these two, namely the *vāgbhava* and the *māyābīja*, by means of the letter *ha* (the *śiva*).
(48) Śrī Śaṅkararāśi says that it should be "connected" (ānvita), meaning it should be joined with what follows by implication. Thus: *aiṃ hsauṃḥ hrīṃ*.

And this is stated in that very [text] due to the variant reading *madhye'ntam* ("the end in the middle"). This is the meaning here: having taken the first letter of each of the first and third *vidyās*—namely, the *vāgbhava* and the *māyābīja*—by implication, one should place the "end" (*antam*) of these very two in their middle.

The remaining sense is that one should honor [the letter] by joining it above—meaning with the seed-syllable of Śakti, namely the letter *Ha*. In this regard, the previous position is disregarded; for, according to the venerable doctrine of Īśvaraśiva, just as the extraction of the Cakrāsana occurs here, so too, according to the view of Rājānaka Kalyāṇavarman, it does not terminate [there]. This is intended by the author who presents the maxim of "whatever it may be" (*yādṛktādṛkprāya*).

It is done. We do not know what fault there might be if it were thus finalized. For in reality, these two teachers alone were the ones who introduced this system into Kaśmīra. And from that point on, it is clearly observed through the lineage of Śrī Viśvāvarta and others that this very [system] has reached everyone down to our own time through the succession of disciples and grand-disciples. Thus, because there is no difference in the reliability (*āptatva*) of those two, [the tradition remains authoritative].

That very doctrine alone is authoritative in every respect. Consequently, because they possess equal authority, it is logical that there should be an option (*vikalpa*) between those two doctrines, rather than the abandonment of one side; on the contrary, the superior strength of the venerable Īśvaraśivācārya’s doctrine is observed, for he alone is universally renowned as the direct propagator of the verses of the *Śrīrasamahodadhi*. As you yourselves have also said:
Our own former teacher formerly obtained this *cakra* from Īśvaraśiva, which had been transmitted through the succession of excellent gurus from the lord of Śrī Śūramaṭha.

Thus [he says]. If these two initial [syllables] and the syllable at the middle and end were otherwise in the fourth [case], that too would merely be a statement whose meaning has not been properly considered; let this matter rest.
He spoke again of the fifth [syllable] situated on the seat of all mantras, the primordial Great Vidyā, conjoined with Śiva and the Moon. (89)
Having performed [this], the Vidyā that grants desires, which resides upon the seat of all mantras,
is once again the primordial Great Vidyā that effects the purification of the hands, because it serves as the foundation for the extraction of each respective subsequent Vidyā.

Having joined each syllable with the letters *ha* and *sa*, which are like Śiva and the Moon, the Vidyā—which bestows whatever desired object it is and resides upon the seat of all mantras—is to be extracted by the Guru; this is the remainder [of the sense]. Thus: *hsaiṃ hsklīṃ hssauṃ*.
As it has been said:
"The first [syllable] should be known as joined with the two ending in *ṣā* and *dha*, situated on the seat of the mantra.
Regarding the phrase "with the two ending in *ṣā* and *dha*," it means with the letter *ha* and the letter *sa* located in those respective positions.

He also speaks of the sixth [syllable], which is situated upon the throne of the accomplishment of the goal, according to the sequence of the previously mentioned Vidyā of the Goddess’s own seat. || 90 ||

O Supreme Goddess, having joined the drops of water (bindu), Indra (ha), and Śakti (i) in sequence at the end of the region [of the letter], one should then join them together with the half-moon (ardhendu). 91.
The Vidyā, established upon its own seat, is to be accomplished through the differentiation of the syllables alone:

*toyaṃ* (va), *śakraḥ* (la), and *śaktiḥ* (the fourth vowel, *ī*), thus forming *vlīṃ*. Then, having removed that from its place—the location of the seed-syllable of Śakti situated at the end of the previously mentioned third Vidyā, the Ātmāsana-vidyā—[one should proceed].

The meaning is that, having sequentially joined *toya* (water) and the others, the *vidyā* situated upon the *āsana* of the *sādhya*—which consists of each one of those [elements] as a single *piṇḍa* through the differentiation of syllables, like the case of Satyabhāmā and Bhāmā—is to be extracted. Thus: *hrīṃ klīṃ vlīṃ*. This has been stated:
"In the reversed position, the two ending in *ra*, marked above by *jha* and preceded by *ū* and *pa*."
Having bestowed [it], from the end of the seed-syllable of desire (kāmabīja) of the third vidyā.
"The sixth Vidyā, seated upon the throne of the *sādhya*, has been revealed.
Thus: "the end of *rā* (*ra*), *la*, and *va*. Regarding "in reversed position," this means that the letter *va* is above and the letter *la* is below. (p.
50) "Having placed *aṃ* above *jha*, and *ī* preceded by *ū*, at the end of the region of the Kāma-bīja"—by this, first comes *Māyā*, then the Kāmarāja.
"This," [it is said].
He also declares the seventh mantra for the invocation of the Goddess: "The Primordial One, mounted upon Haṃsa and Soma, seated upon the throne of fire. (92)
The Vidyā that accomplishes all aims is for the rite of invoking the Goddess;
it is the primordial three-syllabled Vidyā which effects the purification of the hands, wherein each syllable is mounted by the Haṃsa (the Sun) and Soma (the Moon),
with the letter *ha* and *sa* situated above the *repha* (*ra*) in accordance with the rule of *agnyāhitādi*, depending precisely upon the consonant.

Having placed the letter *ra* below the Goddess Satī who is seated upon the fire-seat (*agni*), this Vidyā, which accomplishes all aims, is to be extracted for the purpose of invoking the Goddess; that is to say, *hsraiṃ hsklrīṃ hssrauḥ*. Thus it has been said:
"Having placed above the three seed-syllables the two letters beginning with *ṣa* and ending with *ṣa*."
The very first Vidyā residing within the [seed-syllable] *yāṃ* is supreme in the rite of invocation.
Thus: *ṣa* with a downward stroke is *ha*; *sa* ends in *ṣa*; *ra* ends in *ya*.
Concluding this, he introduces another point:
"In this way, O Goddess, these great vidyās grant the accomplishment of all aims. (93)
O beloved, listen to the root-vidyā of Mahātripurasundarī.
The repetition of the word "listen" is for the purpose of demonstrating the highest degree of reverence.
He describes that very [power]:
Mādanā is below that, Śakti is below that, and Bindumālinī is below that. || 94 ||
The syllable of Indra is situated within the seed-syllable of space (Ā), with the letter of fire (Ra) below it;
joined with Māyā (I), the Bindu (M), and Īśvara (U), it is placed at the very top of all. || 95 ||
O Goddess, this is the Vāgbhava [syllable], which brings about the state of mastery over speech:
*ka* is Mādana; *e* is Śakti; *ī* is Bindumālinī; *la* is Aindra; *ha* is the seed-syllable of space; and *ra* is the letter of fire.

By the phrase "Māyā, Ī, Bindu, and Īśvarā," the outlining of the entire range of mantras and objects of knowledge is indicated through the relationship between the governed (adhiṣṭheya) and the governor (adhiṣṭhātṛ). Thus: KA-E-Ī-LA-HRĪṂ.

Having thus explained the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable], he also extracts the Kāmarāja [seed-syllable] by joining the seed of Śiva in three ways according to the sequence of emanation, maintenance, and dissolution. (96)
The first pair is devoid of the first [syllable]; below that is the syllable of Madana (the letter *ma*).
Again, one should join the seed-syllable of Indra (*la*) below Sthitiśiva.
Likewise, O Maheśvarī, there is also a flaming [syllable] below Layashiva,
conjoined with the fourth vowel and adorned by the Bindu, Khaṇḍendu, and Ardhacandra.

Thus, having joined the great seed-syllable *kāmarāja*, which brings about great prosperity—the seed of Śiva, namely *ha*—the meaning is that one should join and then install it. Furthermore, he states that this should not be installed with immediate contiguity between the two intermediate sections, saying: "the pair is devoid of the first," which refers to the nature of stability (*sthiti*).

The effect is devoid of and unconnected with the first [element], which consists of persistence (*sthiti*), so that there may be room for the two syllables to be described in between. For this very reason, he says: "the letter of passion (*madanākṣara*) below the first," and "the seed of Indra (*indrabīja*) below the persistence-Śiva. The letter of passion is *ka*, the seed of Indra is *la*, fire is *ra*, and the fourth vowel is *ī*.

Thus, *hk-hlhrīṃ*. It should not be said that [the mantra] is devoid of the letter *ā*, which consists of the head-line (*śirorekhā*) of the first [consonant]. For we do not understand by what intention it was stated that two [of the letters] lack a head while one possesses a head. In reality, it is logical that all the *piṇḍa* syllables are indeed without vowels (*anacka*), since [they are formed] by whichever single [consonant] occurs anywhere.
Because some desire non-duality through this [method], it is not only here that such a false explanation has been made by him; rather, following this very same path—
some have been destroyed by those who are themselves destroyed.
In this manner, even the collection of mantras beginning with "In the glorious Ānandeśvara-kalpa, Śiva [united with] Śakti...
has been destroyed; so what can be said of these self-arisen ones who have not seen a Guru?

Let alone the consideration of other texts which, having abandoned the primary method set forth by the Great Teacher—which stands as a royal road—say something or other that is merely a fragment; let this too, which distracts from the matter at hand, rest for now.
Having thus extracted the seed-syllable of Kāmarāja, he also declares the seed-syllable of Śakti:
"O Maheśānī, [the seed-syllable of] Māyā joined with Mādana and Śakra. (99)
O fair-faced one, the seed-syllable of the Moon alone is to be employed:
the seed-syllable of Māyā is *hrīṃ*, Mādana is *ka*, Śakra is *la*, the seed-syllable of the Moon is *sa*, and the absolute is *ha*.
And how is their application to be performed? He says:
"O Goddess, having abandoned the sequence of emanation (sṛṣṭikrama), [it is done] by means of the sequence of prior utterance. (100)
One should extract the seed-syllable of Śakti by means of the yoga of the sequence of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*).
Regarding the seed-syllables of Mādana and Śakra, the reversal of the sequence of withdrawal is shown precisely through their relationship as qualifier and qualified.

However, he states "by the previous sequence of utterance" (*prāguccārakrameṇa*) to indicate that the actual pronunciation must be performed according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*) alone. For this very reason, the word *tu* is used in the sense of exclusion (*vyatireka*). Thus...
Hsklhrīṃ.
He concludes that very point:
"In this way, she is the Great Vidyā, Mahātripurasundarī. (101)
O Great Goddess, she alone, when merely remembered, brings the three worlds under control;
as it has been said:
Having taken the letter *aḥ* situated in the center of *kha*, place it between *ḷ* and *ai*;
then, one should place [the letter] situated above the syllable *aḥ* in the middle of that.
Ending in *ra*, *ṣa*, and *ya*, and joined with *māyā*, the *bindu*, and *nirodhin*,
this is declared to be the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable], which perfectly produces correct realization.
One should place [the letters] upon the seat of each of the three lower castes;
[the letters] beginning with 'ga' and ending with 'ya' above, together with the first letter marked by 'lā~'.
O Great Goddess, the seed-syllable of desire has been revealed along with its secret;
by the mere utterance of it, the agitation of the world is produced.
I shall now fully declare the third seed-syllable of Śakti, which is most wonderful:
it consists of *ṣa-dha* joined with *la*, followed by *ga-ā-dya*, *pha-dha*, and ending with *ṣa-pā-dha*.
The syllable *Aḥ* on its back, joined with the letter above it, is extracted as the seed-syllable of Śakti.
By the mere knowledge of this, one shall effect the destruction of all poisons.
This supreme knowledge has been fully declared, which brings about all wonders;
when correctly understood through this, there is nothing that it cannot accomplish.

Thus: *ka* is the middle of *aḥ-kha*; *e* is the middle of *ḷ-ai*; *ī* is above the syllable *aḥ*; *la* is the end of *rā*; *ha* is below *ṣa*; *ra* is the end of *ya*; *māyā* is *ī*. Such is the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable]. Regarding the letters beginning with *ga* among those below *ṣa*, which are the *ha*s, *ka* is according to their position in the fire-purification (*vahni-pura*); *la* is above that; *ra* is the end of *ya*; *māyā* is the first [letter] because it is the cause of the universe; its letter is *ī*. Alternatively, *ā* is the letter *ā*.

That which has "Ādi" (A) as its first part is *Kāmarāja*. Below *Ṣa* is *Ha*; below *La* is *Sa*; the first of *Ga* is *Ka*; below *Pha* is *La*; below *Ṣa* is *Ha*; below *Pa* is *Ra*; the back of *A* is *Ī*; above *Jha* is *Aṃ*. Thus is the *Śakti-bīja*. Nor should a ninefold nature be asserted here on the basis of a sevenfold nature, even though it is manifest; thus...
(p. 54) Why is it not also said that [the mantra] consists of ten aspects and so forth, with respect to Nirodhinī and the others?

For there is no difference in their being objects of knowledge through mantra. Indeed, in the *Śrīrasamahodadhi* there is a statement concerning Nirodhinī: "It is joined with the Bindu that restrains [the breath]."

Thus [it is said]. As for that which was stated by the venerable Allata in the *Aṅganyāsavidyā*: "However, at the end of the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable (*bīja*) beginning with 'ka', there is 'tatpara'; this is the opinion of Śaṃkara regarding the *kāmarāja* [seed-syllable]. Having understood this, he nevertheless refutes other positions regarding the extraction of the third, fifth, and seventh *vidyās*, excluding the *karaśuddhi-vidyā*, [and instead adopting] the second, third, and fifth.
The mere act of grasping is the seed of Śiva; its objective is the final seed of Śakti.
Furthermore, the threefold division of this Vidyā is that which belongs to it.
By means of the three vowels preceded by the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable], just as in the first-mentioned Vidyā,
one should [place them] in their entirety within the other two wheels by means of the venerable *tripiṇḍa*.
"By means of Śiva (H), Indu (I), Smara (E), Hari (O), and Śivadahana (R), joined with the Fourth Speech (AU) and the Trident (M),
each accompanied by a Bindu and its companion— this is the eighth Vidyā. Thus,
he has devised this alternative Vidyā based on his own imagination, even though it is not approved by his venerable Guru.
By the transposition of the second and third syllables, and by the addition of the letter 'i',
the seed-syllable of Śakti is indeed extracted here from the second, fifth, and seventh [syllables] by those [who know].

It is truly a marvel that they roar with pride here, despite being largely ignorant even of the seed-syllables, the colors, and the ritual stakes (kīlana) of these mantras; by what greatness do they thus boast?
Thus has been declared here the extraction of all the vidyās according to the distinction of the fourfold lineage; their pacification is to be obtained from the mouth of the Guru.
Although this has been taught to me by my gurus through many various lineages,
nevertheless, in this context, the lineage of the fourfold succession alone is the primary one, as it is endowed with reason.
And so forth has been stated; all of that must be disregarded according to the aforementioned reasoning, because there is a lack of consistency in every respect.

Furthermore, as for what is here [presented], which—merely relying on a superficial play upon syllables—is for the most part a web of nonsense, consisting of an unerring and endless sequence of consciousness and so on:

The pervasive nature [of the relationship] and so forth shown in the case of mantras and the like is based on a lack of foundation and a fondness for meager learning; therefore, we should not harbor envy toward the learned. Why is this? Because that [relationship] was not refuted by restating it word-for-word.
Since it ought not even to have been undertaken at its very root when elucidating the meaning of the scriptures, how indeed could it be so openly displayed as to bring about such great expiation?
Even when the meaning of the mantra is being elucidated, the great-souled ones—the people who fear the violation of their commitments—will tolerate it.

For today, wherever and from whatever source, even from an improper place, by misconduct, or ultimately even through theft, those who have obtained merely a fragmentary manuscript will all reverse the established order of the Guru and others; therein, they will even designate their own father or similar kin as the Guru.

Those who turn their backs on the practice of the meaning of the scriptures, whose sole intent is the sale of mantras, and who are devoted only to the accumulation of wealth, are seen to be submerging the entire world. However, out of fear of interrupting the study of the scriptural meaning, I have performed only a very brief consideration of their intent; therefore, enough with this speech which causes headache to wicked people.
Although it possesses such greatness, he states what should be done with it:
"With this, the practitioner should begin the worship of this wheel. (102)
And as to what that [form] is like, he says:
"His body is reddish with saffron, adorned with reddish garments;
his mouth is filled with betel-leaf, and he is made fragrant by the scent of incense. (103)
His limbs smeared with camphor powder, adorned with red ornaments, covered with red flowers, observing silence, and anointed with red perfumes. (104)
Seated upon a red throne, dwelling in a house as crimson as lac, richly adorned with all the finery of amorous passion, his body constituted of the three cities. (105)

Or, the practitioner (sādhaka), whose mind is fixed and who is impassioned by mental resolve, [should perform the rite]. The inversion of the compound order in "vastrāruṇā" (red garment) is for metrical reasons; "raktagandha" (red scent) refers to yellow sandalwood, lac, and so forth. The term "sādhaka" refers to one who is constantly exerted in the means of attaining accomplishment (siddhi); for this very reason, he is described as "sthiramānasaḥ" (of steady mind). And here, the worship with red [substances] is intended.

It has been stated that "or one who is attached to mental resolve" precisely to illuminate its absolute necessity. Thus, even in the absence of external substances, there is no impairment whatsoever regarding the obligatory rites (*nitya*) and so forth; this is what is indicated by this [statement], because engagement occurs therein as far as possible. The sense is that such [impairment] might indeed occur in the case of optional rites (*kāmya*) and the like, where engagement is not necessarily possible. Furthermore, the intended meaning here is as follows:

Whatever material may manifest for the practitioner as being composed of the various degrees of the wonder of supreme bliss (*parānanda-camatkāra*) within his own self, that alone is to be gathered with all one's being. As they have said:
"Whatever gladdens the mind and whatever increases good fortune..."
Having adorned oneself with that, one should always worship the Lord.
Thus [it is said].
Regarding where, how, and of what nature this wheel (cakra) should be made, he says: "On a level and pure patch of ground, smeared with cow dung. (106)
O Goddess, [the ground] strewn with heaps of flowers, fragrant with the scent of incense, and further adorned with vermilion powder or saffron; 107.
First, one should draw a beautiful mandala with perfectly even lines,
possessing the tips of three equal triangles and the śakti, auspicious and exceedingly lovely. (108)

The state of being endowed with splendor (*saśrīkatva*) itself has been elaborated upon as "extremely beautiful. In that regard, the reason is provided through specific qualifiers such as "having parallel lines" and so forth.

Here, it has just been stated [in verse 107] that "one whose body has been made into the *tripurī*," for without the meditator’s cultivation of identification (*tādātmya*) with the respective deity of the mantra to be worshipped, not even a single act such as worship would succeed. || 108 ||
And how that should be done, he says:

"O Goddess, having meditated upon the three cities (the three eyes) as endowed with the three seed-syllables, O Goddess, one should perform the purification of the hands with the *sarvādi-vidyā*. (109)

The "three cities" are characterized by the secret place, the heart, and the space between the eyebrows, but they do not consist of speech, mind, and body; having meditated upon them as endowed with the three seed-syllables, one should deposit the three seed-syllables associated with the root-vidyā therein—this is what is meant. As he will state: "Residing in the center of the navel-mandala, the heart-lotus, and the face-mandala" (4.51).
Thus [it is said]. Our supreme gurus also state:
"One should place the three root-syllables in the secret place, the heart, and between the eyebrows.

Regarding this, the gurus maintain that because the sequence of meaning (*arthakrama*) is more powerful than the sequence of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*), this placement (*nyāsa*) occurs immediately after the placement that will be described next.

It should not be said here that, by virtue of the appropriateness of the mantra of the weapon (*astra*), one should meditate on these three seed-syllables within the three cities consisting of the upper, middle, and lower parts of the sacrificial chamber for the sake of dispelling obstacles. || 109 ||
Thus, when the purification of the hands has been performed, it is appropriate to perform the placement of other mantras upon those hands; so he says:
"Thereafter, O Īśvarī, one should offer the seat of the Self and then the seat of the wheel."
O Goddess, it is the seat of all mantras, as well as the seat of the sādhya and the siddha. || 110 ||

By the force of the name alone, one should install the *ātmasana* as a seat within the self (*ātman*). Since there is no authoritative evidence for restricting the placement of the *cakrāsana* and other seats to specific locations such as the secret region (*guhyakanda*) or the heart, their installation is rightly performed as pervading the entire body, as this is more appropriate given that they take the form of those respective seats. Furthermore, regarding these [external seats], there is no authoritative evidence for determining a fixed front, right, or left side.
The restriction of location, established by the force of traditional designation (*samākhyā*), must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, the worship would remain incomplete.
As I myself have stated: "Now, the seat of the mantra, having taken recourse to the center of the four-gated inner square..."
The wheel-throne (cakrāsana) is situated at the tip of the power that first arose, and in the center of the triangle.
The seat of the one to be accomplished—[blank]—thus [ends]. || 110 ||
Likewise,
one should then perform protection by means of the previously mentioned family-vidyā,
joined with the application of the six-limbed nyāsa and accompanied by the word of salutation.

And it has been stated that here, in these ancillaries (*aṅga*), one should not perform the application of other castes (*jātyantara*) as prescribed in other scriptures, because this is enjoined by the act of salutation (*namaskāra*). Furthermore, this explanation [of the *puruṣasūtra*] as being supplementary to everything must be disregarded;
for since it cannot otherwise be justified as belonging to the *Kula* tradition, the procedure of the *Vainayika* school is appropriate here, as it is logically consistent. || 111 ||
Then,

one should perform the placement (nyāsa) with eight [syllables] in the following locations: the crest-lock (śikhā), the forehead, the space between the eyebrows, the throat, the heart, the navel region, the foundation (ādhāra), and up to the secret organ (ūhaka).
By the term *ūhakam*, the foot presided over by that [deity] is indicated. By the phrase "with eight" (p.

59), it is meant the seed-syllables of Vaśinī and the others, and not the wheels (*cakras*), because those are nine in number and thus cannot appropriately be referred to here. By this much alone, his state of being the "Triad City" (*tripurībhāva*) within his own self is established.
The Vāgbhava seed-syllable is on the right eye, the Kāmarāja on the left,
the Śakti-bīja on the forehead, and [the two remaining syllables] on the right and left ears.

Then, one should perform the ritual placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa) in this sequence: in the middle of the mouth, in the two arms, then in the heart, in the two shanks, and in the middle of the navel.
Having performed the arrangement of the wheel (cakravinyāsa), one should also tear asunder the weapon;
there, in the space of the shaven head (muṇḍavyomana), one should first [place] the lunar wheel (vaidava) as the leader of the wheels.
One should place a three-spoked [cakra] on the crest-lock, an eight-spoked one on the forehead starting from the region between the eyebrows,
and then a second ten-spoked one on the throat.
The heart has a fourteen-spoked wheel, then the navel has an eight-petaled one;
the foundation (ādhāra) has sixteen petals, and the door-wheel is at the feet.
The noose and goad are in the left and right hands; the two bows are at the eyebrows;
the arrows are at the nose; and the intermediate discus is also [there].

Thus, even if some intermediate element is not required, nothing imagined by oneself should be expected, because there is simply no expectation [of such a thing]. For if that expectation were present, one would have to look to another treatise for as long as the expectation persists. In its absence, however, [such an addition] is entirely without basis. If what is stated in another treatise were to be expected, then everything would follow suit, resulting in an infinite regress.
There would be the performance of another scripture. As it has been said:

"It is not proper to perform what is heard in another scripture [in the context of this one], because a scripture is independent of others; for that [performance] would originate from human intellect."

Even if there is dependence, that very dependence is the means of proof; as long as one depends upon something, the effect must arise from that alone, and not from anything else, lest there be an infinite regress.

Thus, let it suffice to ask: even though [the teachings] have been imparted by excellent gurus in various other regions, what can be said at every step for those who are not fit to receive instruction? || 112 ||

Thus, the practitioner, whose body has been made into the triple-city (*tripurīkṛtavigraha*), preceded by the worship of his own self, performs the worship of the Gurus and others— distinguished by the three lineages (*oghatriya*) beginning with the Divine and ending with the Lord of the Gate— at the external mandala and so forth, according to the view taught by our previous Gurus.

He states that, for the sake of omitting the worship of the entire cycle of wheels (*cakra*), one should first perform the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth for the Goddess alone due to her preeminence:
"Then [one should invoke] the Goddess, who resembles a lotus and is as red as the rays of the rising sun..."
Resembling the hibiscus flower and comparable to the pomegranate blossom.
Resembling a ruby and appearing like saffron water,
she was adorned with a shimmering crown and a network of tiny bells set with rubies.
Her sprout-like, curling locks of hair resembled a swarm of black bees,
and her lotus-face was like a freshly blossomed, deep red lotus.
The Supreme Goddess has a forehead slightly curved like a crescent moon with a soft fillet,
and eyebrows as beautiful as the bow of Śiva.
Her eyes were playfully swinging with waves of bliss and joy, and her golden earrings were spread wide by the mass of shimmering rays [emanating from them]. || 117 ||
Her expansive, rounded cheeks surpassed the orb of the moon, and her nose was as perfectly defined as the measuring line for the creation of Viśvakarman and other celestial architects.
Her lips were red like copper, coral, or the bimba fruit, resembling nectar;
they surpassed the very essence of sweetness through the charm of her smile. || 119 ||
She was graced by a chin endowed with incomparable qualities,
possessed a neck like a conch shell, had large eyes, and arms as graceful as lotus stalks.
(61) Her lotus-like hands are as delicate as red water-lilies;
the sky is overspread by the radiance of the moonlight from the nails of her lotus-hands. || 121 ||
Her lofty breasts were adorned with strings of pearl necklaces, and her waist was beautifully graced by the three folds of skin. || 122 ||
Adorned with a navel that resembles the flowing current of the river of beauty,
she possessed shapely hips encircled by a girdle fashioned from priceless gems.
The Goddess, whose curved line of hair on her rounded hips acts as a goad for the two elephants,
and whose thighs are as delicate as the graceful pillars of a plantain tree.
Adorned with a pair of shanks resembling a plantain tree in its loveliness,
her lotus-feet were rubbed by the crest-jewels of Brahmā as he bowed before her.
She who smiles with a continuous stream of splendor resembling a hundred moons,
and whose feet possess the crimson hue of pomegranate flowers and red lac, surpassing even vermilion.
Clad in red garments, with noose and goad raised in her hands, seated upon a red lotus, and adorned with red ornaments. || 127 ||
She has four arms and three eyes, and she holds five arrows and a bow;
her mouth is filled with betel-leaf mixed with pieces of camphor,
and her body is crimson with the intense fragrance of great musk and saffron.
(62) Richly adorned with all the attire of love and decorated with every ornament. || 129 ||
She who generates delight for the world, she who causes the world to be enamored, she who effects the attraction of the world, and she whose form is the cause of the world. || 130 ||
The Goddess who consists of all mantras, beautiful with all auspiciousness, eternally composed of all Lakṣmīs, and delighted by supreme bliss. || 131 ||
Having remembered the Great Tripura-mudrā,
one should invoke [the deity] by means of the Vidyā in the form of an invocation, O fortunate one, accompanied by the utterance of salutation.

The supreme practitioner, having meditated upon Mahātripurasundarī in the center of the wheel according to what was previously described—[the rest of the sentence is omitted]—should remain intent upon that for a moment; this is the implied meaning. By the word "mādhurya" (sweetness), its loveliness and its nature as sweetness are indicated.

Regarding the word *rasa*: she is characterized by her arms. Precisely because she gladdens the world, she is the manifestor elsewhere of the Supreme Reality (para-tattva), which is designated by the term "world-bliss" (*jagadānanda*). By the two qualifiers "possessing all auspiciousness and beauty" (*sarvasaubhāgyasundarī*) and "consisting of all fortune" (*sarvalakṣmīmayī*), the meaning of all the preceding qualifiers is subsumed. Thus, since this description of meditation pertains specifically to the Principal Goddess, it is the same for the others as well.
"Meditation" (dhyāna) is established by implication, because these [deities] possess its expanded form. That which is an ocean of aesthetic flavor (rasa),
beyond the reach of words, consisting of all bliss belonging to the Goddess,
has one face, is deep red, and is seated upon a red lotus throne.
One should meditate upon the pure host of Śaktis in the form of the Goddess’s hands, equipped with four weapons: the noose, the goad, the bow, and the arrow.
"O lady of excellent complexion, for this reason, meditation does not exist for them.

[This means: "meditation does not exist" means something other than the aforementioned meditation. However, it is not intended as a total prohibition from the very root, since meditation is possible even for the primary Goddess, who, being composed of all bliss, is beyond the reach of speech.

Because other [mantras] whose forms expand from that [source] are suitable for that purpose; "the great Tripura-mudrā" refers to the *trikhaṇḍā* due to its proximity to terms such as the "invocation-vidyā" and so forth, as he will state:
"This *trikhaṇḍā* is the great mudrā for the rite of invoking Tripurā. (3.4)
Thus [it is said]. Because of the unsuitability of invocation, it is by means of that which is joined with salutation.

"Now, surely worship cannot be performed without mantras, yet these [deities] have been mentioned as being specifically assigned; by which one, then, is the worship now to be performed? To this he says:
"O Goddess, the drops of Śiva and Agni, and the drops of the Sun and Fire."
O Maheśvarī, they should be applied both simultaneously and in sequential form.

The pair of seed-syllables that has arisen, joined with Māyā (the letter *I*) and the crescent moon (*ardhendu*), consists of Māyā and Lakṣmī; by means of this [syllable], the eight Mothers are to be worshipped there.
[The syllables are: *Śiva* = *O*, *Agni* = *Ra*, *Dinakṛt* = *Śa*, *Vahni* = *Ra*, *Māyā* = *Ī*; thus, *Hrīṃ Śrīṃ*.
As for which of these are to be worshipped and where, he says:
Brahmāṇī is at the western gate, and Māheśvarī is also in the north;
likewise Indrāṇī is in the east, and Kaumārī is in the south. (136)
One should place Vaiṣṇavī in the northwest, Vārāhī in the direction of Ishana (the northeast),
Cāmuṇḍā in the southeast, O Goddess, and Mahālakṣmī in the southwest.
The word "pūjyā" (to be worshipped) should be connected with the nominative case, and "pūjayet" (one should worship) with the accusative case.
In that regard: "O Great Goddess, the eight Siddhis beginning with Aṇimā are established as the manifest Yoginīs in the Cakra called Trailokyamohana" (Yoginīhṛdaya 3.118).

By such statements as these, it is shown that the powers beginning with Brāhmī are designated as *aṇimā* and so forth precisely because they perform those functions; thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Regarding their status as the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*), [she appears] in each respective division of Tripurā and so on—(Yoginīhṛdaya 2.9).

Thus has been stated the worship of the Goddess known as Śrī Tripurā; and regarding the Mistress of the Wheels (Cakreśvarī), [it is said]: "O Goddess, those very mudrās belonging to Tripurā, which are accompanied by the eight Siddhis on both sides of each wheel—those one should worship at the time of worship in all the wheels. (4.65)

According to the perspective that will be explained below, one should worship each individual mudrā together with its corresponding siddhi. For example, here the *saṃkṣobhiṇī* mudrā is accompanied by the *aṇimā* siddhi. And the teachers maintain that these three—[the mudrā, the siddhi, and their union]—are to be worshipped at the very beginning of each cakra. 137.
Having thus described the first wheel, the Deluder of the Three Worlds, he also speaks of the second wheel, the Fulfiler of All Hopes:
"She whose form is the attraction of desire, and whose nature is the attraction of the intellect."
She is the attractor of the ego and has the nature of attracting sound.
The Goddess is of the nature of attracting touch and is the performer of the attraction of form; she is the attractor of taste and likewise the attractor of fragrance. (139)
She is the form that attracts the mind and has the nature of attracting steadfastness;
she is the form that attracts mindfulness and performs the attraction of names. || 140 ||
Another has the form of attracting seeds; another has the nature of attracting the self; she is the attractor of nectar, and the supreme attractor of the body.
Thus, O Great Goddess, one should worship on the sixteen-spoked [cakra] by way of the left path;
this indeed is the group of sixteen digits (kalās) consisting of the digits of Māyā and Lakṣmī. 142.
"By the left path" refers to the practitioner (*sādhaka*); for the Goddess, however, it is by the right, as is established by the sense of the context. As he will state:
"By the sequence of the left path alone, having taken [the transmission] from the Western [tradition] itself to the Southern... (1.148).
Thus: one word *kalā* denotes the vowels (*svara*), while the second refers to the powers (*śakti*).
And here, the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*) is said to be Tripurīśvarī. As the scripture states:
"In like manner, the Guptayoginīs [reside] in the fulfillment of all desires."
The deities beginning with Kāmākarṣaṇī and Rūpākarṣaṇī have been fully described.
Thus—[the first]—and [the second is] Tripurīśvarī;
so it is said. || 142 ||
He also speaks of the third wheel, called the "Causer of All Agitation":
Anaṅgakusumā in the east, Anaṅgamaṅgalā in the south, Anaṅgamathanā in the west, and Madanottarā in the north. (143)
One should worship Anaṅgalekhā in the southeast, Anaṅgavāsinī in the southwest, Anaṅgāṅkuśā in the northwest, and Anaṅgamālinī in the northeast. || 144 ||

In this case, since the sequence of east, west, and so forth is stated for the first wheel independently of any other [system], the sequence of directions according to Prajāpati alone is to be adopted;
and Anaṅgakusumā and the others are [placed] according to the arrangement of the goddesses of the gates.
Statements such as these, however, must be disregarded because they contradict the Śruti. And here, the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśvarī) is Tripurasundarī. As it is said:
"O Goddess, [the form] most secret among the secret resides in the wheel that causes the agitation of all;
and Anaṅgakusumā and the others are established as goddesses within the wheel."
Thus, [in] the third [wheel], Tripurasundarī;
and so it is said. || 144 ||
He also spoke of the fourth, called Sarvasaubhāgyakāraka:
"The power that agitates all, likewise the one that subdues all;
the other which attracts all, and likewise the one that gladdens all. (145)
She is the power that utterly deludes, she whose form is the paralyzing of all;
she is the one whose nature is the crushing of all, and she who brings everything under her control.
She is the power that colors all, whose very nature is universal intoxication;
she is the power that accomplishes all aims and fulfills every hope.
The Goddess consists of all mantras and brings about the destruction of all duality.
Thus, (p. 67) [it is said].
In a counter-clockwise sequence, from the west itself one proceeds to the south.
Having taken [the offerings], one should worship these goddesses, the sovereigns of the three worlds;
"starting from the west" means beginning from the front of the Goddess. The word "having taken" indicates the limit [of the sequence]. And here, Cakreśvarī is Tripuravāsinī. As it has been said:
In the wheel that brings about good fortune, which has come down through the lineage of oral tradition,
the beautiful goddesses are established, beginning with Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī.
Thus,
[the goddess] Tripuravāsinī is in the fourth;
and so it is said.
He also spoke of the fifth, called Sarvārthasādhaka:
"The Śakti bestows all accomplishments and likewise bestows all prosperity. (149)
She is the one who makes all dear, the performer of all auspiciousness, the goddess who grants all desires, and the liberator from all suffering. 150.
She is the pacifier of all death, the destroyer of all obstacles;
she is the goddess beautiful in every limb, the bestower of all prosperity. 151.
And likewise,
O Goddess of the lords of gods, one should again worship this group of ten goddesses in the second enclosure with the primordial vidyā, O Goddess. (152)
"By the primordial ignorance (ādyavidyā)" means by that which was just mentioned, consisting of two syllables characterized as Māyā and Lakṣmī.
As it has been said:
"The great breath (mahāprāṇa), conjoined with the nose (nāsā), having the form of a staff (daṇḍākāra), and accompanied by the bindu."
In that same way, one should keep this secret; this vidyā is considered to consist of two syllables.

Thus [it is said]. "In the same way" means in the first and second [sections]. By the words "once again," it is stated that this very [mantra] is employed in the third and fourth [sections] as well, because it alone was introduced and no other vidyā has been mentioned. However, in the case of the three-syllable vidyā, none of this is consistent, since that [vidyā] has already been employed previously and is not under discussion here. This is also the case in the *Śrīsamudra*.
In the worship of the first cakra, the seed-syllable consists of Māyā (Hrīṃ) and Lakṣmī (Śrīṃ);
for the second [cakra], the sixteen vowels are joined with those [two] separately.

Since there is no mention of other designators such as these, [the text] is intended solely as an illustration of the four wheels; thus, there is no fault whatsoever. The Gurus also state: "In this manner, within all six wheels, the Yoginīs—excluding the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśvara)—are joined with the Māyā and Śrībīja mantras."
Thus it is said;
and here, one must also explain the meaning of the *mātṛkā*, according to the passage: "And they call the first knowledge the *mātṛkā*, the Mistress of Speech (*vāgeśī*)."
Again, the three wheels should be worshipped in the reverse order, turning counter-clockwise,
with the same number of digits and syllables as the mantra, using beautiful flowers.
Thus, likewise,

there is also the denotation of the initial syllables of the eight groups (*varga*) within each triad of eights; since no such division has been heard [stated] for the second enclosure (*āvaraṇa*) with respect to the fourteen spokes at the end of the wheel, [there is] the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*).
Herein lies Śrī Tripurā. As it has been said: "The Yoginīs of Kulakaula are bestowers of all accomplishments;
those beginning with Sarvasiddhipradā reside in the wheel that accomplishes all aims."
Thus:
"In the fifth [wheel] is Tripurā and Śrī... and so forth. || 152 ||
69) He also spoke of the sixth [chapter], called "The Provider of All Protection":
"She is omniscient, omnipotent, and the bestower of all sovereignty."
The Goddess consists of all-knowledge and is the destroyer of all diseases. || 153 ||
She is the very nature of the support of all, likewise the remover of all sins;
she is the Goddess consisting of all bliss and the embodiment of the protection of all. 154.
Furthermore, O Great Goddess, these ten deities, who bestow all desired fruits, are renowned for arising in accordance with their own names. (155)
In this manner, O Goddess, one should worship these great goddesses, who grant the accomplishment of all aims,
in the third enclosure according to the previously stated procedure.

"Arising in accordance with their own names" and "bestowing the accomplishment of all aims" applies to all [the goddesses] without exception. "By what was previously stated" refers to the nature of the application of the two-syllable vidyā, the counter-clockwise rotation, and so forth. And here, the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*) is Tripuramālinī. As it has been said:
"The deities of the Nigarbha [Tantra] reside in the supreme wheel that effects all protection."
O Great Goddess, praised by heroes, Sarvajñā and the others are established there.
Thus, [in the sixth] is Tripuramālinī;
and so it is said. || 156 ||
He also spoke of the seventh [chapter], called "The Remover of All Diseases":
"O Maheśānī, listen to the worship in the first wheel according to the sequence; each name of the deities, as previously stated, is joined with its seed-syllable. (157)
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship from below by way of the left path until reaching the right path with red flowers, O Maheśvarī. (158)

"Beginning from below" means beginning from the west; "with red flowers" applies to all [the remaining items]. And here, the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*) is Tripurāsiddhi. As it has been said:
"O Dear One, the secret deities in the wheel are the removers of all diseases."
The great goddesses, beginning with Vaśinī, are established as the ultimate reality.
Thus, [in] the seventh [chapter], the accomplishment of Tripurā;
and so it is said. || 158 ||
He also describes the eighth wheel, called Sarvasiddhimaya:
"One should worship the fourfold [group] in the center of the wheel in sequence, starting from the northwest, northeast, east, and so on, up to the south. (159)

"In the middle of the wheel" means outside of the root triangle; the sense is that there are four intermediate spaces between the outer and inner [circles] in the four directions. By the word "beginning with the east" (*pūrvādi*), the counter-clockwise direction (*vāmāvarta*) is further reinforced. || 159 ||
"What is the group of four? he asks.
"O Maheśānī, it consists of the arrows of Kāma, his bow, and likewise his noose, together with the goad [formed by] the words *jambha*, *moha*, *vaśa*, and *stambha*. (160)

The term "goad" (aṅkuśa) should be understood as referring specifically to that [deity] due to its proximity to the word "desire" (kāma). By virtue of this commonality, it follows that the worship of the goddesses' weapons should also take place here, and not merely [that of the primary deities]. || 160 ||
O Goddess, one should worship everything within the central triangle with the root-mantra,
both collectively and individually, according to the distinction of each syllable alone.
One should worship Kāmeśvarī in the foremost corner, Vajreśī likewise in the south, Bhagamālā in the north, and Tripurasundarī in the center. (162)

"By means of the differentiation of the individual syllables alone" (kevalākṣarabhedena) means having differentiated each single syllable individually. Therefore, even when the root-vidyā is distributed, one should worship the triad beginning with Kāmeśvarī in all three corners using each individual *puṇḍra* (mark) in counter-clockwise order, and not by omitting them. However, when it is combined as a whole, one should worship Tripurāmbikā, the eighth Mistress of the Wheel, in the center by means of the three *piṇḍas*.

This is the intended meaning (*tātparyārtha*). As it has been said in the *Sarvasiddhimaya-cakra*: "The four deities of the sacred seats (*pīṭha*), beginning with Kāmeśvarī, who abide in the supreme secret, reside within the wheel."
Thus, [in the eighth [chapter], Tripurāmbikā; and so it is said.

Of the syllable whose nature is the final *piṇḍa*, which is indicated by the individual words alone, there is—just as in the case of the *Ādividyā*—a fusion with the three vowels beginning with *vāgbhava*.

As for the claim that the eighth is not rightly called "Vidyā" because it is not taught in the Guru’s tradition, this has already been largely addressed. Thus, even in the case of the eighth and ninth wheels (*cakra*), there is no contradiction whatsoever, since—as in the case of the wheels of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) in the *Śrīdevīpañcaśatika*—each one is designated as a "Vidyā. And so, because this eighth Vidyā is stated to be the designator of the Mistress of the Wheels (*cakreśvarī*) of both the eighth and ninth wheels, [the same applies] to the remainder as well.

It is established that, by the power of the meaning, the status of being the designator of the Mistress of the Wheel (*cakreśvarī*) for the sevenfold group of Vidyās is obtained sequentially across the seven wheels, beginning from the first wheel. By the repetition of the phrase "Tripurasundarī in the middle," it is indicated that [she is] the Mistress of the ninth wheel named *Sarvānandamaya*, namely Śrī Mahātripurasundarī, specifically in the center of the eighth wheel.
The meaning is that one should worship. With this very intention, it is also stated in the *Śrī Rasamahodadhi*:
"Endowed with the final sequence (*prāntakrama*)... and so forth.

For this very reason, [objections] such as "the wheel is attended by the eight Mothers (*ambāṣṭaka*) because it is to be worshipped according to the final sequence" are also refuted. For it is thus...
Otherwise, it would follow that even a tenth wheel has been mentioned, which would contradict the scripture. As it is said on page 72:
"But in the ninth [wheel], O Great Goddess, is Mahātripurasundarī."
This is declared to be the Root-Vidyā, which brings the three worlds under its control.
Thus, even by means of mere worship, she who consists of nine aspects and more returns;
for the primordial Śakti is of a single form, bringing about freedom from old age and death.
Thus,
in the wheel consisting of all bliss, the Great Mistress of the Fullness,
the primordial Mahātripurasundarī who comprises everything, is established.
But she whose nature transcends the world, who is endowed with the ultimate sequence,
who abides in the state of supreme non-duality, and is devoted to the Great Worship, O Dear One.

And so it is said. Furthermore, for those who maintain that the ninth wheel is to be worshipped only in the "sky of the skull" (*muṇḍavyomana*), there would be no worship of nine wheels at all within the *cakra*; thus, there is a contradiction with the subject matter under discussion. Moreover, by whom has the worship of the other wheels in the sky of the skull been prohibited? Enough, then, of this conversation with those ill-taught individuals who have lost the authentic tradition. 162.

In this rite, once the host of mantras has been invoked, an offering of satisfaction (tarpaṇa) should be performed with flowers, all the presented oblations, and incense, arising from the power of faith and devotion.
By such statements as these, he declares that the libation (tarpaṇa) must necessarily be performed:
"Having first performed the ritual of worship in this manner, the best of practitioners should present incense, perfumes, food offerings, and libations. (163)
Following that, there are, in due order: agitation, expulsion, attraction, possession, intoxication, the great goad, the forms of the *khecarī* seed-syllables, and the *yoni-mudrās*. (164)
(p. 73) Having performed [these gestures], the supreme practitioner, being composed, should perform meditation.

"Having performed them in sequence" means for each wheel; thus, in the first wheel, there are the *saṃkṣobhaṇī* up to the eighth seed-gesture (*bījamudrā*), and the ninth, which is accepted by the word "and so forth," is the *trikhaṇḍamudrā* and the *yonimudrā*. And in this context, it is these two mudrās alone that are to be worshipped.
The Teachers [state]: "In this system, the supernatural powers (siddhis) are also exactly ten: atomization (aṇimā), levitation (laghimā), magnification (mahimā), and attainment (prāpti);
likewise, irresistible will (prākāmya), lordship (īśitva), and thereafter, mastery (vaśitva)."
Likewise, the eighth is proclaimed as the power of resolving desires (*kāmāvasāyitva*).

Thus, the eight accomplishments beginning with *aṇimā* have been described in order for the [first] eight wheels; however, in the ninth, there is the accomplishment of the essence (*rasasiddhi*) and the accomplishment of liberation (*mokṣasiddhi*). For here, in the primary sense, the fruits are indeed enjoyment and liberation. Regarding that:

The supernatural powers (*siddhis*), beginning with *aṇimā*, are accomplished individually by means of the eight wheels (*cakras*); however, collectively, they are accomplished by the ninth and principal wheel, in relation to which the accomplishment of *rasa* (*rasasiddhi*) is designated as the object of worship. For it has been stated everywhere in various places in the *Śrīrasasvacchanda* and other texts that this [ninth wheel] alone is the treasury of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhinidhāna*). As it is said:
It bestows the accomplishment of the *piṇḍa* and grants the fruits of all desires;
it shall accomplish everything previously mentioned, beginning with the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā*.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the *Śrīrasamahodadhi*, this Blessed Lady is taught as being seated upon the lap of the illustrious Mahākāmeśvara specifically for the sake of attaining the perfection of the accomplishment of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). As it is stated therein:
"O Mistress of Taste (*Rasanāyikā*), you have heard the entire ritual procedure in its entirety."
And for those who are unfortunate, O Lord, that is never accomplished.
Therefore, O Bhairava, out of a desire for the welfare of men and for the sake of the cause of good fortune,
you have declared this ritual procedure of Mahākāmeśvara.
(74) She who rests upon his lap is Mahātripurasundarī;
by you, some portion of her mantras, meditations, and so forth, has been indicated.
O Lord, O Master of all living beings, please tell me out of compassion how she is worshipped separately by men who seek fortune according to their destiny.

Thus, since enjoyment (*bhukti*) is inseparable from liberation (*mukti*) in our system, it is precisely here that liberation is established as well, due to its primacy as the culmination of all [powers].
This is because the fruits are designated among the very limbs (*aṅga*), beginning with *aṇimā* and ending with liberation.

This and more has been stated by the ancients as well. Furthermore, regarding what others have said here—namely, that having set aside the attainment of the state of "wishing for whatever is reached" (*prāptiyatracchākāmāvasāyitva*), they instead postulate the fulfillment of the desire for enjoyment (*bhuktīcchāsiddhi*) and claim that the eightfold accomplishment (*siddhyaṣṭaka*) itself constitutes the three mudrās, such as the seed-mudrā (*bījamudrā*) and so forth, in the eighth wheel—that is entirely excluded from both reason and scripture, and should therefore be disregarded. "Composed" (*samāhita*)...
The meaning is: the continuous contemplation consisting of one-pointed observation of the nature of the mantra which is supreme and partless.
He says that very thing:
having visualized the *bindu*, one should [visualize] the face and below that, the two breasts. || 165 ||
Below that, one should contemplate the *parārdha* together with it, facing downwards.

This is the supreme reality (*paraṃ tattva*), consisting of the mere experience whose nature is the oneness of Śiva and Śakti; it is of the nature of the non-dual Supreme (*parādvayamaya*), indivisible by essence, indefinable, and the self of the universe composed of the thirty-six principles.

Having conceived the mouth as being of the nature of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), because it is the locus of repose and is predominant, and having contemplated it as such, that very [mouth], through its own sovereignty, when desiring to manifest externally below,
is always the two rays of the Unsurpassed Lord (*anuttaranātha*). I bow to them.
It is renowned as Śiva-Śakti— [the rest of the verse is omitted] —.

Thus, by virtue of being presided over by the state of Śiva-Śakti, consciousness— which consists of the self-reflection of its own nature— through its "cooing" (kūjana), attains a state of division resembling a pair of breasts; having thus reached that stage of differentiation, consciousness was previously transformed into vital breath (prāṇa).
According to this rule, even beyond that, in the state of external form, there is the supreme letter *ha*; its half is the vowel-less *kalā*.

Preceded by the manifestation of the nature of the universal vital breath (*prāṇa*), it assumes the stage of the vital subject and so forth; then, by turning downward from that as well, [it proceeds].

"By the principle that 'from this very letter *sa*, the universe shines forth clearly,' one should contemplate—that is, perceive—the ultimate, final, gross form of the universe, which consists of objects of cognition (*prameya*), beginning from the earth up to Kālāgni; such is the meaning according to the sequence of consciousness (*saṃvit*). It is also [to be understood] according to the sequence of phonemes."

Having conceptualized the face as that form [of the letter *sa*] along with its *bindu*, and having touched upon it, one should likewise [visualize] the two breasts below it in the form of the Sun and Moon, and their two *bindus*.
