Below that as well is the letter *sa*; its lower part is the letter *ra*, which is of the nature of fire, and the supreme half-measure (*paramardha*). Thus, there is the fourth vowel (*ī*) together with its *bindu*. By repetition, below that too is the letter *ha*, which is superior to the letter *sa*.

The half-moon (*ardhacandra*) is the *ha*-kalā; below that is the form of the supreme *ra* (the letter *r*) belonging to the *sa*, which is triangular in shape, known by such terms as "the mouth of the Yoginī," and facing downwards.

The meaning is that one should contemplate and mentally connect this seed-syllable of Māyā, which consists of the partless mantra (*niṣkalamantra*). And its partlessness (*niṣkalatva*) is because, due to no difference from the nature of Śakti, it is identical with the letter *i*.

Because of the similarity between the letter *ha* and the state of intoxication (*mādana*), the letter *ka* is included; because of the traditional teaching that *ra* and *la* are one, the letter *la* is included; and because of its being the final half of the *sa*, the letter *sa* is included.

Thus, this is the condensed, subtle form of the Root-Vidyā itself, consisting of the withdrawal of all the *kalās*. Since the sequence of the abodes (*dhāmakrama*) is essentially inseparable from this, it has already been explained for the most part; so, enough with further elaboration.
And what is the object of focus for such meditation? He says:
"In this way, that imperishable [reality] which has arisen in the form of the aesthetic essence (kalā) of desire. (166)

One should contemplate that very body of one's own as the supreme, eternal abode of the liberation from the poisons of desire and the like, and as the most excellent of all principles (tattvas). (167)

In the manner thus described, although it consists of the three *tattvas*, the syllable in the form of *Kāmakalā* shines forth through its incessant form during manifestation; for this very reason, it is eternal (*dhruva*) and partless (*niṣkala*), and because its nature is exclusively partless, it is supreme (*parama*).
For this same reason, it is the abode (*ālaya*) of desires and the like, as well as of liberation from suffering, having arisen and blossomed solely as the singular essence of perfect experience.

The meaning is that one should contemplate—that is, one should continuously attend to—one's own body itself as the most excellent reality (*tattvapravara*) by virtue of its being a representation of that [reality], specifically because it possesses the same form as that [reality]. For indeed, this very arrangement exists directly within the body for everyone, as is witnessed by one's own experience; so enough with further elaboration. Furthermore, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) here— [...]* *Note: The source text appears to be an excerpt from a commentary on a Tantric or philosophical work (likely related to the Trika or Krama systems), discussing the identification of the individual body with the supreme reality.*

To claim that the term "prakāra" (mode/type) is used here for the purpose of summarizing the minor accomplishments (*kṣudrasiddhi*) and so forth to be presented starting from the second chapter is a futile wandering into a realm beyond the reach of words; for the relationship of subordinate and primary (*guṇapradhānabhāva*) is everywhere indeed specific, owing to its all-encompassing nature. Furthermore, regarding this point, others—whether here or elsewhere—have failed to directly understand the true essence of that meaning from the Guru.
Any attempt to harmonize or elucidate the meaning of the *Śrītantrāloka*— even if it concerns the primary, clear path transmitted through the lineage of one's father and grandfather—
only brings great ridicule upon those who reveal that most profound and obscure path to its knowers, for they are unaware of it and have never heard of, seen before, or traveled along such a route.
As for what they say: "He who is lame and deaf has never seen the exterior of a woman's door, nor has he ever heard from the mouth of any guide anywhere any story at all."
To that merchant who knows every path, this new incarnation of Hāsa provides the means to sever the obstacles encountered while traveling to foreign lands— how wonderful!

Thus it is said. Because this matter is profound, because there is much to be said, because it would result in excessive prolixity of the text, and because it is not useful for the present subject at hand, we have not presented it by dividing it into its parts; therefore, the learned should not be displeased with us. Indeed, all are witnesses that demonstrating this is not at all difficult. Therefore, it should be understood from our teacher’s *Upaśatadviveka*; what is the use of further digression? || 167 ||
Having thus attained immersion into the supreme essential nature, what should he do? To this he says:
"Then, having meditated upon Tripurasundarī together with her wheel (cakra), the lord of practitioners should dismiss her with his own mudrā, saying, 'Forgive me. (168)
"With one's own mudrā" means with that which has the nature of withdrawal; may there be auspiciousness. || 168 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Śrīvāmakeśvarīmatavivaraṇa* composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Jayaratha. 1.
Now begins the second chapter.
Establishing the connection with the preceding section— namely, "What would happen to him when worship has been performed in this manner?"— the Blessed One said:
In whatever country, city, or village this rite is performed by the practitioner according to this procedure, an upheaval of the world arises there. || 1 ||

By this statement regarding the *deśāvakḷpti*—namely, "in the city or in the village"—it is made known that this worship, independent of anything else, brings about all accomplishments (*siddhi*). Therefore, one should not speak of a dependence on the instructions of the *dvīpāmnāya* and so forth; for in those cases, the agitation of the world (*jagatkṣobha*) and other such effects arise precisely through the predominance of the location (*deśa*).
"Variegated with paintings"—enough of this prolixity. || 1 ||
What indeed is this "agitation of the world"? He says:
Women approach from afar according to the analogy of ants carrying bones, their minds scorched by the intense heat of the blazing fire of desire. (2)
For this reason,
O Great Goddess, upon seeing it, all women become bewildered in heart by the mantra and their broad hips quiver. (3)
Now, one might ask: "Does this [attainment] occur merely from worship, or not? To this he says:
"When even a single hundred thousand recitations have been performed, the women on the surface of the earth are agitated.
Now, if by this much alone he does not become extroverted, then what would happen to him? To this he says:
For if the mind of the practitioner is not disturbed even slightly in this way. (4)
Then all the nāga maidens in the netherworld (pātāla) are agitated;
they are agitated when, by implication, the second hundred thousand recitations have been performed.
Even so, when they are likewise oriented toward the attainment of the specific [accomplishment] as before, he does not undergo even the slightest agitation.
Then, when the third hundred thousand has been recited— the word "japte" (having been recited) being understood— the celestial nymphs dwelling in heaven flee away.
He summarizes that very point:
"Having thus recited [the mantra] three hundred thousand times, the excellent practitioner remains established in the vow. (6)
O Goddess of the gods, it agitates the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving.
Having thus explained the application of the mantra, he also spoke regarding the yantra: "If, having drawn a vast wheel, one places an image in its center... (7)
Then, one should write [the name] joined with the Name and meditate upon it as blazing;
even if she is situated at a distance of a hundred yojanas and is invisible, [she will be drawn].
"Even she, freed from fear and shame, comes along, utterly deluded.
This is a reason expressed by means of an epithet (*viśeṣaṇadvāraka-hetu*) regarding the drawing of the image of the one to be won over (*sādhyapratimā*).
Right here he states another alternative:
"Or else, having positioned himself in the middle of that, when he contemplates the mantra... (9).
One should visualize oneself as entirely red and the object of attainment (sādhya) likewise made red;
from that, O Goddess, one becomes beautiful with all auspiciousness.

O Supreme Goddess, he is the beloved of all the world and the achiever [of all goals]; this is indicated by the very phrase "situated in the midst of that. For this reason, it was previously stated that [the seat] is "vast. The syntactical connection is as follows: when one contemplates everything—namely oneself, the mantra, and the object to be accomplished—as being ruddy.
He states the third position as well:
"She is worshipped with all red-colored offerings, accompanied by the mudrā. || 11 ||
By the mere mention of whose name one becomes submissive like a servant—
by means of this "mudrā," which, as will be described, takes the form of a *yoni*— and by the name alone, and not even by means of an image or the like.
He spoke also of the fourth:
"But that which is called the 'unseen' (adṛṣṭā) is to be joined, situated in the center of the wheel. (12)
Having formed the yonimudrā, he attracts in an instant a yakṣiṇī,
or a gandharvī, or a kinnarī, or a mistress of the asuras.
A maiden of the Siddhas, a maiden of the Nāgas, a maiden of the gods, and a sky-walker; a Vidyādharī, an Apsaras, a maiden of the Ṛṣis, and Urvaśī. || 14 ||
"From her waist hung [a garment] dripping with the agitation arising from passion.
This is a distinguishing feature compared to what preceded it, namely that she was unseen and that [the garment] was being drawn out;
"dripping" (jharat) means by means of a liquid flow.
He also said by way of meditation and recitation:
"By meditating on the Mahākāmakalā, one may agitate all women. (15)
Likewise,
having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over equal parts of yellow pigment (rocanā), saffron (kuṅkuma), and sandalwood (candana), the wise man should apply the tilaka mark. 16.
To the question "What then?", he says:
"Therefore, whoever one looks upon, speaks to, touches, or thinks of, that person will necessarily fall into servitude through both wealth and body. (17)
Furthermore, O Maheśvarī, flowers, fruits, perfumes, drinks, or garments—
having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times over these, whichever woman they are directed toward [shall be won]. (18)
He would immediately attract that virtuous woman, whose heart was bewildered; "her" is the ellipsis, meaning the one who is currently virtuous.
For this forceful attraction, O blessed lady, is never obstructed anywhere. (19)
He describes the yantras by another method as well:
"In a secluded place, one should draw an image on the surface of the ground with yellow pigment (rocanā)—an image that is beautiful and adorned with lovely amorous attire and ornaments. (20)
Then,
[he should visualize] the Great Vidyā of his birth-name, joined with the circles arising from his forehead, heart, and navel, and pierced by the goad.
Having inscribed the syllables of passion (madanākṣara) joined within all the joints of his limbs,
he turned toward that direction, his body composed of the three cities (tripurīkṛtavigraha).

Having bound the *kṣobhiṇī* mudrā, one should recite the *mahāvidyā* one hundred and eight times, together with the name [of the person]. This is a *madhyapadalopa* (middle-term elided) compound meaning "the great knowledge along with the name. Regarding the phrase "having written it interlaced with the *aṅkuśa*," the meaning is that the *aṅkuśa* mantra should be applied once between the name and the *vidyā*.
And "the syllable of Madana" is the ellipsis.
And he says that one should not draw the image on the bare surface of the earth alone,
but rather after having appointed it within the fire-chamber, which is the abode of the digits of the moon and sun.

Thus, having drawn an upward-facing triangle on the ground, its apex encircled by two rows of vowels including the *ṣa* and *ṭha* [consonants], one should draw the image within it; this is the essential meaning. || 23 ||
When this had been done, he said:
"Then [she was] one whose outer corners of the eyes were agitated, who was tormented by the arrows of the Bodiless One (Kāma), and whose hips were trembling with waves of surging passion. (24)

(82) [She is] one who has swallowed up [all things] by the whirling of the power that surges from the wheel of powers, and who has cast away the goad of fear and shame regarding her own conduct. || 25 ||
Her heart was captivated, her fortitude lost, and her life-breath had departed;
she was well-guarded by embankments, walls, moats, and mechanical devices.
Her lotus-heart trembling from the union of fresh passion,
her garment was snatched away by the force of a great mantra more powerful than the mind itself.
She appeared as if bewildered, as if agitated, as if scorched, as if drained of life,
as if painted in a picture, as if unconscious, and as if crushed.
She appeared as if crushed, as if bewildered, as if overcome with terror;
she seemed as if dissolved, as if shattered, her mind utterly distraught. (29)
One may bring that woman from even a hundred yojanas away, appearing like a leaf tossed by the wind of a whirling mantra, as she revolves in the sky.
He also spoke of protective devices:
"Alternatively, having written the entire Mātṛkā on the outside of the wheel, whoever wears it at the root of the arm shall be invulnerable to all living beings. (31)
In that very same way, O Great Goddess, through the application of the sequence of one's own designations,
one shall attain freedom from old age and death by means of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor. (32)

"Likewise" (tathaiva) indicates an extension of all the points previously stated; however, the connection with a name is an additional factor. But [the example of] sandalwood and so forth should also be applied to the preceding case.

Likewise, even that which is written according to this very procedure with yellow pigment (rocanā), agallochum (aguru), and saffron (kuṅkuma) by means of the wheel-yoga, remains [efficacious] wherever it is placed. || 33 ||
Having interlaced the name of the one to be accomplished with his own name within the circle, he brings the entire world under his feet before long. || 34 ||
"Etadeva" refers to the wheel (*cakra*). "By means of the wheel-yoga" refers to the letters of the *mātṛkā*. "In this or that" refers to the base of the arm, the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and so forth.

Within the wheel is the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*); after that, one's own name; and that [name] must be interlaced at the end with the mantra (*vidyā*) placed once. This is the core statement (*garbhavākya*). || 34 ||
Likewise,
O Dear One, by means of the seed-syllable situated in the center, which consists of the Great Kāmakalā, one should seize each individual syllable of the name of the person to be accomplished.

The syntactical connection is as follows: "One should encircle each individual syllable of the name of the target (*sādhya*) with all the letters of the *mātṛkā* even on the outside. By the phrase "situated in the middle," it is indicated that this should be done within the wheel itself; otherwise, the statement "even on the outside" would be inconsistent. [The word] "having firmly grasped" (*avaṣṭabhya*).
Each syllable of the subject matter, however, is encased within the syllables of the yantra; it should be known as strung together by the practitioners of mantra—[the rest of the verse follows].
By the expression "ityuktyā," the meaning is "having woven together."
Then, having placed it in the center of gold, one should wear it on the left arm. || 36 ||
The word "I shall protect" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 36 ||
Not only here, but wherever one may wear it— whether on the crest-lock, on a garment, or anywhere else—
this is protection.
For it indeed makes the three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, become its servants. || 37 ||
It deludes the king, the horse, and the wicked elephant;
it [deludes] the thief, the lion, the serpent, and the great planet of supreme mantras. (38)
When worn in the form of a wheel, it [protects against] enemies, the thunderbolt, weapons, as well as ḍākinīs and śākinīs, and bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas. (39)
He now describes the yantra that causes the agitation of the cities and so forth:
"O beautiful one, having joined it with that wheel, one should place the yantras named after the cities either in the center, at a crossroads, or in the four directions. (40)

"By that" means by what was previously stated, namely, its internal and external nature and so forth. "Having joined together" (saṃdarbhya) does not mean having woven it again. "In the middle" refers, by implication, to the centers of the cities; the same applies elsewhere. "One should cause to be placed" refers to the yantra. || 40 ||
"What would happen thus? he asked. [The Lord] replied: "O Goddess, from that there arises for the world a great calamity, and especially for women, O Īśvarī, even those who have not seen you. (41)
Likewise,
one should visualize the earth situated in its center, together with its mountains, forests, and groves, extending to the four oceans and blazing with light. (42)
"Pṛthvīm" means, as before, preceded by the writing of the name [of the disciple]. || 42 ||
Then,
through the yoga of six months of meditation, one becomes like Madana;
to the question "What then?", he says:
By her very glance she attracts the world; by her very glance she brings it under her control. || 43 ||
With a glance she agitates a woman; with a glance she withdraws poison;
with a glance she effects possession; with a glance she brings about the delusion of all. (44)
By its mere sight, one shall quickly destroy fevers such as those occurring on the fourth day.
Regarding this very [mantra], he also states another result based on a fixed time: "This, when worshipped at night and decorated with vermilion... (45).
This wheel, containing the aforementioned earth-mantra situated in the midst of fire, effects a great attraction of women even from a very great distance.
He speaks with certainty regarding the directions: "In this manner, in all cardinal and intermediate directions, the Goddess is worshipped. (46)
"Then the entire world is under [his] control by means of the sequence of the directions.

"In this manner" means by the sequence beginning with the night being smeared with vermilion (*sindūra*) and so forth. "By the sequence of the directions" means according to each respective direction, such as the east and so on.
Regarding another machine for the initial agitation of the city and so forth, he says on page 86:
"Having written [the mantra] upon birch bark with yellow pigment (rocanā), agallochum (aguru), and saffron (kuṅkuma)... (47).
In the center of that, one should delineate either a city,
or else a vast region, or a province, or a district.
Having composed [the mantra] by interweaving one's own name—

[fill in the gaps]— and having thus inscribed the wheel, the intended meaning is that one should interweave the name of the city or other location with one's own name within the center of that wheel by means of the Vidyā-mantra. || 48 ||
When this has been done—
[filling in the ellipsis]— if one should cause it to be placed on the ground,
or hold it in the hand, or around the neck, or at the base of the arm; || 49 ||
Whether it be on the crest-lock, on a garment, or situated anywhere else—
at that time,
O highly fortunate lady, this supreme wheel causes the agitation of the city.
He has also stated another protection:
"Milk of the *arka* plant, saffron, likewise the juice of *dhattūra*, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), lac-dye, lac-resin, and abundant musk. (51)
When this wheel is drawn by combining [the syllables] under its name,
for that person there is [protection] from thieves, seizing spirits, diseases, enemies, lions, serpents, and horses.
[It wards off] the floods of yakṣas, rākṣasas, and bhūtas, as well as the evil-minded śākinīs;
likewise, it prevents the occurrence of spider-bites, "donkey-flames" (gardabhajvālā), and the outbreak of "cold-fever" (śītalikā).
No fear exists— [as before]— for him;
likewise, [as before]—
his supreme mantra is an exorcism against malevolent incantations.
And because of constant maintenance [of this practice], Yama, the god of death, and others [have no power]. || 54 ||
For they are never able to harm even a single hair properly;
he now states another method by means of the application of a yantra:
"Or else, [one should place] the Goddess in the center and likewise in both triangles. (55)
He who makes [the image] joined with the name at the bottom and marked with gorocanā and saffron shall,
within seven days, become a servant like a slave.
"Going to both triangles" means situated within the hexagon; even there, it is situated in the center, and not in the intermediate corners. || 56 ||
Likewise,
having drawn [the figure] with a yellow substance and wearing it facing the direction of Indra (the East),
even one who has become omniscient becomes mute at that very moment by means of [this] name.

"One should hold" means that one should [hold] the Goddess situated in the middle of the six lotuses, joined below with the name of whichever [deity], by virtue of whose name he becomes such. (57) Likewise, having joined the name with the juice of mahānīla as before, [one should proceed].
Facing south, having burned it in the fire, one should kill him in an instant. || 58 ||
"Of whom" refers to the name; "having burnt" refers, by implication, to the yantra. || 58 ||
Likewise,
having smeared it with buffalo dung, horse dung, and cow urine,
and having placed it in the midst of sour gruel (āranāla), [the practitioner] becomes hated by all living beings. (59)

The meaning of the statement is as follows: if the wheel written with the name of the person [targeted] is thrown into the midst of a mortar (āranāla) along with buffalo and horse dung mixed with cow urine, as previously described, that person shall become hated by everyone. || 59 ||
Having thus applied it with yellow pigment (rocanā) to the center of a crow's wing-feather,
that which hangs suspended in space is a supreme means for causing expulsion.
Having joined [the syllables] below the Goddess situated in the middle of the hexagram; by making [the name] that which occupies the center, it effects the eradication of that person.
Likewise, O Goddess, having written it with milk, lac, yellow pigment (rocanā), and the juice of the mahānīla plant and so forth, one who wears it shall bring the four castes under control.

Regarding the word "dugdha" (milk): the phrase "having written" means by the very method previously described. One should wear the wheel on the arm and so forth. One brings [others] under control: by that written with milk, Brāhmaṇas; and up to that written with the juice of mahānīla, Śūdras. || 61 ||
Likewise,
if one should cast this very [substance] into the midst of water according to the prescribed rite,
there is no doubt that he will attain incomparable good fortune through bathing and drinking it. || 62 ||
"Etat" refers to the wheel as previously described. "By the procedure" means by way of scraping with milk. "Of that" refers to the fourfold caste system (cāturvarṇya).
"From bathing and drinking" refers to the water from the wheel cast into the center. || 62 ||
Likewise (p.
O Goddess, [one should contemplate] a city or a beautiful woman situated in the midst of this.
Having meditated upon her as blazing, one will truly cause agitation within seven days.

Now he describes the specific types of worship: "O Goddess, even one whose soul is burdened with great sins, if he should perform worship with *śamī* sprouts, *dūrvā* grass, *aśvattha* leaves, or those produced from the *arka* plant... (64)
Within a month, a person destroys the defilement created over seven lifetimes;
by the word "one should worship," it is implied that this refers to this wheel.
Having written it thus, when one worships this yellow-colored wheel, || 65 ||
Facing the eastern direction, one should paralyze all disputants;
likewise,
facing the northern direction, one should worship that which has been drawn with vermilion powder.
When that is done, the world is always under his control.
Likewise,
having drawn a wheel with red ochre, he should worship it while facing the west.
To the question "What would happen thus?", he says:
"And that [mantra] shall become one that attracts all women, brings them under control, and causes agitation.
Likewise:
When one, facing southward, worships that which is black in color; || 68 ||
O Supreme Goddess, in that same manner, when it is worshipped in the intermediate directions, the mantra of whoever [performs it] suffers constant loss. (69)
By the phrase "it is like that," whatever is desired—

such as yellow color and counter-clockwise rotation— is applied; thus, in the northeast (īśakoṇa) corner, the color is yellow, with the result being immobilization (*stambha*), up to the southeast (āgneya), where the color is black, and the result is the eradication of enemies (*śatruccāṭana*).
He states that there is also a difference in its fruit due to the difference in the substrate:
"O Goddess, when written with red ocher on the surface of milk, it brings about subjugation. (70)
Thrown into the midst of cow urine, it causes the eradication of enemies;
the wheel placed within buttermilk is supremely effective for creating enmity. (71)
[He is] situated in the midst of blazing fire, the destroyer of all enemies.
Now he describes specific modes of worship according to the particularity of place, time, and so forth:
"Alternatively, O Goddess of the gods, [worship performed] at a crossroads in a secluded spot... (72).
Near that, O Maheśvarī, one should draw a wheel of great luster with vermilion,
beginning from the outermost edge and proceeding to the center.
One should install the Mātṛkā, beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa', therein.
Whoever worships such a wheel at night according to the sequence of the Kula practice, [attains success]. (74)
At that very moment, O Maheśānī, the practitioner becomes a *khecarī* (a sky-farer).

This means by way of the sequence of the *kulācāra* (the practice of the Kula) and through the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the supreme non-duality (*parādvaya*). Indeed, nothing whatsoever is accomplished for the practitioner without the firm support of identity with the mantra-deity, which consists of the non-duality of the supreme consciousness within one's own self; therefore, it is said:

All of this has been stated here without exception. Furthermore, regarding the claim made by others that whatever external action is performed here cannot become internal without knowledge—namely, the proposition that "only an action performed when based upon the internal *lakṣa* bears fruit externally"—this is an excessive argument brought forward at the wrong time. (p. 91)

Having become intent upon inner realization, it is explained here that worship of the goddesses must be performed with substances appropriate for the *kula*, such as honey, meat, and so forth, using the *kulamantra* lineages within this wheel drawn with vermilion (*sindūra*). Although this contradicts the intended meaning [of the primary injunction], it is irrelevant, as its purpose is already covered by the phrase "one should worship. For in our system, worship consists precisely of these very implements.
And let this matter rest: even when relying on internal definitions, if this meaning is being elaborated upon, it is not right to forget it.
Having worshipped in that manner, O Great Goddess, likewise on a mountain, one [should act] in the same way. || 75 ||
One correctly attains the state of being free from old age and death; there is no doubt about this.
"In that same way" is an extension of everything previously stated.
Likewise, if one should worship on the day of the great elements or even in a cremation ground; || 76 ||
As before, O Goddess of gods, at night the practitioner, with a steady mind, [attains] the sandals, the sword, the vetāla, the siddha, the kravya, and the manaḥśilā.
The collyrium, the opening, the servant, and likewise the yakṣiṇī—whatever collection of accomplishments exists within the three worlds [is attained]. (78)
The best of practitioners should accomplish all of that suddenly;
"suddenly" means without delay. What excellence of variety could there possibly be in the attainment of that? May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Śrīvāmakeśvarīmatavivaraṇa* composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Jayaratha. || 2 ||
Now begins the third chapter:
Having formed the yoni-mudrā— [text missing] — (2.13).

In such passages as these, [the author] establishes a connection with the *pāṭalika* (chapter) by asking how their arrangement might be: Śrī Devī said: "O Blessed One, why did you indicate the mudrās of Tripura but not reveal them?
Tell me, O Śaṅkara, how is their arrangement performed? (1)
Desiring to dispel such a doubt of the Goddess, Śrī Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Goddess, for I shall describe the mudrās that grant the accomplishment of all aims; by performing which Tripurā becomes present before one. (2)
In that regard, concerning the passage:
"Therein, [the rites of] agitation, driving away, attracting...
(1.164), although [the specific method] was not explicitly indicated there—

"Having remembered the Mahātripuramudrā with the mantra of invocation" (1.132). Since invocation was previously indicated [in the preceding verse], he first describes the Trikhaṇḍāmudrā, which must be performed at the very beginning because it precedes the invocation.
Having turned the two hands over, one should make the two thumbs clearly even;
having placed the two index fingers in a curved shape within the ring fingers. (3)
O Maheśvarī, one should place the little fingers in their own positions;
this is the Mahāmudrā consisting of three sections for the rite of summoning Tripurā.

"Having turned the hands" means having placed them in the position of the añjali-gesture. "With the two ring fingers (anāmikā) situated in the svastika-bindu and inserted within"—this is the compound construction. "One should employ [them]" implies that they should be held level. In this way, it is established by the sense that the middle fingers (*madhyamā*) also remain in their own natural state without being altered. || 4 ||
Now he defines the nine [mudrās], beginning with Saṃkṣobhaṇā, in their proper order:

Having placed the two little fingers in the middle of the middle fingers, and having blocked them with the thumbs, one should hold the two index fingers like a staff above the middle fingers, with the ring fingers [placed] upon the middle fingers. (5)
This, however, is the first mudrā, which causes universal agitation;
it consists of the little fingers and the ring fingers [forming a swastika shape], and the thumbs [forming the shape of two staffs].
When the two middle fingers of this very mudrā are straight, [it is as described]. (6)
O Supreme Goddess, these two are performed and are known as the "all-enchanting" (sarvavidrāviṇī).

[The fingers] were previously straight (sarale), but now they have become curved (kuṭile); otherwise, how could the inclusion of the little finger (kaniṣṭhā) take place? Thus it is established that the arrangement is indeed the same as before.
The middle and index fingers [are extended], while the little and ring fingers are held level.
O Supreme Goddess, when [the two hands] are positioned in the middle with forms shaped like hooks,
this is the Ākarṣiṇī mudrā, which effects the attraction of the three worlds.
"Equal" means, as before, by way of having the form of a svastika; "situated in the center" is understood by implication. || 8 ||
Having made the two hands into distinct forms with the two index fingers shaped like hooks,
they should be positioned one below the other in the middle, following the sequence of rotation.
Gradually, O Goddess, by that same method, all the fingers beginning with the little finger and the ring finger should be joined closely together at the tips of the thumbs.
"O Supreme Goddess, this mudrā is known as that which effects all types of possession (*āveśa*).
Having performed [this]—it should be applied elsewhere as well. 'By way of rotation' means by way of the form of a *svastika*.

'By that very sequence' means by the characteristics such as being positioned below in the form of a *svastika*. The word 'etc. (*ādi*) indicates a manner; [the phrase refers to] 'the two thumbs,' by implication."
These two are clear, just as before.
Having placed the two hands facing each other, with the little fingers positioned between the middle fingers.

The two ring fingers (anāmikā) should be straight, with the two index fingers (tarjanī) outside them; there, the two thumbs (aṅguṣṭha) should be shaped like staffs, and the middle fingers (madhyamā) should reach the region of the nails.

This mudrā is named Unmādinī; she causes all women to become moistened. Having performed [this] elsewhere as well, it should be applied everywhere. Regarding the phrase "with the middle finger situated in the middle," the word "middle" (madhya) refers to the middle finger (*madhyamā*); by means of this, since these two are established, the state of being the region of the nails of the two thumbs becomes consistent. [It is] on the younger brother.
On the little finger; "the two index fingers" means they should be straight.
Having placed her pair of ring fingers below in the shape of a hook (aṅkuśa), || 13 ||
One should also apply the two index fingers in that same sequence;
this is the Mahāṅkuśā Vidyā, which accomplishes all desires and aims.

"Downwards" (*adhaḥ*) means facing downwards; for previously, due to its straight form, it was facing upwards. For this very reason, its "hook-like form" (*aṅkuśākṛtitva*) has been mentioned, [meaning] by that same sequence—that is, by way of having the nature of a downward-facing hook—and thus it applies to all six as well.
The fingers should take the form of a goad. || 14 ||
O Great Goddess, having placed the left arm in the right position and the right arm in the left position, one should rotate both hands.
O Goddess, having joined the little fingers and the ring fingers in that same sequence,
both middle fingers should likewise press down upon the two index fingers from above.
O Maheśānī, one should also make the two thumbs straight;
this, O beloved, is the mudrā named Khecarī, the most excellent of all.

"Savyam" means "left," in consideration of the form and action; it should be construed with "saṃparivartya. Otherwise, this manner of binding would not be easily accomplished. "Hastau" (the two hands) implies that the fingers are interlaced behind. "Saṃparivartya" means by way of forming the shape of a *svastika*. "Tena krameṇa" means by that sequence characterized by the *svastika* shape. Regarding the phrase "sarvordhvamapi" (also entirely upwards): [Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding "sarvordhvamapi."]
The word "yuktvā" (having joined) is to be connected [to the preceding]. By the word "api" (also), the straightness of the index finger and the middle finger is also implied. || 17 ||
It demonstrates its very supremacy: "O Great Goddess, she alone is fashioned to take away all splendor;
O Goddess, only when bound by her is one seen as the best of practitioners. (18)
He was like a blazing fire surrounded by all the hosts of yoginīs,
as well as by the multitudes of śākinīs and ḍākinīs, and the throngs of rākiṇīs and lākinīs.
O Supreme Goddess, this [mantra] is meditated upon by the Kākinīs and Hākinīs;
therefore, O Goddess, by knowing this, one becomes dear to the Yoginīs. (20)

And therefore, because Śākinīs and others are meditators upon this [deity] with their entire being, I have bestowed this sequence of commitments (samaya-paripāṭī) upon all the Yoginīs, such that they must show affection even toward a practitioner who knows this. || 20 ||

Therefore, it says: "Hence, this is proclaimed as the *samayamudrā* of them all. Furthermore, its identity with the *samayamudrā* described in the *Śrītantrarāja* is difficult to establish; for this [mudrā]—
And there is the accomplishment of the fifty [letters]! Even there, in the case of being excluded from the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth—enough of this prolixity!
Now, since she possesses such greatness, one might ask: is there any restriction regarding the state of bondage for her, or not? To this he says:
"Whether disciplined or undisciplined, in a pure place or an impure one. (21)
Whether standing or sitting, walking or remaining motionless, whether impure or having become pure, while eating or engaged in sexual intercourse—(he should always remember). || 22 ||
The word "should bind" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. || 22 ||
He has also stated another variety of this very [mudrā]:
"By turning the two middle fingers of the mudrā in succession and assuming the earthly posture (pārthiva-sthānaka), one shall immediately attain the state of moving through the sky (khecaratā). (23)
"Having rotated in sequence" means having positioned them in the shape of a swastika, starting from the little toes.
"The earthly stance" refers to what was stated:
"The left foot is placed doubled over, while the right is held above."
Having placed each other's palms together, one assumes the heroic posture (*vīrāsana*), which is characterized by such valor.

Thus, the intention is that the "hero" (*vīra*) is indeed said to be the "earthly" (*pārthiva*). Those who do not know even the mere coming and going of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), yet explain the "earthly" station (*sthānaka*) by means of the "intoxicated scent" (*mattagandhaka*), are of coarse vision; though they appear not to be of coarse vision, this discussion is inclined toward the mere instruction on the physical configuration of the body. However, the investigation of *vīrya* (vital energy) pertains to all [of them].

Regarding the word "equal" (*samāna*), what is the purpose of such a designation here? Furthermore, since that [state] resides only in the minds of certain great souls, what is the use of this mockery of verbal ostentation?

Moreover, it has already been stated that it is not logical for these [energies] to possess the nature of powers such as *raudrī* based on their specific configurations; this is further explained in the *Śrī Rasamahodadhi*:
When both the prāṇa and apāna are completely restrained and established,
there in that middle is the supreme reality, arising from the state beyond existence and non-existence.
In that regard, one should form the *cita* mudrā in the middle; this is the supreme *khecarī* mudrā.
All other [mudrās] established in all the scriptures are formed by the binding of the hands.

By such statements as these, another *khecarī-mudrā*—possessing a majesty proclaimed in various other scriptures and serving as the very life-force of all *mudrās*—has been described; thus, the laborious efforts of others are misplaced. Enough of this prolixity. || 23 ||
O Dear One, having turned the two hands over so that they clearly take the shape of a half-moon,
one should then simultaneously form a pair of index fingers and thumbs.
One should place the two middle fingers pressed down from below;
likewise, one should join the two ring fingers at the very bottom in a curved position.
This is the seed-seal (*bījamudrā*), which swiftly brings about all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*).

The binding of the *svastika* with the little fingers and middle fingers accomplishes one's purpose. "At the very bottom" means at the base of all four pairs beginning with the index fingers; for this reason, these two [the little and middle fingers] remain almost entirely submerged within.
Having made the two middle fingers curved and positioned above the index fingers. || 26 ||
Likewise, when the ring fingers and little fingers are similarly positioned, all [the fingers] should be joined together and pressed by the thumbs. (27)

This, however, is the first mudrā, known as the *yonimudrā*. Regarding the term "slightly curved" (*kuliṭe*), it means slightly; by implication, the slight curvature of the two index fingers is also established, for otherwise, how could these [middle fingers] be positioned above them? Regarding the term "ring fingers" (*anāmikā*), it refers to those which are downward-facing and curved. Regarding the term "pinky fingers" (*kaniṣṭhike*), it is understood by implication.
"Abiding in the svastika-bond": "in one place" means with density; "the first" means the primary.
And what is the occasion for their application? He says:
"O Maheśānī, these mudrās of Tripurā have been declared by me. (28)
They should be employed at the time of worship according to the sequence;
"according to the sequence" means in the acts of invocation, worship, and dismissal. As it has been said:
"One should subsequently display the mudrās in three ways during the ritual actions of the three times."
Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śrīvāmakeśvarīmatavivaraṇa* composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Jayaratha. || 3 ||
Now begins the fourth chapter.

Without being submerged in the knowledge of the non-duality of supreme consciousness (*parasaṃvidadvaitajñāna*), nothing whatsoever—such as worship, recitation, or mudrās—would exist; thus [ends] the chapter.
Seeking the connection [between the topics], the venerable Goddess said:
"O Blessed One, you have explained everything—the supreme knowledge of the mudrās. Now, please speak of the practice for each individual syllable of the Great Goddess. (1)

O Supreme Lord, [you have described] the power of great gnosis, its pervasiveness, its arising from the locations, and its dissolution within the body, according to the distinction between the gross and the subtle.

"Knowledge" refers to the act of creation, because that [creation] is preceded by knowledge. "Arising from the locus and dissolution" means characterized by emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal; or else, it means from what locus does it arise and where does it become dissolved? || 2 ||

And desiring to provide a comprehensive response to this very point, the illustrious Bhairava said: "In that regard, setting aside the sequence as previously indicated, he begins first by defining the nature of knowledge according to its preeminence:
'Listen, O Goddess, to the Great Knowledge, the supreme which transcends all knowledge.'"
By the mere performance of which one does not sink into the ocean of existence. || 3 ||

That which is supreme, full, and for that very reason great and unsurpassed— the pair consisting of both Śakti and the Possessor of Śakti (Śaktimat) in a state of equalized flavor— is the highest knowledge because it illuminates all manifestations of knowledge belonging to the nature of Śiva, Śakti, and the individual soul;
such [knowledge] exists by virtue of possessing an excellence of skill in inquiry.

(100) While [the Self] is shining forth, listen attentively and grasp this: by the mere act of reflecting upon it, this entire delusion consisting of non-recognition (akhyāti) shall be specifically pacified for everyone. || 3 ||
He says that very thing:

"O Dear One, Tripurā is the supreme primordial Śakti; from the beginning of birth, she is the Mātṛkā who brings about the creation of the three worlds through the division of the gross and the subtle. (4)

She whose nature consists of the entire aggregate of principles swallowed up [by her], who is "from the beginning" according to the manner previously stated, [arising] from Paramaśiva—who is primordially established as a single mass of consciousness and bliss—is the Supreme [Power].

Because she is inherent in him, she is the supreme collection of all powers, whose essential nature is non-differentiation; for this very reason, because she cannot be designated by fixed names, she is the Inexplicable (Anākhyā).

Precisely because she is spontaneously established (*sahajasiddha*), she is primordial; for this very reason, since no other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) arise, she consists of the wonder of the supreme "I-consciousness" (*parāhaṃcamatkāra*), is of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and though one, her true essence is the capacity to manifest thousands of various appearances.
By her own majesty alone, with the desire to overflow outwardly, she exists in the supreme state (*paradaśā*) as the nature of will, knowledge, and action, and in the subtle state (*sūkṣmadaśā*)...
By virtue of her characteristics as Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī, and in her gross state as the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa, she is divided into three;
thus, because she possesses the nature of the three cities—those abodes which, according to the aforementioned process, fulfill the functions of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal—she is Tripurā.
She is the Mātṛkā, the Mother, who manifests during the origination of the triple world consisting of transcendence, immanence, and worldly existence; and furthermore:
The meaning is that she became designated by the word *ambikā*, having manifested as such.

Now, one might object: "If there exists only the one, peaceful, supreme Brahman, and the phenomenal world (prapañca) is produced by ignorance (avidyā), what is the purpose of accepting such a [dualistic] position?
Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"But when that [ignorance] has undergone transformation, no other [reality] whatsoever is admitted. (5)

Regarding the word *turyārthe*: for when that very power (*śakti*) exists, nothing else—be it conceived as having the nature of protection or fulfillment—is desired; the meaning is that even the Supreme Brahman would not be established in this way. Here, there is no disagreement that pure light alone is reality (*tattva*); moreover, it is logical that it must possess self-reflective awareness (*savimarśa*). Otherwise, however—
Even though it manifests those respective objects, there would be no distinction between this [consciousness] and inert things such as a crystal; as they say:

"They know that the essential nature of manifestation is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); otherwise, even if light is colored by an object, it is like an inert thing such as a crystal" (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.5.11).

Thus, this is not some excellence of its own nature (*svarūpa*), but rather its very nature is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), which, in its state of manifestation, does not depend on the assistance of another. And that very [nature], when disregarding external objects, latent impressions (*vāsanā*), or ignorance (*avidyā*), is called "sovereignty" (*svātantrya*)— namely, the capacity for the simultaneous emergence of thousands of various appearances— by means of which all of this is established.

For if there were a difference between ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth [and Brahman], the principle that "Brahman is one" would be lost; yet if there were no difference, then everything would be merely Brahman, and thus all [distinctions] would be sublated.
Therefore, Brahman alone, whose nature is absolute sovereignty (*svātantrya*), is everything. || 5 ||
He says that there is no way [to act] without power;
for indeed, one who is devoid of power is not able to do anything.
Therefore, he says that power must necessarily be accepted.
But when, O Supreme Goddess, he becomes capable and endowed with power, || 6 ||
The word "tadā" (then) is to be supplied from the preceding context; "bhavet" (it would be) refers to the supreme light. || 6 ||
Furthermore, in Śiva, who is subtle, there exists neither name nor abode without Śakti.
"In the subtle" means that which is unknowable because it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). For the supreme light, which is the nature of ultimate bliss, is indeed self-luminous.

Precisely because it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), it is never capable of being made manifest by another; thus, for this [Self], there exists neither determinate (*savikalpaka*) nor indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition as its locus (p. 102), since its nature is solely that of the knower (*pramātṛ*). The meaning is that it cannot become an object of knowledge (*prameya*). And since it is unknowable, it is impossible to conceive of it as being taught or meditated upon; therefore, the Self is established.

"Because of the elaborate scriptural injunctions such as 'it must be known, it must be reflected upon, and it must be meditated upon,' one should either remain silent or accept the empowered (śākta) form; for although this [Self] is in reality of the singular nature of pure subjectivity (paramātmaika-rūpa), by its own sovereignty, without ever falling away from that very nature, it brings its own form into the state of being an object of knowledge (prameyatām āpādayati) for the sake of establishing its capacity to be taught and so forth."
All this worldly and transcendental activity would be established; as they say:
"But by its own sovereignty, its innate nature does not deviate from the nature of the cognizer, for the sake of establishing the ultimate reality of instruction and that immersion."
"Bringing about the state of being an object of awakening, the Lord is clearly manifested.
(Tantrāloka 12.11) Thus it is said.

Thus, even though that supreme light has become an object of knowledge, it is power alone that performs all purposeful action; so he says: "O Great Goddess, even when known, there is no action whatsoever that brings happiness. (7)
For, in relation to the Supreme Light, nothing whatsoever exists apart from it that could manifest; thus, everything is indeed the Light itself.

In such a state, what kind of action could possibly bring benefit to the practitioner? Therefore, one must strive for the very entry into the state of Śakti, by which the arising of all accomplishments (siddhis), such as omniscience and the rest, may occur. As they say:
But in the first *tuṭi*, everything has everywhere attained oneness in fullness;
what object of knowledge or what effect could there be therein that is subject to designation?

Therefore, the wise seek out that primordial Goddess Pratibhā, who is the first digit of the manifestation of differentiation, for the sake of attaining omniscience and other perfections. (Tantrāloka 10.210) || 7 ||
(p. 103) For this very reason, even the status of being an object of meditation (*dhyeyatā*) is not appropriate here; thus he says:
"But at the time of relying upon meditation, there is neither delight, nor intellect, nor stability.

For meditation (*dhyāna*) is a state of identity (*aikātmya*) fixed upon a specific object of meditation, and that is characterized primarily by non-duality (*abheda*). Indeed, when [the subject and object] are distinct...
A person becomes attached to an object, and because of his stability therein, a progressively superior knowledge regarding that object arises.
However, this cannot be the case here, because [the ultimate state] consists of a single mass of perfect light, wherein the relationship between the meditator and the meditated ceases to exist;
therefore, in our system, it must be accepted that the Power consisting of the wonder of the supreme self-reflection (*parāhaṃparāmarśa*) alone is the locus of rest. This very [Power]...

In various places throughout [the scriptures], she is awakened by such terms as *spanda* (vibration), *sphurattā* (manifestation), *sāra* (essence), *ūrmī* (wave), *hṛdaya* (heart), *sadbhāva* (true being), and *saṃkarṣiṇī*, as well as by the word *Tripurā* and others.

Thus, she herself, existing in identity with the supreme subject, is the manifestor of the creation, maintenance, dissolution, and so forth, of the entire universe consisting of the signified and the signifier; as it is said:
"Having entered within the supreme path, she exists in the form of a subtle nature. (8)
Vāmā, having swallowed the entirety of the seeds and so forth, has become the state of the sprout;
from that, Śikhā becomes Jyeṣṭhā, having assumed the form of a triangle (śṛṅgāṭa).

O Supreme Goddess, Raudrī is the one whose form is the devouring of the universe. Because she has entered into the interior of the supreme path, she is of the singular nature of the supreme subject; because her essential nature consists of a subtle form, she is unknowable (*avedyā*) precisely because she is inherent in that [supreme subject]. Being primordial (*ādyā*), she abides in her own very nature, having assimilated the entire causal manifold (*kāraṇaprapañca*) into her own self.

Moreover, that supreme power (parā śakti), desiring to manifest externally through the majesty of her own sovereignty and being oriented toward the expansion of the universe, has attained the state of a sprout;
assuming the form of Kuṇḍalinī, she vomits forth the entire swallowed world as Vāmā, and thereafter, with the desire to cause it to arise.

The Śikhā, presiding over the form of a distinct line that constitutes the entire staff (daṇḍa) of the paths extending as far as the Fire of Time (kālāgni), is Jyeṣṭhā; furthermore, when she desires to withdraw the universe by means of the process of uncoiling, she manifests the form of a triangle (śṛṅgāṭa) consisting of the equilibrium of the triad of powers beginning with Will (icchā), and is thus called Raudrī.

The meaning is that she illumines the primordial phoneme (A), which is the animator of all letters and the triad of abodes (the three worlds) whose creation, maintenance, and withdrawal are inscribed upon the wall of her own self. As it has been said:
"But above is situated the creation, which rejoices in supreme bliss."
The supreme digit of the bindu rains down a shower of nectar.
Below, he should be known as the performer of dissolution, the great fire who brings about the end;
he is difficult to withstand, a treasury of lights, endowed with a series of terrible flames.
Between those two is the supreme splendor, beautiful with the bliss of both;
that is to be known as the descent, Śiva, who pervades both.
The moon and fire are mutually interpenetrated within the *iṣṭibha* asterism;
one should know that the moon is creation, while fire is said to be dissolution.
"O Supreme Goddess, the Sun is said to be the descent situated in the center."
It is not only as the nature of the signifier that she manifests the universe, but also as the nature of the signified; thus he says:
"In this way, that supreme power is indeed one, the Supreme Goddess. (10)
The goddess Tripurā is threefold, having the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa;
she consists of the power of knowledge, the power of action, and the power of will, O beloved. (11)
She creates the three worlds— [the rest of the sentence is omitted]—

meaning that she consists of the triad of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, and so forth. This very point is reinforced by the passage beginning with "she who has the forms of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa," and even so, she remains never separate from her supreme nature which is beyond all designation.

It has been stated [in the previous verse] that she is "Supreme," "One," "the Supreme Goddess," and "Divine. "The three worlds" refers to the forms of existence, non-existence, and so forth. "She creates" means that, according to the analogy of a city in a mirror, although she does not deviate from her own essential nature, she manifests them as if they were distinct.
For this very reason, he states that her name is used here in its etymological sense.

"— — — — — — because of this, she is celebrated as Tripurā. 'Because of this' means because of the bringing together (*saṃsarga*) of the three cities; thus, the meaning is that she is called Tripurā because she brings the three cities together. It should not, however, be explained as 'she who precedes (*pūrvabhāvinī*) the three [powers], namely Śakti, Vyāpinī, and Samanā.'"

Because of the prohibition of a genitive *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound with indeclinables (*avyaya*) by the rule *pūraṇaguṇasuhitārthasadavyayatavyasamānādhikaraṇena* (Pāṇini 2.2.11), and because even in that context the word *purā*— by virtue of its technical definition (*nipātana*)— denotes only place or time and cannot possibly denote a substance (*dravya*), it cannot be referred to [in the compound]. Therefore, enough with this consideration of the prattle of a child!
Thus, in order to describe its dissolution and emergence even within [the central channel], he says: "When she, whose form is crooked, flashes forth from the seat of the śṛṅgāṭa... (12).
Having pierced the solar disc of Śiva and melting the lunar disc,
she is delighted by the intoxication of the flowing nectar arising therefrom.
A woman of noble family, having abandoned her own family, goes to another man who is devoid of auspicious marks, lacking virtues, and bereft of noble lineage and beauty.
Indeed, when this very Supreme Śakti, who rests upon the state of vital breath (prāṇa) and supports the abode of the Kula,

issues forth from the seat of the triangle (śṛṅgāṭapīṭha)— which is designated by such terms as "source of emanation" (prasara-ākara) and is the support of birth— she assumes a curved form, appearing as the vowel-less digit of the letter *ha*.
Because she brings about the attainment of the state of Śiva, she pierces the solar orb of *prāṇa* and dissolves even the lunar orb of *apāna*.
Having struck the two channels characterized as right and left— which function according to their own inherent nature— she,
being delighted by the intoxicating bliss arising from that very striking, which consists primarily of a flow of nectar easily obtained through the constant central channel, [attains her goal].

When [the breath], by the mere process of carrying the *udāna*, rises upward and expands clearly in form according to the analogy of a snake struck by a staff, then it leaves behind the *kula*—the body—and abides in the supreme, full *akula* state; for this very reason, it is without defining marks (*nirlakṣaṇa*), because it is excluded from those qualities that grasp a specific, fixed form, and thus it possesses an indefinite shape. Therefore, by means of *kula*...

It means that [the yogi] attains identity with that Supreme Person (puruṣa), the subject (pramātā), who is devoid of body, its attributes, and form, whose nature is free from obscuration, and for that very reason is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa). || 14 ||
And it is not in this very state that she finds her rest; thus he says:
"Then, having wandered through the world again in her own free form, she, being satisfied by that movement, becomes once more solitary. (15)

She rejoices— [in the state of] — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — | Again, from that supreme state of the form of space (*parākāśa*), which is *akula*, she who is of the nature of absolute freedom (*svacchanda*), shining forth spontaneously by her own essence alone according to the sequence of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), pervades the world characterized as *kula* and, through that movement consisting of emanation, [proceeds].

Although she partakes in the satisfaction born from the experience of the *kulabhūmi* (the plane of the Kula), she nevertheless, by her own free will and through the upward-moving nature of the process of withdrawal (*saṃhārakrama*), leaves behind the *kulabhūmi* and plunges into the sky of *Alaka*. Standing alone, assuming a form that transcends the universe, she delights right there and attains a state of aesthetic identity (*sāmarasya*) with Paramaśiva.

The meaning is this: having abandoned the non-family (*akula*) within the family (*kula*), and the family within the sphere of the non-family (*akulagocara*), she— by means of this vision, through the state of constant flux (*ājavañjavībhāva*) at every moment, by resorting to the sequence of emission and reabsorption (*sṛṣṭisaṃhārakrama*),
and by consisting solely of dissolution and emergence (*layodayamayata*)— shines forth, yet does not attain manifestation through any fixed form whatsoever.

Furthermore, since the conduct of a courtesan is also hinted at here, there is the suggestion (dhvani) of the figure of speech *upamā* (simile). She too, in the end, having exhausted her life as a courtesan, remains alone; though she is like an ascetic woman (*tapasvinī*), she still enjoys herself in secret. Let it be that even a woman of noble family (*kulayopit*) is of such a nature—thus the *virodha* (contradiction) is also suggested—but enough of this irrelevant matter.

Thus, although her essential nature is not perceived even through causes and the like, she, manifesting externally solely by virtue of her own sovereignty, attains a state of being accessible to all once she has reached manifestation through a determined form. Thus he says:
"This very Tripurā, though unmanifest, has attained manifestation."
She is designated as the three principles and consists of the three powers of the phonemes.

The meaning of the sentence is this: although this Supreme Power (parā-śakti) is thus unmanifest, having attained manifestation through the nature of the triad of principles, phonemes, and powers, she is called the venerable Tripurā, who is to be worshipped in our system. || 16 ||
He explains this very point by dividing it:

Vāgīśvarī is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), consisting of the *vāgbhava* syllable and having the form of liberation; Kāmarājā is the digit of desire (*kāma-kalā*), consisting of the *kāmarāja* syllable and having the nature of action (*kriyā*). (17)

The supreme power (*parā śakti*) is the seed-syllable of Power (*śaktibīja*), which is indeed Will (*icchā*) in the form of poison. Here, there is a triad of principles (*tattva*)—namely Knowledge, Action, and Will—which correspond respectively to the three seed-syllables of Speech (*vāgbhava*), Passion (*kāmarāja*), and Power (*śaktibīja*). Furthermore, this corresponds to the syllables and the powers of Knowledge, Action, and Will, in accordance with the respective nature of the seed-syllables beginning with *vāgbhava*.
Three qualifying attributes have been employed: "Vāgīśvarī," "Kāmakalā," and "Parā Śakti."
Thus, by means of this sequence of transmission, she who is fully known accomplishes the supreme goal of human existence;
so it is said: "In this way, O Goddess, the three-syllabled Mahātripurasundarī [is the supreme reality]. (18)
"Known through tradition as the liberator from the bonds of existence, it not only does so, but reveals various supernatural powers (siddhis) as well; thus he says:
'When remembered, it removes sins; when recited, it destroys death. (19)
When worshipped, she destroys suffering, poverty, disease, and misfortune;
when offered oblations, she pacifies the flood of obstacles; and when meditated upon, she accomplishes all goals.
And by this, its state of possessing great power has been stated. || 20 ||
Having thus resolved five questions in a single stroke, he proceeds to resolve the remaining sixth as well:
"O Mistress of the Gods, hear now the practice of the three seed-syllables of this [goddess]."
He says that very thing:
"Clad in white garments, situated in the midst of white garments. (21)
A man devoted to celibacy should worship with white flowers and with white food offerings such as curd, milk, boiled rice, and so forth. (22)
In the absence of this,
even by means of those purified by intention (*saṃkalpa*)—
[the rest of the verse follows]— he states another alternative (*pakṣāntara*) in that regard as well.
"— according to desire, according to what one may obtain;
that is to say, according to wish, according to acquisition."
Having thus worshipped, O Supreme Goddess, one should meditate upon the supreme Vāgīśvarī.
Manifesting in the form of a seed-syllable, awakening consciousness and bliss, one should pierce the knot of Brahmā at the tip of the tongue, [visualizing it] in the form of a lamp. (24)
Thus, following the worship,

the practitioner should know that the *kula* is below the penis, while that which is designated as "poison" (*viṣa*) is in the middle; at the base, however, it is called *śākta*, which, through awakening, sets [the flow] in motion.
And then, regarding the passage "the one designated as fire...

and so forth—here, having extracted the term *anaṅga* (which is expressed by the word *meḍhra*), which is a synonym for *kāmarāja*, [one considers] the designation of that which is called "fire" as being below the *janmādhāra* and the *mūla*; [this occurs] when the *kula* is indicated as being above.
The Brahma-knot is said to be situated between the fire and the poison;
one who has mastered it becomes a poet who knows all subjects and all sciences.

By saying this, [one should contemplate] the Supreme Central Power (madhya-śakti) which, having burst asunder with particular firmness and entirely— not as something partial— the Brahma-knot (brahma-granthi), that specific power-base (śākta-mādhāra-viśeṣa) situated at the root of the birth-base (janmādhāra) between the two bases of fire and poison; which, by its very nature, awakens consciousness and bliss, and, through that awakening, sets [the yogin] in motion, being of the nature of a seed (bīja-rūpā).
"Vāgīśvarī is Vāgīśvarī; she is the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), whose form is the seed-syllable Vāgbhava.

By this statement, [one should contemplate her] as having an essential nature inseparable from the emerging Vāgbhava, which is the very expansion of the power of knowledge; likewise, she is in the form of a lamp upon the tip of the tongue.
The meaning is that one should meditate upon her as blazing and contemplate her with one-pointed concentration. The reading "ito 'naṅgapadāvadhi" (up to the station of Anaṅga) is a corruption;

for this very purpose is already attained by the piercing of the *brahmagranthi* (the knot of Brahmā). Therefore, the statement beginning with "having pierced the knot of consciousness in the ground of the heart by means of the citi of the nature of Nāda, [she goes] upwards," etc., is also not well-said.
To the question, "What would happen to such a person? he says:
"One whose heart is ruined, who is vulgar, foolish, and a great sinner—even one who is deceitful and unable to speak even a single word clearly—[would be ruined]. (25)
Though he be dull-witted, mute, of poor intellect, lacking wisdom, or even one whose mind is lost, he becomes eloquent, like a second Vācaspati. (26)

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: even one who is of such a nature, if he should contemplate [this], he too becomes eloquent. "Mute" means one whose faculty of speech has been stolen away. "Of dull intellect" means one with a sinful mind. "One whose wisdom is gone" means one who lacks innate intelligence from the very beginning. "One whose intellect is lost" means one whose wisdom, though it had arisen, has been destroyed by the employment of deceitful arts and the like. (26)
He further describes his own status as a second Vācaspati:

"The conqueror of the assembly of true scholars, possessing unimpeded brilliance, he is a knower of the essence of the six systems of logic, the meaning of words and sentences, and the ornaments of speech. (27)
One should compare [them] to rows of waves in the ocean tossed by the wind;
"to equal things" means, by implication, to verbal elaborations.
Likewise, [it is characterized] by extremely delicate and expansive styles and ornaments. || 28 ||
O Goddess, by means of the composition of verses, one becomes a creator of mahākāvyas;
moreover, one becomes a master who has reached the further shore of knowledge regarding the Vedas, Vedānta, the Siddhāntas, and the Vedāṅgas. (29)
He was a knower of the statements of the Mīmāṃsā and Smṛti, as well as astronomy, history, and other sciences;
he was a knower of many mantras from the Purāṇas, the Rasas, the Vādas, and the Gāruḍa tradition.
He was a knower of the true meaning of the Pātāla-śāstras, the sciences, and the tantras concerning elemental beings;
he was highly skilled in many arts, such as various types of painting and other crafts. || 31 ||
(111) His speech is refined by the noble words of the Great Prophecy; he knows all languages and sounds, and is skilled in all forms of writing. || 32 ||
O Goddess, one who is renowned for various weapons, sciences, arts, and so forth, as well as the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, and who knows all branches of learning, becomes omniscient. (33)
In the statement "an omniscient one is born," everything such as being a master of the Vedas and so forth is the cause.
Having thus concluded the section on Vāgbhava, he introduces Kāmarāja:
"O Maheśvarī, when she takes the form of Kāmakalā within the range of the sprout of passion, she possesses the luster of the rays of the young, reddish sun. (34)
Having the form of a flickering lamp-flame, raining down a stream of bindus,
she has swallowed up the life-force of the entire expanse of the worlds.
Having destroyed the ground of egoity by treading upon the greatness of the Great Sound (Mahāsva),
she then gradually emerges, shining forth even from the limit of the "Bodyless" (Anaṅga).

O Goddess of the Gods, from each part of the body up to the extremities of the limbs, she possesses both natures; therefore, she becomes [the source] for those who pride themselves on every kind of amorous charm.
O Goddess, for those possessed of passion, she is the accomplisher who surpasses even Madana in her power to obstruct.
Indeed, in this world, when the central energy (madhya-śakti) itself, arising from the support of the vital breath (vijā-dhāra) as the first vibration, manifests in the form of the Kāmakalā;
That Kāma, who is headless and whose abode is the heart of the beloved woman—
thus described as being composed of the vowel-less *ha* and the *kalā*— shines forth in a red form like the newly risen sun,
like the bimba fruit, and like the flame of a lamp; and there, somewhere, she incessantly rains down a torrential shower of distress.

One should meditate upon the Mind-born (Kāmadeva) in the form of a drop (*bindu*), residing right there within the womb of any woman who is the object of one's desire— his birthplace being the cause of his manifestation— and whose life-force and ego have been rendered helpless by the mere pervasion of his own majesty from afar. One should contemplate him as having a curved form situated precisely therein.
Resembling the fresh dawn, it was crowded with many rays of light.
Above that is a subtle crest, the power of desire, possessed of great splendor.

By such statements as these, the sprout— which consists of the *bindu* and the crest (*śikhā*) and is situated near the uvula (*ghaṇṭikā*)— is contemplated for some time within the womb of women in its forward range, by means of the method of the Tantra of "looking toward the future" (*anāgatāvekṣaṇatantra*). (4.42)

Thus, with reference to the subsequent statement, the [energy] is considered sequentially as both the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhaka*), becoming dual-natured through the mutual blending of their vital powers (*prāṇa-śakti*) in a state of equalized flavor (*samarasita*). From there, from the very tip of the sprout at the limit of the bodiless one (*anaṅga*,
i.e., Madana), it proceeds intensely toward the limit of the bodiless *akula* space— that is, up to the *dvādaśānta*— within the body of the goal itself.

"Recitation (japa) should be performed equal to one's vital breath"— according to this principle, [the mantra] which shines forth as inseparable from the utterance of Kāmarāja, when contemplated repeatedly, [attains its goal]. For this reason— namely, from such contemplation— it does not merely carry the attachment of other passionate people who, for that very reason, pride themselves on the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), but rather...

The collective meaning is that because he generates such dejection as "We too are exactly like those who are manifestly amorous—why do we not become so?", he becomes an obstacle; yet, being superior to Madana, he is also a means of accomplishment.
For any woman who comes within the range of his vision— whether she be a goddess or even an asura— (38) [is overcome by him].
Whether she be a Vidyādharī, a Kinnarī, or the wife of a Yakṣa or Nāga, or the daughter of an exceedingly fierce king, or a Siddhakanyā— (39)
Their minds were scorched by passion, making them difficult to look upon due to the blazing circles [of light];
drenched, with their limbs trembling, they were bewildered and overwhelmed by intoxication.
O beloved, those who have offered their entire being become subject to one's will.
Regarding this very point, he states another perspective:
"She is like the moon reflected in rippling water, and as red as the rays of the rising sun. (41)
When meditated upon within the womb of women, she causes agitation at that very moment.

"Meditated upon" means, by implication, the central power (madhyaśakti) in the form of the *kāmakalā*. Although it resembles the moon reflected in moving water, its specific distinction is the redness of the rays of the rising sun; for coolness is indeed its natural quality.
Likewise, when that very same one, possessing the luster of the color of vermilion, is meditated upon in the heart; || 42 ||
She is remembered as the one who causes delusion, intoxication, possession, and the attraction of the mind;
"she herself" refers to the aforementioned form of the Central Power (*madhyaśakti*), [located] "in the heart," which, by implication, refers to that of women.
Or else, applied to the head, it rains down drops of blood. || 43 ||
Through the application of *dhāraṇā*, he renders the world powerless.
Where "drops of blood" (*raktabindūn*) should be said, the reading "drops of blood" (*raktabindavaḥ*) is an archaic (*aiśa*) form. Through the application of *dhāraṇā* (p.
114), that Kāma, though headless, has his abode in the hearts of women.
Then, with that [consciousness] mounted upon the eyes, one should withdraw the gaze of power.
By the reasoning stated in such passages, the meaning is that [the soul] acts through the channels of the sense organs, such as the eyes, in the form of entering another's body and so forth.

Right here, because it is a secret and its meaning is concealed, he makes a formal promise to state another ritual application that is difficult to find on earth: "Now I shall fully explain another ritual application, rare upon the earth. (44)
By the mere knowledge of which the practitioner becomes intoxicated;
"difficult to obtain" means it is impossible to attain in such a way.
He says that very thing:
Abiding in desire, situated in the midst of desire, and enclosed within the hollow of the belly of desire. || 45 ||
One should accomplish desire through desire; one should cast desire into desires. Having fulfilled what is desired by means of desire, one who abides in desire may agitate the world.
In this context, indeed, the practitioner (*sādhaka*), desiring the awakening of the initial vibration of power (*śākta-parispanda*) through desire, remains "situated in desire" (*kāmastha*)—
that is, abiding within the womb (*janmādhāra*), the place of its arising; there, having fixed his continuous contemplation by means of the dissolution of all other objects of knowledge,
he [perceives] that which resides in the center of desire, namely, in the middle of the source (*yoni*).
"— within the range of the sprout of passion" (2.34).

According to such statements, [the syllable] consists of the vowel-less *hakalā*, which is the nature of the central power of breath (*madhyaprāṇaśakti*). It is "desired" (*kāmita*) by *kāma*, that is, the seed-syllable *kāmarāja*, because its essential form is inseparable from its utterance; it is "loved" (*kānta*), being encapsulated within the womb of desire.
As for the seventeenth digit (*kalā*) of the head of *Ka*, it has the form of nectar (*amṛta*).

In the belly of that *amā* whose nature has been thus described—specifically at the location of the *ghaṇṭikā*, which is the *tālu-granthi* (palate-knot) because it is difficult to pierce—the breath is folded and encapsulated;

being restrained right there, it abides in *kāma*. It is situated in *ke* (the head), remaining there as it is naturally inclined to go to the *dvādaśānta* (the limit of twelve finger-breadths) and having reached that point, one should certainly accomplish *kāma*, bringing it to the state of being ready for success (*siddhi*).

Then, by means of that [power] mounted upon the eyes, one should withdraw the gaze of power (*śakti-dṛṣṭi*) from those things designated by that term— which are characterized by the movement of entering and exiting among objects of desire—

according to the principle beginning with "one should withdraw the gaze of power," and project it into the eyes and other senses of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), such that it has emerged from one's own two eyes and entered into the eyes of the object to be accomplished.

One should meditate on [the light] emerging from the eyes of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and entering into one's own eyes; thus, by means of the process of the swing-mechanism (*dolāyantra*), the repeated coming and going should not only affect a specific, fixed object to be accomplished, but should agitate the entire world— the cycle of living beings as they are born— by way of turning toward oneself, preceded by the rejection of rest within one's own self.

The meaning is that one should lead [the opponent] into a state of helplessness. This has been explained many times by others through various word-plays and difficult constructions as being the ultimate sense of "explaining words by means of other words. Therefore, in this and other instances, those who possess intelligence and inward knowledge alone are the authority. And so, the former teachers have also said:

Indeed, from the time of Āśrī Dīpakanātha until now, commentaries on this [work] have been composed by countless others, and will continue to be composed by other eminent teachers according to the propriety of their own individual inclinations.
O Goddess, I am one who has taken refuge in the dust of your lotus feet; [I shall compose this work] beginning with the words "O Kāmasthā... and so forth.
Who is that fortunate person who truly understands the meaning of that verse worth ten thousand pieces of gold?

When the syllable *hrīṃ*, which is the form of the seat for the Primordial Desire (*Ādikāma*), has been spoken, O Goddess of Gods, one should place the mantra of the target (*sādhya-aṇu*) upon its head;
by this statement, [the deity] remains present merely through the placement of the letters of the name upon that head.
O Goddess, O sinless one, from the syllables *aṃ-ya-ā* belonging to those who dwell in the third station, Manmatha is born through their conjunction.

Thus, situated in the middle of the second Kāma, designated by the word *manmatha*— namely, the syllable *klīm*— is the letter preceded by *am*, which is written between the letters *ka* and *la*, and likewise possesses the number of elements (*bhūta*).
O Goddess, from the union of these two, Kandarpa is born.
