Thus, having encased and encapsulated [the syllable] within the womb— the interior— by means of the third *kāma*, denoted by the word *kandarpa*, which consists of two *e*-vowels and exists in the form of a hexagon;
and having done so within the six corners produced by the aforementioned *kāma* known as *kandarpa* among the objects of desire (*kāmeṣu*).
The pair of syllables beginning with *kṣa* arises from *rasa*; this is Makaradhvaja.

The meaning is that one should write the fourth *kāma*, the syllable *blaṃ*, as presented by Makaradhvaja. This quartet of *kāmas* also arises when preceded by *ha-tha-la-u*, and thus the Mind-born (Manobhava) is produced.

Thus, one should accomplish [the goal] by means of the fifth *kāma*, known as *manobhava* (mind-born), which consists of the syllable *strīṃ*; the meaning is that one should accomplish it by casting [it] within the belly. This is how this perfected *yantra* is accomplished by means of the first *kāma*, the syllable *hrīṃ*.
Then, one should again provide the support for the wheel with another *kāma*.

Thus, because it serves as the substratum according to the sacred scripture (*śruti*), by wearing [the *khaṭvāṅga*] upon the head as if it were a king, one makes the desired object beloved; and when these objects of desire are certainly worn on the crest-lock (*śikhā*) and other parts, one remains bowed down in devotion amidst these desires, or rather,
in the place where the power of desire (*kāma-śakti*) arises.

(117) The practitioner, remaining attentive while situated in the Śākta Ādhāra located at the base of the penis, should not only certainly agitate that [seed] alone, but even the entire universe; thus, this Yantra is composed of the five Kāmas. And here is the extraction [of the mantra]: *ha* precedes *kṣa*, *ra* for *la*, *ī* for the vowel *u*, and *aṃ* for the vowel *aḥ*; thus, *hrīṃ*. [The extraction] of the syllable *aṃ*...

From its own city [the letter *ka*], the third position is the letter *la*; with the vowel *ā*, it becomes *ī*, thus forming *klīṃ*. For it is said: "That supreme seed-syllable which stands at the number of Rudra (eleven) should be made the head of all five desires."

Thus: from the letter *u*, the eleventh seed-syllable (*aṃ*) is established according to the number of Rudras; before the letter *aṃ* is the fifth, having the number of elements (*e*); and likewise after the letter *ṛ* is the one with the number of elements (*e*). "From these two" refers to the two *e*s. For this very reason it has been said:
"One should make the Temple of Kandarpa (Kandarpamandira) divided into two parts, O Pārvatī.
Thus, from the letter *kṣa*, the sixth syllable arising from the *rasa* (taste) group is *va*; from *ha* comes *la*, thus *blaṃ*. From *ha* comes the one situated before it, *sa*;
from *tha* comes *ta*; from *la* comes *ra*; from the vowel *u* comes *i*; thus *strīṃ*. In this way, there are five *kāmas*. And it is said in this regard:
That which is called Māyā, situated within Kāmarāja and encircled by the Kula-bīja,
is enclosed by that very same [bīja] which assumes the form of a hexagon.
One should pierce it with the arrow of torment from Kāma situated in its corner;
one should cast that [mantra] ending with the word *strī-arṇa-kāma*, and by means of the first [syllable], one should effect the desired object.
Thus, one who is established in power may either meditate upon or even wear this fivefold seed-syllable mantra accompanied by the goad, and thereby agitate the world.

Thus [it is said]. And here is the specific distinction: that in the fourth *kāma* (triangle), there is another vowel and the external seed-syllable *aṅkuśa* (hook); with this very intention, the venerable Kalyāṇavarman stated that one should place the syllable *blūṃ* in the middle of the six corners (*koṇa*), and outside of that, the eight syllables *kroṃ* in the eight directions.

(p. 118) This has been explained. Thus, you—who do not know how to compose even a single faultless word or meaning—have somehow seized and taken away from your kinsmen the entire collection of ancillary materials, such as corroborative evidence and the like, which were gathered by your great-great-grandfather and were capable of making those various points understood, having done so through forceful deception or, at the very least, by theft.

We understand that [the author] has said, "Relying on what skill [could we hope to succeed]? and will say later, "Salutations to me, the fortunate one," and so forth—[implying]: "Relying on what skill could we, who have revealed the true nature of the tradition even in these specific commentaries (vyākhyāviśeṣa)—whether in this chapter alone or elsewhere—despite their being composed by others and surpassing other commentators, be encouraged by those possessing an abundance of creative intuition? Or rather, [this refers to] those who speak according to their own whims (*svacchandābhidhāyin*).
What indeed could serve as the basis for a limit when defining that [infinite]? As they say:

"For rivers whose nature is to follow their breaches and which are unpleasant to touch due to the vomiting of dullness, the ocean is the limit; but for those of base speech, there is no limit at all."
Thus [ends the section]. || 46 ||
Having thus concluded the section on Kāmarāja, he speaks in order to also explain the practice of the Śakti-bīja:

"One should contemplate within the body the form of the Śakti-bīja, from the limit of emanation up to the limit of reabsorption—that is, throughout the entire process of emanation and reabsorption. (47)
In this practice, the adept, within his own body, perceives the central power (*madhyaśakti*)— whose essential nature is inseparable from the emerging seed-syllable of Power—
as flowing forth from the limit of withdrawal (*saṃhṛti*), beginning from the *dvādaśānta* and extending down to the heart by way of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*).
Then, having turned back again, he perceives it as returning from the heart— the site of the arising of that emanation— to the *dvādaśānta* itself, which is the site of withdrawal.

The meaning is that one should contemplate and connect [the mind] with it by going back and forth repeatedly, in every direction and on all sides, until it shines forth from within the object. || 47 ||
(119) He says what will happen for him by reflecting in this way:
"O Goddess of the Gods, because of this he becomes like another Vainateya;
merely by the sight of snakes, he causes them to be paralyzed. (48)
He is like a steady rain-cloud pouring down a shower of nectar for the right name;
he is the destroyer of the artificial poison known as doubt and of all secondary poisons. || 49 ||
Likewise,
surrounded by hosts of malignant diseases, seizing spirits, and many *ḍākinīs* in female form,
along with floods of *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*, he appeared as if he had three eyes. (50)

Regarding what has been explained by others in this treatise on the practice of the three seeds (*bīja*), even though it is being superimposed upon our words, it is merely a cause for shame, utterly useless, and results only in an expansion of the text; therefore, those with discernment should not be envious of us as to why we have not repeated that [explanation] and refuted it. Furthermore, concerning the three *piṇḍas* therein...
Thus, this practice of the three seeds has been taught here according to its divisions;
herein, the extraction of the *piṇḍa* (syllabic cluster) as it occurs spontaneously has been declared by the Lord.

Because they have failed to discern the intended meaning of this statement, we do not know by what verbal operation the deluded ones have performed the extraction [of the mantra]. Or rather, for those who do not know the direct extraction of the mantra,
here indeed— by means of this pair of verses concerning their own essential nature and so forth— the two deities [are revealed].
Indeed, our Guru himself declared that Manu spoke with the essence of pervasiveness.
One's own true nature is established in its own path, self-perceived, self-luminous,
consisting of its own bliss, and situated within its own power— thus described by these six qualifiers.
The Śākta portion is indicated as beginning with the letter *ū* and ending with the letter *kṣ*;
or alternatively, the Śākta portion of these two is that which begins with *kṣ* and extends up to *ū*.
[She who is] her own current, situated on her own path, innate, born of her own family, her own bliss, and established in her own state— thus she is indicated by these six [attributes].
Since the portion belonging to Śakti extends from the letter *ra* up to the *nāda*,
the portion belonging to Śiva is then indicated as extending from the *nāda* down to the letter *ra*.

By such statements as these, those who claim that its extraction is without foundation—speaking according to the process of creation and dissolution—have no fear of having their tongues cut out, nor do they fear the palate falling upon them.
One may speak without hesitation; what shameless person is not a scholar?
Thus, by this artful turn of phrase, their minds are rendered entirely free from doubt; what need is there for us to say to you, those self-existent ones, what has been stated by the learned:
"We do not know which lord of yogis bestowed the divine eye upon you at the very beginning, so that you might perceive objects that are utterly beyond the senses"? || 50 ||

She resides in the center of the navel-circle, the heart-lotus, and the face-circle.
O Great Goddess, she alone, possessing a luster equal to a ruby,
quickly brings about for him the eightfold sovereignty.
Thus, he states that even the mere recollection, chanting, and meditation upon her name bestow a distinguished fruit:
"O Dear One, when a practitioner recollects even her name with the mind, at that very moment he becomes known to the circle of Mothers. (53)
At the very moment one recites the mantra of Mahātripurasundarī,
the command of the circle of Mothers (mātṛcakra) immediately transfers into his body.
O Supreme Goddess, through meditation alone, the practitioner shall become as dear as a son to all Yoginīs, regardless of their various forms. 55.

(121) Having thus described the majesty of Vidyā alone, he speaks also of her when combined [with Śiva]: "But when, O Supreme Goddess, one worships her in her complete form, then the Khecarīs bestow upon him the highest siddhi. (56)
If it is asked: "If the worship of this [goddess] together with her wheel is performed, why then do the *khecarīs* grant supreme accomplishment? he says:
"Because there are sixty-four crores of yoginīs of great power."
O Goddess worshipped by heroes, they remain established by relying upon this wheel.

Stating the specific excellence in this very context, he also speaks of the particular result: "Having meditated upon the eight seed-syllables within the word associated with the beginning, and outside of it the *kalā*, [one becomes] like the bodiless one (Kāma) in the bodiless woman (Rati), O Beloved. (58)

In the word—that is, the position—belonging to the initial *vāgbhava*, when the *kāmarāja* is placed in the middle (that is, when there is an exchange between *vāgbhava* and *kāmarāja*), such is the *vidyā*. Outside of that, there is merely the eight seed-syllables (*bīja*) denoting Vaśinī and the others, and the sixteen vowels denoting the Kalās beginning with Kāmākarṣiṇī; this much constitutes the *cakra* for a certain practitioner (*sādhya*).
The meaning is that by meditating upon the "Anaṅga"—the female organ designated by terms such as *madana*—the practitioner becomes like Anaṅga himself, capable of withering the entire world. || 58 ||
[The opponent asks: "But why has no ritual procedure for accomplishment been stated for the other vidyās, just as for the Mūlavidyā? To this he replies:
"O Supreme Goddess, in the Rudrayāmala-tantra, I have previously taught a ritual procedure for each one of the vidyās beginning with Karaśuddhi. (58)
Then, he speaks [as follows] regarding the fate of the practitioners situated within the eighth wheel (p.
122): "Having become Madana through the intoxicating [powers], one should agitate the women of the heavens, the earth, and the netherworld with the noose, the hook, the bow, and the arrows. (59)
Having thus described how intoxicants bring women under control, he extends this principle to show that they likewise bring men under control for those who follow the Śākta path:
"In the same way, O Goddess of the Gods, one whose body has been rendered as the triple city (tripurīkṛtavigraha) by the Śāktas may accomplish even gods, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Vidyādharas. (60)

"Having become Madana"—this is stated because they share the same trunk (*samaskandhatayā*). By the phrase "with his body made of three cities" (*tripurīkṛtavigraha*), the method of worship described for the weapons of Madana is extended (*atidiṣṭa*) to these [deities] as well.
As for the question, "What is the meaning of this word?"—since that [method] is established simply by the similarity of their weapons (*āyudhasājātyāt*), what is the point of this? Let it be. 60.
Now, one might ask: "What indeed is the essential nature of these [weapons] by which the accomplishment of their respective subjugations occurs?
To this he says: "In that regard, the arrows of the Śāktas are produced from the *mahāvajraprastāra*.
Here, the *mahāvajraprastāra* is that which is taught in the *Śrīnityākāla*, and not the four-peaked Meru, for that is never [referred to as such] anywhere.
Because it cannot be fully expressed. Nor can the power of this wheel be described by me in this manner; it is impossible—[to do so]. (1.56)
Thus,
in such passages as "thus situated here in the great wheel (*mahācakra*)—
[blank]— ," there is a certain distinction based on the inclusion or exclusion of the word *mahat* ("great"). And it has been said in this regard:
The seed-syllable situated in the middle of *jhañ*, standing above the center of *ūḍha*,
is conjoined with the one located at the end and differentiated by the center of *ūḍha*.
O Goddess, the first means of accomplishment is the drying [element], resembling blood;
that very reality, O fortunate one, is adorned by the first bindu.
The *pṛṣaṭka* known as *mohana* is the supreme deluder in the three worlds; it is the reality situated between *dha* and *sa*, pierced by the middle of *ṣa* and *ha*.
The supreme inciter is the arrow joined with the quiescent bindu;
the seed-syllable situated between *cha* and *ja* is adorned with the quiescent bindu.
The fourth arrow, said to be situated above the middle of the letter *ṣa*, is named Tāpana;
this arrow can scorch even the gods.
O Dear One, the fifth arrow, beginning with *ha* and ending with *na*, is perfectly pure and undifferentiated;
it is named Unmādana, the one that causes the three worlds to go mad.

Thus [it is said]. This is the meaning here: *da* situated between *jha* and *ña*; *ra* situated between *ū* and *ḍha*; *ā* located at the end; *aṃ* situated between *ū* and *ḍha*. Thus, *drāṃ*. That very thing is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of reality, namely *drāṃ*; however, there is this distinction: *īṃ* preceded by *m*. Thus, *drīṃ*. *ka* situated between *dha* and *sa*; *la* situated between *ṣa* and *ha*; *i* at the end of *y*. Thus, *kliṃ*. *va* situated between *cha* and *ja*.
The end of *śa* is *u*, the middle of *ṣa* is *la*; thus, *blūṃ*. The end of *na* is *sa*, the beginning of *ha* is *aḥ*; thus, *saḥ*.
The venerable *Rasamahodadhi* also extracts the middle of *ña* and *dha* in two ways, marked by the middle of *pa* and *ṣa*.
It is endowed with the back [of the letters] from *au* to *aḥ*, and joined with the head preceded by *ka*.
The first letter of the *ga*-class, that ending in *la*, those two situated above accompanied by the vowels *a* and *i*,
those joined with the *ka*-class, that ending in *ṣa*, and that marked by the *kha*-class— these are the five arrows of the deity.

Thus: the middle of *ña* is *da*; the middle of *pa* is *ra*; the back of *au* is *ā*; the back of *aḥ* is *ī*; the head of *ka* is *aṃ*. Likewise, *drāṃ* and *drīṃ*. The beginning of *ga* is *ka*; the end of *la* is *va*; above *sa* is *la*; the end of the letter *a* is *i*; the end of the letter *i* is *u*; the beginning of *ka* is *aṃ*. Likewise, *kliṃ* and *blūṃ*. The end of *ṣa* is *la*; the beginning of *kha* is *aḥ*. Thus, *saḥ*. For this very reason, of these...

The specific detail mentioned regarding the extraction from the center of Meru is not to be adopted, because it belongs to another tantra. For in this way, even of the root mantra produced by the Vajraprastāra,
there is a twelve-syllable mantra according to a particular division of the Vajraprastāra.
It is devoid of the three natures, for it is indeed [devoid] at the beginning, middle, and end.
Having begun thus:
"This is that supreme knowledge, the bestower of all accomplishments;
this fifteen-syllable knowledge has arisen from the center of Mount Meru."

Thus, the aforementioned distinction would follow as a logical consequence. If this were not accepted, it would be because [the teaching] was spoken by extracting [the essence] according to the difference in the qualified recipients (*adhikārin*); otherwise, the omniscience (*āptatva*) of the Supreme Lord would be undermined. If that were invalid, what basis would there be for its authority? And thus: "As for those five arrows which have been mentioned, within them are the elemental syllables (*bhūtākṣara*)."
Having extracted each one from the beginning, they become complete.
Having extracted the first of the eleven [vowels] up to the end of *bh* (i.e.,
*au*), and having taken that preceded by *rudra* (the letter *r*) and joined with *jhiṇṭhīśvara* (the letter *ṣ*).
One should know that the fourth letter above the syllable *ha*, which is at the top of the seasonal enclosure (*ṛtukoṣṭha*), is the supreme abode of Rudra, known as Sādhu.

Within the center of the nine [syllables] and in the middle of the *vilas*, there is the seat for the gods of the [respective] colors; it should consist of those situated beginning with the letter *ka*.
O Goddess, without the third [vowel], the three forms and the three [consonants] would be divided;
all [the syllables] should be joined with the Bindu and placed outside the four-syllable [mantra].
The fifth [letter] should be placed at the beginning, joined with the bindu at the end of *dha*;
through their union with the bindu upon the head, these five are the bestowers of success (*siddhi*).
These five seed-syllables are the illuminators within the five arrows;
O Goddess, deprived of these, they become fruitless.
The seat consists of the five arrows, the messenger of the root-vidyā and the others;
O Goddess, this was previously described by me in the context of the Ruru-bheda in its center.
This seed-mantra was previously extracted by me through the method of expansion;
by this very procedure, may they become fruitful for you.
Those devoid of seed-syllables do not succeed at all when they are bereft of the oral tradition;
indeed, those with seed-syllables are fully described, whereas those without seed-syllables are never [effective] in worship.
Thus, by this agreement, [your] effort was in vain. And here is the extraction: *ka* is the first of the eleven; *ma* is that which ends with *bha*;

*da* is the first of the Rudras; *e* is Jhiṇṭhīśa; by these, *de*. The sixth [letter] in the square of the seasons (*ṛtu*) is *va*, situated therein; thus, *kamadeva*. *La* is situated in the middle of *vi*; by this, [the syllables] *kla*, *mla*, and *bla* are on the petals. *Trimūrti*. Now...

"If it is argued that this is stated thus solely on the strength of the dialogue in the *Śrīrasamahodadhi*, which says, 'Those endowed with the oral tradition (*saṃpradāya*) should be appointed by means of those [initiations] possessing seeds (*sabīja*),'— let it be so; however, since this text has emerged from your own house under a disguise,
this very point is not seen in such a way by some of your own followers who have proclaimed it as belonging to the *Vuppārāhula* school."

And since it has not been touched upon in the *Mantra-saṃketapaddhati*, we have doubts as to whether this [system] is substantially real or non-substantially real. Regarding that, if it were substantially real, this fault would not be ours, because it was previously stated that the illustrious Viśvāvarta himself was the direct proponent of this system in Kashmir; that is so.
"—the disciple shall become a denizen of hell.

Having forgotten the meaning of this quarter-verse, why was it taught [to him] while omitting these five seed-syllables? For if the Guru himself gives the instruction of the mantra in a different way, what fault is there on the part of his disciples? If the verses of the *Śrīrasamahodadhi* were [interpreted] otherwise...
Let that which has been done remain as it is; for by that, only the mere denial of the reality is established, but there is no harm whatsoever to the reality itself.

It would be a great negligence to instruct otherwise those mantras which have been received directly from a guru. Likewise, if even physicians were to administer poison, then the earth would be easy to describe as being free of the sick. By this line of reasoning, enough of such misconduct on your part.

Even by exposing the faults of those Easterners who persist in their former views, we incur no fault that would defile us in either world, for our engagement is directed solely toward touching upon the reality of things. As they say:
"One should not engage in censure or the like against those who have been initiated out of malice. (p. 126)
There is no fault in our instruction, for it is preceded by a lack of hatred.
Thus, if it were a non-existent entity, our own position would indeed be superior; so enough of this subduing of the ill-behaved!
Having thus described the Śaktas, he speaks of the Mādanas as well:
"The Mādanas, however, are joined starting from the beginning and ending at the very bottom. (61)

The meaning of the sentence is as follows: the "interdentals" (antaḥsthā), which denote all the elements situated at the bottom of the entire path—that is, the four elements beginning with air—are joined after the letter *ha*, which is the first of those [elements] and denotes space; furthermore, they become the "intoxicating arrows" (*mādana-śara*). Thus, the sequence is *ha ya ra la va*. || 61 ||
Likewise,
the great noose pertaining to the person (puruṣa), which pervades from beginning to end, is proclaimed; the power of Rudra called Kuṇḍalinī, which is Māyā, is said to be the female noose (strīpāśa).
O Pārvatī, the fourth [syllable] is from the group of vowels (aruṇa-varga), and the second [syllable] likewise;
[these form] the pair of male and female bows, while the goad is that which pervades the fire of desire.
The letter *ā* is situated at the end of the first letter [which is *ka*]. She is known as being surrounded on all sides by the two earrings-like *i*-vowels;

she is the power of Rudra (*rudraśakti*), consisting of the fourth vowel (*ai*) which arises from the union of those two. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that she is here called *māyā*, and not the four-fold *strīpāśa*. And thus:
The letter *ī* is like [the letter *i*], bestowing half [of the power]; even *māyā* possesses four *kalās* in women.
By this statement, the position of the three-syllable [mantra] is refuted;
however, this is not so merely by taking up the infinite victory of the perfect awakening accumulated by the great-grandfather (*vṛddhaprapitāmaha*).

The purposelessness of employing three syllables would be resolved [on page 127]. From the *aruṇā* group—that is, from the *tavarga*—the fourth is *dha*, the second is *tha*, *kāma* is *ka*, *agni* is *ra*, and the pervasive one is *o*;
thus, *kroṃ*. As for the *kāmāṅkuśa*, it has already been explained in the first chapter.

By virtue of the context of the section on mantras, it should be understood that these [syllables] possess the bindu (m). And it has been said: "The pair of syllables beginning with *ū* and *ū*, joined with the head [letter] from the *ka*-group, is declared to be the two nooses (*pāśa*), which are Śākta and Mādana."
One should extract one goad (aṅkuśa) joined with the words beginning with *jambha*;
the second [goad] extends from the letter *ka* to the end of the womb (*yoni*), reaching the end of the letter *aṃ* and the end of *laya*.
The pair of bows is declared to end in *ṇa*, begin with *sa* and *ka*, and end in *ca*;
likewise, it consists of *ṣa* and *dha*, *rā* and *tha*, ending in *la* and *ya*, and *vā* and *dha* accompanied by *la*.
With the seed-syllable situated between *au* and *aḥ*, all [the syllables] are struck by the head;
this is declared to be the supreme fivefold arrow of Kāmadeva.

Thus: the pair of vowels preceded by *ū* is *ī* and *ā*; *ka* and so forth up to *aṃ*, thus *īṃ* and *āṃ*. *Ka* and so forth up to *aṃ*. Within the *yoni* (the letter *e*) is *o*; within the letter *aṃ* is *ka*; between *la* and *ya* is *ra*; thus *kroṃ*. With respect to its position within the interior of the *yoni*, the end of *ṇa* is *tha*; the beginning of *pa* is *dha*; *ka* and so forth up to *aṃ*, thus *thaṃ* and *dhaṃ*. Below *ṣa* is *ha*; below *ra* is *ya*; between *la* and *ya* is *ra*; below *va* is *la*; the end of *la* is *va*; *au* and *aḥ*.
The seed-syllable *aṃ* is situated in the center; likewise [are] *haṃ*, *yaṃ*, *raṃ*, *laṃ*, and *vaṃ*. || 63 ||
Now, it was previously stated that there is only the [displaying of] mudrās and not worship; therefore, one might ask whether these are to be worshipped anywhere or not. To this he says:
"O Goddess, those very mudrās of Tripurā which are endowed with the eight siddhis—one should worship them at the time of worship in all the cakras. (64)
By the term "the eight siddhis," because of its association with the ten mudrās, the two [siddhis] characterized by the release of rasa are also implied;
this has already been stated previously. || 64 ||
(128) And because she possesses such greatness as has been described, she is unique and without equal; thus he says:
"Therefore, this supreme Goddess Tripurā is the preeminent Vidyā.
O Mistress of the Gods, there exists no Vidyā whatsoever that is her equal. (65)
For it was by propitiating this very Vidyā Tripurabhairavī in the past that the Blessed Lord Hari assumed his form that deludes the three worlds.
Likewise,
O Goddess of the gods, Kāmadeva also, having propitiated Mahātripurasundarī,
became the most beautiful and fortunate one in the world. (67)
Likewise,
O beautiful one, that which is still performed by me today while established in my vow—
the recitation at the three junctions of the day— is for the sake of attaining this very state. (68)
In this context, he describes the difference in results arising from the worship of the wheel both individually and as a whole:
"O Goddess, by worshipping the center, a man becomes a lord of speech;
likewise, by worshipping the outer, the middle, and the inner, he becomes another Kandarpa. (69)
O Pārvatī, by means of this [practice] entirely, at all times, and joined with all the goddesses,
one should accomplish the siddhi of Khecarī, which is endowed with the qualities of aṇimā and the rest.

The supreme [attainment] of the central root-triangle is achieved solely by means of the four goddesses situated in the eighth wheel; furthermore, by worshipping the ninth wheel—which is situated at the very center of the external eight-spoked wheel—one shall achieve mastery of speech (*vākpatitva*) and the power of desire (*kāmatva*). Thus, there is the worship of the wheel in its two distinct parts, as well as in its entirety.

Through worship, the perfection of moving through the sky (*khecaratva-siddhi*) arises, accompanied by the eight perfections beginning with *aṇimā*. As for the three groups of eight [perfections] that are without a fixed basis, who indeed is capable of discerning the underlying intention? May there be auspiciousness! (70)
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Śrīvāmakeśvarīmatavivaraṇa* composed by Rājānaka Śrī Mañjaratha. || 4 ||
Now begins the fifth chapter:

here, [the author] addresses the section concerning how success might be achieved through recitation and fire-offerings for the Vidyā, whether taken individually or as a whole, in the absence of these two practices.

Seeking a connection [to the subject], the illustrious Goddess said: "What is it that you have spoken? You have declared the entire supreme knowledge of Tripura, as well as the triad consisting of the principle of desire (*kāmatattva*), the knowledge of poison (*viṣajñāna*), and the principle of liberation (*mokṣatattva*). (1)
Now, O Śaṅkara, tell me the procedure for recitation and fire-offerings, by the mere performance of which even one of dull fortune attains success. (2)
The word "trayam" (the triad) means as a collective whole. || 2 ||
To provide an answer to this very point, the venerable Bhairava said:
"Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the practice for the realization of the Tripurā mantra, along with the rules for recitation and fire-offerings, which bestows all desired fruits. (p. 130)
In that regard, he first states the procedure for recitation:
"O Supreme Goddess, having worshipped the entire wheel according to the rule,
O Goddess, [one may worship] either the center alone, or that which is situated between the outer and the middle."
Standing before it, O Supreme Goddess, the practitioner of mantra should recite [the mantra] a thousand times while observing the vow; thereupon he shall obtain infinite fruit.

The meaning of "only the middle" is that it consists solely of the form of the root-triangle (*mūlatrikoṇa*). For in that case, the primary sequence of worship is indeed through the eighth and ninth wheels; the intention is that since effort expended toward the principal [element] becomes fruitful, what is the use of any other secondary worship? The phrase "situated between the external and the middle" means by means of the external...
The meaning is that it is joined with a seven-spoked seat-wheel (*saptāsana-cakra*) which serves as the locus for the inner retinue consisting of the eight deities beginning with Vaśinī;

thus, one should worship the three-spoked wheel situated in the center—this is the intended sense of "possessing eight spokes" (*sāṣṭāra*). "In front of that" (*tadagre*) means in front of that wheel which has been worshipped with the three options. "If" (*yadi*) is used in the sense of a reason. By the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*), [it implies] even a lesser [number of spokes].

The acceptance of a specific number means that by reciting [the mantra] a hundred times or a thousand times, one shall obtain infinite fruit; this is the logical connection (*anvaya*). Furthermore, since it is established here that the recitation (*japa*) itself is the primary constituent (*aṅgin*), the clamor raised by others is in vain. Enough, then, with these conceited and false conceptualizations! || 5 ||
Regarding this very point, he states another alternative:

"Or, having meditated upon the wheel situated in the heart and having contemplated the Supreme Goddess residing therein through the yoga of meditation previously described, one should begin the recitation. (6)
The word "wheel" (cakra) refers to all three types as well.
And regarding the commencement of *japa* here in its various forms, he says (p.
131): "O you of good vows, [it may be performed] by means of loud recitation (*nigada*), or in a whisper (*upāṃśu*), or even mentally (*mānasa*).
By 'loud recitation' is meant with sound. As it has been stated:
That which the self does not hear is proclaimed to be mental (mānasa);
that which is heard by the self alone is known as whispered (upāṃśu).
O Goddess, that which others hear is called "with sound" (saśabda).
To the question of how, to what extent, and what is its fruit, he says: "Equipped with the previously mentioned nyāsa, his body armored with mudrās. (7)
It may be made of pearl necklaces, or produced from large lapis lazuli gems,
or originating from putrajīvaka, padmākṣa, rudrākṣa, or crystal.
It was fashioned from red sandalwood, such as young sprouts and rubies,
and adorned with saffron, agallochum, camphor, and musk.
Having taken up a rosary and made his body threefold,
O Goddess, he who recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times is liberated from great sins.

It has been stated that "the body is rendered as the triple-city" (*tripurīkṛtavigraha*) precisely because it is equipped with the previously mentioned ritual placements (*nyāsa*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of *saṃkha* and so forth is intended; therefore, one should not say that there are only nine [types of beads]. Nor is it logical [to limit them] merely on the basis of a difference in the reading;
for when the attainment of the principle of Speech (*vāktattva-siddhi*) is primary, [beads made of] pearls, crystal, and so forth are used.
They arise from various jewels, such as lapis lazuli, rubies, and others.
Or else, for the accomplishment of the reality of desire, it may be made from red sandalwood,
or fashioned from putrajīvaka, lotus seeds, rudrākṣa, and so forth.
Regarding the primacy of the great siddhi of Nirañjana—thus has the division been stated; likewise, on page 132:
"The triad beginning with Muktāphala [is assigned] to the deities of the one, three, and eight-spoked [mandalas], and so forth."
In front of the eight goddesses on the eight spokes, there should also be [the mantra] beginning with *putrajīva*.
A common rosary made of red sandalwood, or one consisting of crystal, coral, lotus seeds, ruby, and so forth, should be fashioned for the goddesses of the central wheel.
Thus stated, even this division is not logical, because it is merely a difference in recitation and lacks scriptural authority.
Now he demonstrates the respective increase in both the number [of repetitions] and the fruit:
"By two hundred thousand [repetitions], the Goddess Tripurā destroys even the sins committed over seven lifetimes for the practitioner; of this there is no doubt. (11)
Having recited the mantra three hundred thousand times, the practitioner, restrained and embodied by the mantra,
shall quickly destroy even the sins accumulated over seven thousand births.
Having recited the vidyā four hundred thousand times, one becomes a great lord of speech;
and by five hundred thousand, one is no longer poor and truly acts like Vaiśravaṇa himself.
Having recited this [mantra] six hundred thousand times, one becomes a lord of the great vidyādharas;
having recited it seven hundred thousand times, one shall go to the assembly of the sky-farers (khecarīs).
O Maheśvarī, by reciting this vidyā eight hundred thousand times,
one becomes the master of the eight siddhis, beginning with aṇimā, and is honored by the gods.
Having recited the mantra of Tripurasundarī one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rite,
the practitioner of mantra becomes like another embodiment of Rudra.
This very fact reveals his nature as the form of Rudra:
"O Gaurī, he is himself the creator and the destroyer, possessing unimpeded splendor in the world;
he is eternally joyful, the Hero, the Lord whose movement is independent. (17)
The word "it becomes" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 17 ||
Now, one might ask: "Is there any mutual distinction between these three modes of recitation—namely, *nigada* and the others—or not?
To this he says:
"That which is recited as *nigada*, and that which is performed as *upāṃśu* [to the extent of] a hundred thousand (*lakṣa*)."
O Great Goddess, through mental recitation one obtains the fruit of ten million recitations. || 18 ||

The meaning here is that if it is recited even slightly, once or twice, by the practitioner in an audible manner (*nigada*), he obtains a result exactly commensurate with that amount; however, if it is recited even in a whispered manner (*upāṃśu*) a hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*), he would obtain a result a hundred-thousandfold greater than in comparison to the audible recitation. Likewise, when recited mentally (*mānasa*), it is a ten-million-fold (*koṭi*) increase; thus, the essential point is that there is a progressive excellence among these methods.
He also states the distinction regarding recitation according to the difference of location:
"O lady of excellent vows, in whatever place there may be a linga facing west— whether it be a self-manifested (svayambhū) one, a bāṇa-linga, or even another kind— " (19).
Staying there, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, having made one's own body threefold.
"The other" refers to the linga established by perfected beings (*siddhas*) and others, which is of many kinds, facing westward, and situated within the womb (*yoni*). It is thus proclaimed.
The self-existent, which is the expressive power of the arrow, is situated within the heart-knot and the point.

Furthermore, there exists in many Āgamas various descriptions such as "situated in the intermediate space," and so forth, in numerous ways. Therefore, diligent yogis should themselves infer from those very sources according to their own inclination and until they reach direct experience. Moreover, others have explained this in many ways, but in a manner that is merely like chewing the cud (superficial).
Let it be that we have no dogmatic attachment (*abhiniveśa*) toward this detailed exposition, as it involves a stubborn adherence (*durāgraha*). (p. 134)
To the question "What would happen thus?", he says:
"From that, O Goddess of Gods, the man becomes a shaker of the three worlds. (20)
Concluding it in this manner, he states the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*):
"Having first performed the recitation (*japa*) according to his capacity in this way, the best of practitioners should perform the *homa* with a tenth part [of that number]..."
By what means and in what manner? He says: with flowers born from the Brahma-tree. || 21 ||
Or else, with safflower blossoms smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) according to the prescribed rule;

"the sacrificial *brahmavṛkṣa* tree" refers to the *palāśa* and others. "The three sweets" consists of various types such as sugar, ghee, and milk. In the reading *svayaṃbhukusumaiḥ*, the meaning is "with wild [flowers]. Regarding "according to the prescribed rule," in that context:

Having observed one pit from among the eight pits to be described according to the perspective of others, one should sprinkle it with the *astra-mantra*, scratch [the ground], sprinkle [water] over it,
contract [the lines], smear [it with cow-dung], prepare the crossroads and the axle-pit (*akṣavāṭa*), and solidify it. Then,

having covered the inside and outside with *kuśa* grass consisting of a mass of light, and for the sake of removing obstacles, one should install and worship the triad of powers beginning with Vāmā upon the girdles (*mekhalā*).

Then, having visualized a triangle within the crossroads, having invoked Ambikā with the *māyābīja*, having placed her upon the seat and worshipped her, having brought the fire, sprinkled it, rendered it nectarine (*amṛtīkṛta*), and worshipped it, having meditated upon it as semen (*śukra*), having circumambulated it three times by way of the left and right, and having cast it into that womb, having sprinkled that womb with the *astra-mantra* and covered it with *darbha* grass, one should kindle the fire and [form] the flame-gesture (*jvālāmudrā*).

Having demonstrated the rites of conception (*garbhādhāna*), the male-impregnation (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*), the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*), and the naming (*nāmakaraṇa*), and having performed them by means of the science of limbs (*aṅgavidyā*) with one oblation for each,

he places the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles face-down upon the *darbha* grass to his left as Śiva and Śakti. Then, having consecrated the collection of sacrificial materials such as clarified butter (*ājya*) by means of the sprinkling of droplets from the *arghapātra*, [he proceeds] for the fulfillment of the purificatory rites.

Having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* and dismissed the Mother of Fire (*agnimātṛ*), and having fully worshipped the circle of mantras (*mantracakra*) within the fire of desire (*kāmāgni*), one should perform the oblation (*homa*) while visualizing the entire sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) as the mouth of the Fire-god; this means that one must not transgress the procedure taught in both similar and dissimilar tantras.
To the question "What would happen thus?", he says:
"From that, this knowledge arises which destroys the flood of great obstacles. (22)
O Goddess, you are the bestower of all desires and the giver of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.
As for where one should perform this, it says: "In a vulva-shaped pit, or marked with the sign of the womb, or circular, or crescent-shaped. (23)
"Either in a nine-triangle wheel, or in a square, or in an eight-petaled [lotus];
'marked with the vulva' refers to the triangle; 'nine-triangle wheel' is a *dvandva* compound meaning two equal doors; and 'eight-petaled' refers to an eight-leaved lotus."
Now, one might object: "Since the oblation can be accomplished with a single *kuṇḍa*, what is the purpose of specifying eight? To this he says:
"In a *yonikuṇḍa* one becomes eloquent; in a *bhagāṅka* there is excellent cultivation. (24)
In a circular pit, there shall be prosperity; in a semi-circular one, one obtains the three [goals];
and in a nine-triangular pit, one attains the power of moving through the sky.
In a square [mandala], there shall be peace, prosperity, nourishment, and freedom from disease;
in one marked with a lotus, all success arises without delay. (26)
In an auspicious eight-cornered circle, one shall obtain the desired fruit.
Thus, he says that a difference in results also arises from the difference in the substances offered in the fire-oblation:
"With jasmine, mālatī, and jātī flowers, drenched in clarified butter... (27).
O Supreme Goddess, even one who is mute becomes the lord of speech through these oblations.
O Pārvatī, [one should offer] Karavīra and Japā flowers mixed with clarified butter. (28)
Having offered [this] into the fire, the mantra-practitioner draws forth the women of the heavens, the earth, and the netherworld;
O Goddess, having mixed saffron with camphor and musk. (29)
Having offered oblations, he shall become even more fortunate than Kandarpa through his own good fortune;
and by offering Caṇpakas, Pāṭalas, and other such flowers, one shall indeed attain prosperity.
O Goddess, by offering incense made of sandalwood, agallochum, or camphor combined with *pura*, one becomes a disturber of the women of the city.
Having offered a piece of meat smeared with the three sweets and having performed the rite while recollecting Maheśvarī,
O Goddess, one becomes a sky-walker by going to a crossroads at night.
Then, O Maheśvarī, by offering parched grain mixed with curd, honey, and milk,
one is not afflicted by diseases, nor by the fear of untimely death and other such calamities.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: having gone to a crossroads at night, having smeared [the offering] with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), having recollected Maheśvarī, and having offered a *pala* [of the substance], one becomes a sky-walker (*khecara*). Herein lie the intended meaning (*bhāvārtha*), the traditional meaning (*saṃpradāyārtha*), the innermost secret meaning (*nigarbhārtha*), and the Kaula meaning.
Likewise, it is the meaning of all secrets and indeed the meaning of the great reality.
"Thus it is, O Great Sovereign: this sixfold exposition of all the Tantras of the Supreme Lord is obtained through the oral tradition. (Yoginīhṛdaya 2.15).

Having thus explained word by word what was stated in these passages, which is being performed in its sixfold manner, [I shall now address] that which results merely in the burden of voluminous texts...

(p. 137) It is stated by way of grasping the intended meaning alone (*tātparya*). For instance, the meaning of the verbal root (*bhāvārtha*)—whatever is intended as the mere literal sense—is indeed, even when it appears external, the "meaning of the tradition" (*saṃpradāyārtha*), provided it is of the nature of great awakening (*mahābodha*), conforms to the words of Śiva, and is not contradicted by the Guru and others, because it is intent upon establishing the knowledge of the Self and so forth.

It is said: "The Self is to be known, it is to be contemplated," and "This Self is once-for-all manifest. This twofold explanation consists of the means (*upāya*) for attaining the nature of the individual soul (*āṇava*), such as the phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth. How is this so? Because the Self—whose sole form is Śiva, appearing continuously precisely because it is once-for-all manifest—is of the very nature of the knower; therefore, [the statements] such as "this is to be known" are appropriate only insofar as they refer to the object of knowledge (*jñeya*).
"It is fitting that there should be a reflective awareness of 'this-ness' (idantā);

thus, the Lord, through His sovereignty, having fashioned by His will [the world] as a self liberated from sovereignty—though its nature is non-dual—engages in worldly transaction. (Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā 1.1.47)

In this manner, even while not abandoning its singular nature as the subject (*pramātṛ*), it manifests itself within its own self as the object (*prameya*), by which it is able to arouse such a state of reflective awareness (*parāmṛśyatā*). Thus, taking recourse to the state of being cultivated (*bhāvyatā*), this third mode—designated by the term *nigarbha* because of its internal nature—should enter the domain of the pure Self, which is otherwise divided by distinctions such as the Guru and so forth; that is to say, "this is Śiva. Thus [it is said].

"The Self alone, manifesting within all existents, is Śiva— whose nature is blissful consciousness, whose flow of will is unobstructed, and whose powers of vision and action are ever-expanding" (Pratya-bhijñā Hṛdaya 4.1.1). Likewise:
"One's own Self alone is the one Great Lord (*maheśvara*) of all living beings;
I am the universal form (*viśvarūpa*), nourished by the undivided reflective awareness (*akhaṇḍāmarśa*) that 'this is I'. (4.1.1).
According to this and other views taught by the venerable former gurus, such is the Self, even within all those states consisting of the self-awareness of limited subjects.

In all states (*daśāsu*), being perceived as the very nature of pure consciousness— which consists of the supreme light and is composed of the reflective awareness of the "I" that transcends all others—
one attains the supreme, innate sovereignty of Śiva even without effort; this is [the teaching].

"But the *kula* is the very nature of the Self—[the rest of the verse follows]—thus, because it exists within the *kula* which is the form of the Self, the fourth [empowerment] is designated by the term 'Kaulika'. This [fourth empowerment] also consists of two modes, which, being of the nature of the purification of conceptual thought (*vikalpa*), belong to the means of power (*śākta-upāya*). Even so, here itself, according to their respective [applications]...
Then, by ascending the stream of supreme excellence, consciousness— augmented by that very nature of most vivid and noble clarity— attains its stainless, non-conceptual state. (Tantrāloka 4.6)
Through such a perspective, one should immediately attain the non-conceptual cognition characterized by the direct realization of the Self;

because it is not perceivable by ignorant people, this fifth [means], which consists of the Śāmbhava-upāya, is designated by the term "secret" (rahasya). Thus, for one who, even while possessing a physical body, has reached the supreme pinnacle through the power of contemplation (bhāvanā)— [The text continues: ...even though the body remains...

May they attain the perfection consisting of pure consciousness alone, free from the stain of all mental constructs such as existence and non-existence; for them, even this entire circle of objective phenomena, though appearing before them, shines forth as nothing other than the universal sphere of Being.
"Situated right before one, dissolved by the fire of the Bhairava of consciousness" (*Tantrāloka* 2.35)—
since he abides in the state described by such passages as being composed of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), he shines forth from every side entirely independent of anything else.
Because he exists above the state thus explained and because he excels all others, he is designated by the term "the Great Supreme Reality" (*mahāparamatattvārtha*).
Regarding the "sixth":
as the scripture states, "O Supreme Goddess, the meaning of the syllables is indeed the meaning of the state of being in its absolute purity;
the oral tradition, which consists of great awakening, resides in the mouth of the Guru. (Yoginīhṛdaya 2.16)
O Great Goddess, the Nigarbha [Tantra] has as its scope Śiva, the Guru, and the Self;
the Kaulika [Tantra] is the self-awareness of one's own nature, preceded by the awareness of the Self.
The secret meaning is greatly guarded and produces immediate conviction;
it is the meaning of the supreme ultimate reality, established like the Supreme Self.
(139) It reveals the true meaning by means of the dialogue between Śiva, the Guru, and the Self,
preceded by a state in which all conceptual constructions and mental fluctuations have been cast aside.
"Established in those bound to the seats of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha), he bestows the perfection of the body (piṇḍasiddhi).
Thus it is said. And although these [seats] are generally not found in this way everywhere, indeed, the very same essential meaning is obtained in the external scriptures.
It consists of the essence of verbal ornaments, elegant expression, refinement, and composition.
The essential meaning and the oral tradition exist within the dualistic scriptures,
residing in the mouth of the great Guru during the dialogue concerning the external objects of Śiva.

O Goddess, in the Trika scriptures, a threefold exposition is found: the meaning of the essential nature (bhāvārtha), the meaning of the oral tradition (saṃpradāyārtha), and that which is endowed with the sequence of the innermost secret meaning (nigarbhārthakrama).
The meaning of the essential nature, the meaning of the tradition, the meaning of the innermost core, the Kaula meaning,
and likewise the meaning of all secrets— these are the fivefold forms of the Tantras.
The meaning of the essential nature, the meaning of the tradition, the meaning of the innermost core, and the Kaula meaning;
likewise, the meaning of all secrets and the meaning of the Great Reality.

"O Pārvatī, the group of six is seen here in this tantra within the great ocean of knowledge," and so forth; thus, with the intention of highlighting its preeminence, its fixed presence in various locations has been stated. Enough, then, of this restlessness in unveiling paths that have not yet been unveiled. Therefore, this matter should be inferred by oneself in each respective place according to what is possible.

Furthermore, regarding those other [interpretations]— such as the literal meaning (*bhāvārtha*), the traditional meaning (*saṃpradāyārtha*), and the esoteric meaning (*nigarbhārtha*)— which are demonstrated to those seeking peace according to the logic of the "hot salt-water portion," many predecessors as well as contemporaries of our own have exerted great effort in explaining them in detail;
therefore, this [work] is illuminated here only briefly, by way of indicating merely another appropriate method of exposition.

Having thus promised [to explain] in a manner that does not conform to the mere enumeration [of categories], the Great Lords have explained words by means of words themselves— on the grounds that the secret meaning, the esoteric meaning, and the ultimate reality of the Kaula tradition are established upon the self-awareness of one's own nature consisting of *sāmarasya*, act as immediate means of conviction, and bring about the dissolution of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Since for some who are in their final birth (apaścimajanman), this must be revealed in secret through oral tradition alone, who would engage in the great transgression of committing it to writing? Thus, at various intervals, even this mere name has been mentioned without any formal basis; that is [the case].

This [work], which is solely intent on concealing the lack of understanding of everyone, is merely the empty clangor of one who bears the burden of a teacher; thus it concludes. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Śrīvāmakeśvarīmatavivaraṇa* composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Śrī Jayaratha. || 5 ||
Having gathered [the teachings] bit by bit from this and that source, this small work has been explained by some according to the words of their own teachers. (1)
By what cause, and by whom, has this been analyzed through a path of words and meanings that are everywhere difficult, ill-joined, and confused? (2)
With a mind that desires nothing more than the great ocean of aesthetic essence fashioned by their fathers and grandfathers,
[this work] does not attain its true meaning even though it has been explained by others.
It has gone [to ruin] because his intellect was excluded from sacred learning. || 3 ||
Therefore, having understood this exactly as it is from the venerable and most excellent Guru, I, Jayaratha, have thus elaborated upon this matter to some extent. (p. 141)
In this matter, virtuous people should disregard that moment [of the statement] with indifference;
one should speak without even deliberating upon it, for there is neither fault nor merit therein.
Thus ends the *Śrīvāmakeśvarīmatavivaraṇa* composed by the illustrious Rājānaka Jagaratha.
